title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 3.1 Describing the COVID shock with intervention variables
text:
3.1 Describing the COVID shock with intervention variables
A regression can absorb the shock if it is given explanatory variables whose shape matches how the event unfolded. This follows the transfer function idea from the notes. With \(t_0\) = April 2020 and everything on the log scale:

Decaying shock: \(D_t(\delta) = \delta^{\,t - t_0}\) for \(t \ge t_0\) and 0 before. Its coefficient \(\omega\) is the immediate effect in April 2020, which then dies out geometrically at rate \(\delta\). This is the transfer function \(\omega / (1 - \delta L)\) applied to a pulse at \(t_0\).
Pulses for March 2020 (lockdown started on 27 March, so the month was only partly affected) and May 2020 (the industry stayed almost completely closed, so the bottom of the collapse lasted two months rather than one).
Level shift: \(S_t = 1\) for \(t \ge t_0\), allowing a permanent difference between the pre-COVID and post-COVID levels.



Code
covid_vars <- function(df, delta) {
  k0 <- month_num(shock_month)
  df |>
    mutate(k     = month_num(Month) - k0,
           decay = if_else(k >= 0, delta^pmax(k, 0), 0),
           mar20 = as.numeric(k == -1),
           may20 = as.numeric(k == 1),
           step  = as.numeric(k >= 0))
}

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
3.2 Model A1: static regression
The simplest time series regression (fpp3 Chapter 7) has a linear trend, 11 seasonal dummies and the intervention variables, with independent errors:
\[
\log y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \omega D_t(\delta) + \kappa_1 P^{\text{Mar20}}_t + \kappa_2 P^{\text{May20}}_t + \lambda S_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2).
\]
\(\delta\) is fixed at a provisional value of 0.80 here; it is chosen properly in Section 3.3.1.


Code
train_static <- covid_vars(train, 0.80)
test_static  <- covid_vars(test, 0.80)

fit_static <- train_static |>
  model(TSLM(log(nights) ~ trend() + season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step))

static_glance <- glance(fit_static)
static_res    <- augment(fit_static)$.innov
dw_static     <- sum(diff(static_res)^2) / sum(static_res^2)          # Durbin-Watson
lb_static     <- Box.test(static_res, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
r1_static     <- acf(static_res, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]




Code
fit_static |> gg_tsresiduals(lag_max = 36)








Figure 2: Residual diagnostics for the static regression (Model A1).





The fit looks impressive: the adjusted \(R^2\) is 0.965. The residuals tell a different story (Figure 2). They drift in long runs above and below zero, the lag 1 autocorrelation is 0.73, the Durbin–Watson statistic is 0.53 (far below the value of 2 expected for independent errors) and the Ljung and Box test on 24 lags gives p < 0.001.
This matters for more than tidiness. With positively autocorrelated errors, the least squares estimates are still unbiased but no longer efficient, the reported standard errors are too small, so the intervention terms look more significant than they are, and the prediction intervals are too narrow. The static regression also ignores useful information: if this month was above the fitted line, next month probably will be too. The remedy, following fpp3 Chapter 10, is to let the error follow an ARIMA process.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 3.3 Model A2: regression with ARIMA errors
text:
3.3 Model A2: regression with ARIMA errors
The dynamic regression replaces the independent error by an ARIMA process:
\[
\log y_t = \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \omega D_t(\delta) + \kappa_1 P^{\text{Mar20}}_t + \kappa_2 P^{\text{May20}}_t + \lambda S_t + \eta_t, \qquad (1 - L)\,\phi(L)\,\eta_t = \theta(L)\,\varepsilon_t .
\]
Two choices from the static model are revisited. First, the deterministic trend is dropped in favour of a first difference in the errors: after the shock the level does not follow a straight line, and a wandering (stochastic) level is more realistic. With \(d = 1\) the intercept and trend are differenced away, which is why they do not appear. Second, the seasonality is kept deterministic (dummies) rather than handled with a seasonal difference. In Project 1, the airline model fitted with the COVID months included estimated a seasonal MA coefficient of -1.000. A seasonal MA factor \((1 - L^{12})\) that cancels the seasonal difference is the classic sign that the seasonal pattern is fixed rather than evolving, so that seasonal differencing is over-differencing. The seasonal plots in Project 1 point the same way, and the exponential smoothing models below confirm it independently: every seasonal ETS model puts the seasonal smoothing parameter \(\gamma\) at or near its lower bound, so the seasonal pattern barely changes over ten years.

3.3.1 Choosing the decay rate by profile likelihood
The decay rate \(\delta\) enters the model non-linearly, so it cannot be estimated by ARIMA() directly. Instead I profile it: for each \(\delta\) on a grid from 0.70 to 0.96, the model is fitted (with the ARIMA error orders chosen by AICc) and the AICc recorded. The value of \(\delta\) with the smallest AICc is used. Because \(\delta\) is estimated, the model really has one more parameter than ARIMA() reports; this does not change the ranking along the grid.


Code
delta_grid <- seq(0.70, 0.96, by = 0.02)

profile <- bind_rows(lapply(delta_grid, function(dl) {
  f <- covid_vars(train, dl) |>
    model(reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                        pdq(d = 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0)))
  tibble(delta = dl,
         AICc  = glance(f)$AICc,
         spec  = format(f$reg[[1]]))
}))

delta_hat <- profile$delta[which.min(profile$AICc)]




Code
ggplot(profile, aes(delta, AICc)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = filter(profile, delta == delta_hat), colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  labs(x = expression(delta), y = "AICc")








Figure 3: Profile of AICc against the decay rate. The selected value is marked in red.





The AICc is minimised at \(\hat\delta\) = 0.76 (Figure 3). A decay rate of 0.76 means that the temporary part of the shock halves every 2.5 months and has fallen to 4% of its initial size after a year.


3.3.2 Seasonal dummies or Fourier terms?
Fourier terms (\(\sin(2\pi k t/12)\) and \(\cos(2\pi k t/12)\) for \(k = 1, \dots, K\)) are the other standard way to put seasonality into a regression. With small \(K\) they describe a smooth seasonal shape with fewer parameters; with \(K = 6\) they are equivalent to the 11 dummies. I compare the two at \(\hat\delta\) by AICc. All the models have the same response and the same order of differencing, so their AICc values are comparable.


Code
train_reg <- covid_vars(train, delta_hat)
test_reg  <- covid_vars(test, delta_hat)

seas_forms <- c("Seasonal dummies" = "season()",
                "Fourier, K = 1"   = "fourier(K = 1)",
                "Fourier, K = 2"   = "fourier(K = 2)",
                "Fourier, K = 3"   = "fourier(K = 3)",
                "Fourier, K = 4"   = "fourier(K = 4)",
                "Fourier, K = 5"   = "fourier(K = 5)")

seas_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(names(seas_forms), function(nm) {
  f <- as.formula(paste("log(nights) ~", seas_forms[[nm]],
                        "+ decay + mar20 + may20 + step + pdq(d = 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0)"))
  m <- train_reg |> model(r = ARIMA(!!f))
  tibble(`Seasonal terms` = nm,
         `Seasonal parameters` = c(11, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10)[match(nm, names(seas_forms))],
         `Error model` = format(m$r[[1]]),
         AICc = glance(m)$AICc)
}))

seas_tbl |> kable(digits = 1)
best_seas <- seas_tbl$`Seasonal terms`[which.min(seas_tbl$AICc)]

The low-order Fourier models are clearly worse: the accommodation seasonal pattern has a sharp December peak, a smaller Easter and mid-year bump and a dip in winter, which needs many harmonics to describe. Fourier terms pay off mainly for long seasonal periods (weekly data with period 52, or daily data), where dummies would need many more parameters. Seasonal dummies are used from here on.


3.3.3 Fitting the model


Code
# Residuals from the regression part, before choosing the ARIMA errors
ols <- train_reg |>
  model(TSLM(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step))
ols_resid <- augment(ols)




Code
ols_resid |>
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(.resid), plot_type = "partial", lag_max = 36)








Figure 4: Identifying the error process: first differences of the residuals from the regression part, with their ACF and PACF.





As in Projects 1 and 2, the regression residuals are examined before choosing the error model. Without the trend the residuals from the regression part wander, so a first difference is taken. Figure 4 shows the differenced residuals with their ACF and PACF, which point to a low order ARMA structure with no seasonal spikes left (the dummies have removed the seasonality). The orders are then chosen by AICc, and the model is estimated by maximum likelihood.


Code
fit_reg <- train_reg |>
  model(
    Reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                  pdq(d = 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0))
  )

reg_spec <- format(fit_reg$Reg[[1]])

  filter(term %in% c("decay", "mar20", "may20", "step"))

  select(Term = term, Estimate = estimate,
         `Std. error` = std.error, `p-value` = p.value) |>

effect <- train_reg |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(log_effect = rc("Reg", "decay") * decay + rc("Reg", "mar20") * mar20 +
           rc("Reg", "may20") * may20 + rc("Reg", "step") * step,

Figure 5: Contribution of the intervention terms (decay, pulses and level shift combined) in the regression with ARIMA errors, expressed as a percentage reduction in demand. The later recovery is carried by the ARIMA error and is not shown.





The selected error model is LM w/ ARIMA(2,1,1) errors. The estimates have a direct interpretation on the log scale. The decaying shock has \(\hat\omega\) = -3.19; combined with the May 2020 pulse and the level shift, this reproduces a loss of almost all demand in April and May 2020. The level shift is \(\hat\lambda\) = -0.515 (p < 0.001). This needs careful interpretation. Because the error \(\eta_t\) has a unit root, it has its own wandering level, and the slow two-year recovery is carried by the error rather than by the intervention terms: the decaying shock dies out quickly (see the half-life above), and \(\hat\lambda\) is the part of the April 2020 drop that did not decay geometrically. It is therefore not the gap between the pre- and post-COVID levels; that gap is estimated directly in Section 4.2. Figure 5 shows the contribution of the intervention terms alone, which is why it stays flat after 2020; the recovery towards the post-COVID level happens in the error process. The standard errors are now valid only because the errors are modelled; compare the static regression, whose standard errors were too small.


3.3.4 Residual diagnostics


Code
reg_aug <- augment(fit_reg)

n_arma <- tidy(fit_reg) |>
  filter(grepl("^(ar|ma)[0-9]+$", term)) |>
  count(.model, name = "dof")

reg_lb <- reg_aug |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(n_arma, by = ".model") |>
  mutate(dof = coalesce(dof, 0L)) |>
  group_by(.model) |>
  summarise(lb_p = Box.test(.innov, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box",
                            fitdf = first(dof))$p.value,
            .groups = "drop")

lbp <- function(m) reg_lb$lb_p[reg_lb$.model == m]




Code
fit_reg |> select(Reg) |> gg_tsresiduals(lag_max = 36)








Figure 6: Residual diagnostics for the regression with ARIMA errors.





The Ljung and Box test on 24 lags (degrees of freedom reduced by the number of ARMA coefficients) gives p = 0.556. The innovations of the regression model are consistent with white noise and show no remaining seasonal structure, so the deterministic seasonal dummies are adequate. Compared with the static regression, the long runs in the residuals have disappeared: the ARIMA error has absorbed the autocorrelation. The model passes the residual check and can be used to forecast.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.1 Model B1: ETS on the raw training data
text:
4.1 Model B1: ETS on the raw training data
The ETS() function selects the error, trend and seasonal forms (additive, multiplicative or none) by AICc and estimates the smoothing parameters and initial states by maximum likelihood. Exponential smoothing cannot skip missing observations, so the first attempt simply fits ETS to the training data including the COVID months, on both the original and the log scale.


Code
fit_ets_raw <- train |>
  model(`ETS raw (original scale)` = ETS(nights),
        `ETS raw (log scale)`      = ETS(log(nights)))

ets_par_tbl <- function(fit) {
  tidy(fit) |>
    filter(term %in% c("alpha", "beta", "gamma", "phi")) |>
    select(.model, term, estimate) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = estimate) |>
    left_join(tibble(.model = names(fit),
                     Form = vapply(names(fit), function(m) format(fit[[m]][[1]]), "")),
              by = ".model") |>
    relocate(Form, .after = .model)
}

raw_tbl <- ets_par_tbl(fit_ets_raw)
alpha_raw <- raw_tbl$alpha




Code
raw_tbl |> rename(Model = .model) |> kable(digits = 4)

This is the exponential smoothing version of the problem Project 1 had with SARIMA. On both scales the level smoothing parameter is at its upper limit (\(\hat\alpha \approx\) 1.000): the only way the method can follow a collapse of more than 95% and a two-year recovery is to reset the level to the latest observation every month. On the log scale the selected model even has no seasonal component: on the log scale the April 2020 drop is many times larger than the seasonal swings, so the likelihood gains nothing from tracking the season. A model with no seasonality for a series this seasonal is clearly wrong. With \(\alpha = 1\) the forecasts are simply the last observation (plus the seasonal pattern, if there is one), the residual variance is inflated by the COVID months and the prediction intervals are very wide. The COVID window has to be dealt with before exponential smoothing can work.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.2 Imputing the COVID window with a regression
text:
4.2 Imputing the COVID window with a regression
Three ways of handling the window are possible: (1) fit only to the post-COVID months, which leaves just over two years of data to estimate 12 seasonal effects (tested as a check in Section 4.5); (2) remove the estimated intervention effect from Part A; or (3) replace the COVID months by values that describe what demand would have looked like without the pandemic. Option (2) does not help much: the regression explains the shock partly through its ARIMA error, so the “adjusted” series still contains most of the recovery dynamics. I therefore use option (3), with a regression as the imputation model.
The imputation regression is fitted only to the non-COVID months:
\[
\log y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \lambda R_t + \varepsilon_t,
\]
where \(R_t\) is a ramp: 0 before March 2020, 1 after March 2022, and rising linearly through the window. Since \(R_t\) only takes the values 0 and 1 in the months used for fitting, \(\lambda\) is the difference between the pre- and post-COVID levels; inside the window the ramp produces a straight-line transition between the two levels, with the usual seasonal pattern on top. The fitted values in the window are used as the imputed values.


Code
impute_covid <- function(df) {
  n_win <- month_num(covid_end) - month_num(covid_start) + 2
  df <- df |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(t      = row_number(),
           mon    = factor(month(as.Date(Month))),
           in_win = Month >= covid_start & Month <= covid_end,
           ramp   = pmin(pmax((month_num(Month) - month_num(covid_start) + 1) / n_win, 0), 1),
           y_obs  = if_else(in_win, NA_real_, log(nights)))
  fit <- lm(y_obs ~ t + mon + ramp, data = df)   # lm drops the NA months
  df |>
    mutate(log_fit     = predict(fit, newdata = df),
           nights_imp  = if_else(in_win, exp(log_fit), nights)) |>
    select(-t, -mon, -y_obs, -log_fit) |>
    structure(imputation_fit = fit)          # keep the fitted model for reporting
}

train_imp_tbl <- impute_covid(train)
imp_lm        <- attr(train_imp_tbl, "imputation_fit")
train_imp     <- train_imp_tbl |> as_tsibble(index = Month)

imp_r2   <- summary(imp_lm)$r.squared
imp_ramp <- coef(imp_lm)[["ramp"]]




Code
train_imp |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month))) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date(covid_start), xmax = as.Date(covid_end),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15, fill = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = nights), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = nights_imp), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands)")








Figure 7: Training data on the original scale (grey) and the series used for exponential smoothing, in which the COVID window (shaded) is replaced by the regression-imputed values (red).





The imputation regression explains 94.8% of the variation in the non-COVID months, and the estimated difference between the post- and pre-COVID levels is -0.212 on the log scale (-19.1%). This is the clearest estimate in the project of how far demand remains below its pre-COVID path. It is much smaller than the level shift in the regression with ARIMA errors (\(\hat\lambda\) = -0.515), which confirms the point made there: in that model the error process carries part of the recovery, so \(\hat\lambda\) is not the long-run gap. The imputed values (Figure 7) carry the seasonal pattern smoothly across the gap. Their weakness is that they contain no noise, which I return to in the discussion.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.3 Model B2: Holt–Winters from first principles
text:
4.3 Model B2: Holt–Winters from first principles
To make sure I understand what ETS() is doing, I implement the additive Holt–Winters method myself (fpp3 Section 8.3). With \(y_t\) the log of the imputed series, \(\ell_t\) the level, \(b_t\) the trend and \(s_t\) the seasonal effect, the one-step forecast and the error are
\[
\hat y_{t \mid t-1} = \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + s_{t-12}, \qquad e_t = y_t - \hat y_{t \mid t-1},
\]
and the components are updated in error-correction form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \alpha e_t, \\
b_t    &= b_{t-1} + \beta e_t, \\
s_t    &= s_{t-12} + \gamma e_t .
\end{aligned}
\]
Each update moves a component in the direction of the latest error, and the smoothing parameters say how far. The \(h\)-step forecast is \(\hat y_{T+h \mid T} = \ell_T + h\, b_T + s_{T+h-12k}\), where \(k\) makes the seasonal index refer to the last observed year. With additive errors, maximising the Gaussian likelihood is the same as minimising the sum of squared one-step errors (the error variance can be profiled out), so I estimate the three smoothing parameters and the 13 free initial states (\(\ell_0\), \(b_0\) and 11 seasonal effects; the 12th is set so the seasonal effects sum to zero) by minimising the SSE with optim(). The parameter bounds match those in fable (between 0.0001 and 0.9999).


Code
# Additive Holt-Winters filter -------------------------------------------
# par = (alpha, beta, gamma, l0, b0, s_{-11}, ..., s_{-1});
# the last seasonal state s_0 makes the 12 initial effects sum to zero.
hw_filter <- function(par, y, m = 12) {
  alpha <- par[1]; beta <- par[2]; gamma <- par[3]
  level <- par[4]; trend <- par[5]
  s     <- c(par[6:(4 + m)], -sum(par[6:(4 + m)]))  # s[1] is the effect for the next month
  n <- length(y); e <- yhat <- numeric(n)
  for (t in 1:n) {
    yhat[t] <- level + trend + s[1]
    e[t]    <- y[t] - yhat[t]
    new_level <- level + trend + alpha * e[t]
    trend     <- trend + beta * e[t]
    s         <- c(s[-1], s[1] + gamma * e[t])        # rotate the seasonal states
    level     <- new_level
  }
  list(e = e, fitted = yhat, level = level, trend = trend, season = s)
}

hw_forecast <- function(state, h, m = 12) {
  state$level + (1:h) * state$trend + rep(state$season, length.out = h)
}

# Estimation by least squares --------------------------------------------
y_imp <- log(train_imp$nights_imp)
sse   <- function(par) sum(hw_filter(par, y_imp)$e^2)

# Starting values: classical decomposition of the first two years
first2 <- y_imp[1:24]
s_init <- y_imp[1:12] - mean(y_imp[1:12])
start  <- c(0.3, 0.01, 0.1,
            mean(first2[1:12]), (mean(first2[13:24]) - mean(first2[1:12])) / 12,
            (s_init - mean(s_init))[1:11])

own_opt <- optim(start, sse, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = c(rep(1e-4, 3), rep(-Inf, 13)),
                 upper = c(rep(0.9999, 3), rep(Inf, 13)),
                 control = list(maxit = 10000))
own_hw  <- hw_filter(own_opt$par, y_imp)

# The same model in fable --------------------------------------------------
fit_hw_fable <- train_imp |>
  model(HW = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("A")))
fable_par <- tidy(fit_hw_fable)
fable_sse <- sum(augment(fit_hw_fable)$.innov^2)
fp <- function(t) fable_par$estimate[fable_par$term == t]




Code
tibble(
  Quantity = c("alpha", "beta", "gamma", "Initial level", "Initial trend",
               "SSE", "Optimiser converged"),
  `Own code` = c(fmt(own_opt$par[1:3], 4), fmt(own_opt$par[4], 3),
                 fmt(own_opt$par[5], 5), fmt(own_opt$value, 5),
                 ifelse(own_opt$convergence == 0, "Yes", "No")),
  `fable ETS(A,A,A)` = c(fmt(c(fp("alpha"), fp("beta"), fp("gamma")), 4),
                         fmt(fp("l[0]"), 3), fmt(fp("b[0]"), 5),
                         fmt(fable_sse, 5), "")
) |> kable()

The two fits agree closely (Table 4). My optimiser actually reaches a slightly lower SSE (0.08502 against 0.08541), so the small differences in the parameters come from the two optimisers stopping at different points on a very flat surface, not from a difference in the model. Both put \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) at the lower bound, which means the trend and the seasonal pattern are essentially fixed at their initial values, while the level adapts with \(\hat\alpha \approx\) 0.55. This matches the finding from Project 1 that the seasonal pattern is very stable. The 24-month forecasts from the two implementations differ by at most 0.3% (part of this is that fable’s forecast is the bias-adjusted mean, while mine is the back-transformed median). Writing the recursions out also made something clear that is easy to miss when calling ETS(): the initial states are parameters too, and with 13 of them against three smoothing parameters they dominate the estimation.

Figure 8: Components of the damped Holt-Winters model on the log scale: level, slope and seasonal effects.





The results sort the models into two groups (Table 5). The non-seasonal methods (SES, Holt, damped Holt) have far higher AICc values and their innovations are strongly autocorrelated (Ljung and Box p < 0.001), because they leave the whole seasonal pattern in the errors. They fail the residual check immediately. The seasonal models all pass the white noise check, and the automatic selection chooses ETS(A,A,A).
The seasonal models differ mainly in what they do with the trend:

ETS(A,N,A) has no trend: forecasts are flat apart from the season. Its AICc is -236.6.
Holt-Winters has an additive trend with \(\hat\beta\) at the lower bound, so the slope is fixed at its initial value. The forecasts extrapolate that slope linearly for the full 24 months. AICc -240.1.
Damped HW multiplies the slope by \(\phi\) = 0.965 each month, so its effect fades and the long-run forecast levels off. AICc -236.5.

The AICc differences between the three seasonal models are small (less than 4), so the training data alone cannot separate them clearly. The choice matters much more for long horizons than for one-step fit, so the test set below is the real arbiter. My prior expectation, from the literature on damped trends (Gardner and McKenzie, 1985), is that a damped trend will forecast better than a linear one over two years.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.5 Model B4: a check using the post-COVID years only
text:
4.5 Model B4: a check using the post-COVID years only
The imputation approach keeps all ten years of data but fills the COVID window with values that were never observed. A simpler alternative is to drop everything before April 2022 and fit exponential smoothing only to the post-COVID months. At first sight little should be lost, because exponential smoothing already gives the most weight to the latest observations. That is true for the level, but not for the other components here. In the models above, \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) sit at or near their lower bounds, so the seasonal pattern and the slope are hardly updated at all: they stay close to their initial values, which are estimated from the whole series back to 2015. The early years therefore still shape the seasonal pattern and the trend, however small their weight in the level. Fitting to the post-COVID months only is the one way to let those components reflect current behaviour. The cost is data: April 2022 to June 2024 gives just 27 months to estimate up to four smoothing parameters and 13 initial states.


Code
post_start <- yearmonth("2022 Apr")
train_post <- train |> filter(Month >= post_start)
ets_forms  <- c("ETS(A,N,A)", "Holt-Winters", "Damped HW")

fit_post <- train_post |>
  model(
    `ETS(A,N,A)`   = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
    `Holt-Winters` = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
    `Damped HW`    = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A"))
  )

# Test set forecasts from both versions of each model
fc_ets_tbl <- function(fit, label) {
  forecast(fit, h = 24) |>
    hilo(level = 95) |>
    unpack_hilo(`95%`) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    select(Model = .model, Month, mean = .mean, lo95 = `95%_lower`, hi95 = `95%_upper`) |>
    mutate(Data = label)
}

post_fc <- bind_rows(
  fc_ets_tbl(fit_ets |> select(all_of(ets_forms)), "Imputed series, 2015 to 2024"),
  fc_ets_tbl(fit_post, "Post-COVID only, 2022 to 2024")
) |>
  left_join(as_tibble(test) |> select(Month, actual = nights), by = "Month") |>
  filter(!is.na(mean)) |>
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = ets_forms))

sn_rmse <- train |>

  forecast(h = 24) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(test) |> select(Month, actual = nights), by = "Month") |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - .mean)^2))) |>
  pull(RMSE)

post_acc <- post_fc |>
  group_by(Model, Data) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - mean)^2)),
            MAPE = 100 * mean(abs(actual - mean) / actual),
            `Cover 95%` = mean(actual >= lo95 & actual <= hi95),
            `Mean 95% width` = mean(hi95 - lo95),
            .groups = "drop") |>

  arrange(Model, Data)

  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 10: Seasonal effects (log scale) at the end of the training period, from the ETS(A,N,A) model fitted to the imputed series and to the post-COVID months only.





What happens with less data. With only 27 months, each seasonal effect is effectively estimated from two or three values. Across the three post-COVID fits (Table 6), the level parameter ranges from \(\hat\alpha\) = 0.000 to 0.844, and the largest seasonal parameter is \(\hat\gamma\) = 0.0028. As on the full series, the seasonal pattern is held essentially fixed: two years of data contain no evidence that it is changing. The level parameter, in contrast, differs widely between the three forms, a sign that the short sample cannot pin down how quickly the level should adapt.
Forecast accuracy. On the test set (Table 7, Figure 9), the best of the post-COVID fits is Damped HW (RMSE 75.3), against 72.5 for the damped Holt–Winters model on the imputed series and 132.6 for seasonal naive. Dropping the earlier years helps Holt-Winters but not the other two, so the ranking of the three models changes with the training window. The ETS(A,N,A) model moves from an RMSE of 95.9 to 117.5, Holt–Winters from 151.7 to 80.7, and damped Holt–Winters from 72.5 to 75.3. With two years of data, the trend each model estimates comes from a very short stretch of the recovery, so which model forecasts best depends heavily on how that short-run slope happens to continue.
The large improvement for Holt–Winters shows where the problem with the undamped model on the imputed series lies. There, the slope is fixed at the value estimated for the start of the series in 2015, which is slightly negative, and it is extrapolated for two full years, so the forecasts drift steadily below the data (Figure 9). Fitted to the post-COVID months, the slope comes from the recovery instead, which happened to continue through the test period. But this version is not a better model so much as a different gamble. Its smoothing parameters are all close to zero (\(\hat\alpha\) = 0.0003), so it is essentially a fixed straight line plus a fixed seasonal pattern drawn through 27 months. Its 95% intervals are the narrowest of all (mean width 251 thousand nights), yet they still miss 12% of the test months.
The damped model is the most revealing result of the check. Fitted to completely different training windows, it gives almost the same forecast accuracy (RMSE 72.5 and 75.3), because damping makes the long-horizon forecast depend much less on exactly how the slope is estimated. That robustness is a stronger argument for the damped trend than its single best test-set score. The short window still has a cost: the damped model’s 95% intervals are wider when it is fitted to the post-COVID months only (mean width 813 against 543 thousand nights), reflecting the extra uncertainty in parameters estimated from two years of data.
Seasonal pattern. The seasonal effects learned from the post-COVID months alone are close to those from the full imputed series (Figure 10): the largest difference in any month is 2.9%. This confirms, from a different angle, the finding from Project 1 that the seasonal shape survived COVID unchanged, and it means that the long history is not distorting the seasonal pattern. Its value lies in pinning down the level and the trend, which is exactly where the short-window fits are least stable.
Conclusion of the check. Using only the post-COVID years avoids imputation entirely, and for some model forms it forecasts well. But the results are fragile: with so little data the outcome depends on the choice of trend, and there is no way to tell in advance which choice will work. The imputed series gives the models enough history to estimate the seasonal pattern and the trend reliably, which is why it remains the main approach in this project.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
5.2 Rolling-origin cross-validation
A single 24-month test set gives one realisation of each model’s forecast errors, so the ranking could be luck. As in Project 1, I also use an expanding window: the models are refitted at each of 13 origins from June 2024 to June 2025 and forecast 1 to 12 months ahead, and the errors are averaged by horizon. The imputation regression is refitted at every origin. To keep the computation manageable, the regression keeps \(\hat\delta\) and its ARIMA error orders fixed at the values chosen above; the ETS forms are also fixed, but all parameters are re-estimated. All the origins fall inside the test period, so the cross-validation is not independent of the test set; it checks whether the ranking holds when the forecast origin moves.


Code
reg_pdq <- fit_reg$Reg[[1]]$fit$spec
cv_origins <- 13
cv_h       <- 12

cv_data <- nights_sold |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = nrow(train), .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id <= cv_origins)

cv_fc <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(cv_origins), function(i) {
  d   <- cv_data |> filter(.id == i) |> select(-.id)
  fut <- new_data(d, cv_h)

  # seasonal naive and Project 1 SARIMA
  dB <- d |> mutate(nights = if_else(period == "COVID window", NA_real_, nights))
  f1 <- forecast(d  |> model(`Seasonal naive` = SNAIVE(nights)), h = cv_h)
  f2 <- forecast(dB |> model(`SARIMA (Project 1)` =
                               ARIMA(log(nights) ~ 0 + pdq(0, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 1, 1))), h = cv_h)

  # regression with ARIMA errors (orders fixed)
  dR <- covid_vars(d, delta_hat)
  fR <- covid_vars(fut, delta_hat)
  f3 <- forecast(dR |> model(Reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                                           pdq(reg_pdq$p, 1, reg_pdq$q) + PDQ(0, 0, 0))),
                 new_data = fR)

  # exponential smoothing on the imputed series
  dI <- impute_covid(d) |> as_tsibble(index = Month)
  f4 <- forecast(dI |> model(
    `ETS(A,N,A)`   = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
    `Holt-Winters` = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
    `Damped HW`    = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A"))),
    h = cv_h)

  bind_rows(as_tibble(f1), as_tibble(f2), as_tibble(f3), as_tibble(f4)) |>
    select(.model, Month, .mean) |>
    group_by(.model) |>
    mutate(h = row_number(), origin = i) |>
    ungroup()
})) |>
  left_join(as_tibble(nights_sold) |> select(Month, actual = nights), by = "Month") |>
  filter(!is.na(actual))

cv_by_h <- cv_fc |>
  group_by(.model, h) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - .mean)^2)), .groups = "drop")

cv_overall <- cv_fc |>
  group_by(Model = .model) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - .mean)^2)),
            MAE  = mean(abs(actual - .mean)),
            MAPE = 100 * mean(abs(actual - .mean) / actual),
            n    = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(RMSE)

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
5.3 Results
Overall ranking. On the test set the lowest RMSE is achieved by the Damped HW model (72.5 thousand nights). Among the models that passed the diagnostic step, the best is Damped HW. For reference, the Project 1 SARIMA has an RMSE of 101.6 and the seasonal naive benchmark 132.6. In cross-validation the best model is SARIMA (Project 1) (RMSE 83.5), followed by Damped HW (89.5), with seasonal naive at 112.2 (Table 9, Figure 12). The two evaluations therefore do not fully agree, which is exactly why a single test set is not enough: the cross-validation forecasts start later (up to June 2025) and are at most 12 months ahead, so they reward models that track the recent level and penalise less for how the trend is extrapolated in the second year.
Static regression. The static regression has an RMSE of 233.8, worse than seasonal naive. Its deterministic trend is estimated from the whole training period, including the gentle decline before 2020, and is extrapolated through the test period, so the forecasts drift away from the data. Its 95% intervals happen to cover 100% of the test months, but only because the COVID months inflate the residual variance; with autocorrelated errors the interval formula itself is not valid, so this coverage cannot be relied on.
Regression with ARIMA errors. Modelling the error process gives an RMSE of 98.8 and a MAPE of 4.51%, better than the Project 1 SARIMA. Its intervals cover 100% of the test months at the 95% level and 100% at the 80% level, so they are too wide: a correct 80% interval should miss about one month in five. The reason is visible in Figure 6. The intervention terms capture the collapse but not every month of the uneven recovery, so the innovations in 2020 and 2021 are several times larger than normal and inflate the estimated error variance, which then widens every forecast interval (mean width 1,060 thousand nights against 545 for the SARIMA, which ignores those months). By June 2024 the temporary part of the shock had died out (\(\hat\delta^{\,50} \approx\) 1.1e-06), so the forecasts rest on the post-COVID level and the seasonal dummies. The main advantage of this model is interpretation: it estimates the size, shape and persistence of the shock (Figure 5) instead of discarding it.
Exponential smoothing on the raw data. ETS fitted with the COVID months included reaches an RMSE of 130.0, only just beating seasonal naive. With \(\hat\alpha = 1\) it is close to a seasonal random walk, and its 95% intervals are on average 2,292 thousand nights wide, against 1,060 for the regression.
Exponential smoothing on the imputed series. Imputing the window transforms exponential smoothing. The best of the seasonal models on the test set is Damped HW (RMSE 72.5), and the ranking among them is decided by the trend: the undamped Holt–Winters model (RMSE 151.7) extrapolates a fixed negative slope for two years, the no-trend model (RMSE 95.9) holds the level flat, and the damped model (RMSE 72.5) lets the slope fade. AICc preferred Holt-Winters, which is a useful reminder that AICc measures one-step-ahead fit in the training data, while the test set measures forecasts up to 24 months ahead, where the treatment of the trend dominates. The undamped model’s intervals also cover only 88% of the test months at the 95% level: its forecasts drift away from the data while the intervals stay narrow, partly because the noise-free imputed months shrink the estimated error variance. SES, which ignores the season, is far behind (RMSE 225.9), confirming the diagnostics.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
7.1 Key findings

A static regression is not enough. Trend, seasonal dummies and intervention terms give an adjusted \(R^2\) of 0.965, but the residuals are strongly autocorrelated (Durbin–Watson 0.53), so the standard errors and intervals cannot be trusted. Its test RMSE was 233.8.
Regression with ARIMA errors fixes this. With deterministic seasonal dummies (preferred to Fourier terms by AICc), a decaying intervention with \(\hat\delta\) = 0.76 (half-life about 2.5 months), two pulses and a level shift, the innovations are white noise (Ljung and Box p = 0.556), and the test RMSE is 98.8 against 101.6 for the Project 1 SARIMA. The shock is described with five parameters instead of 25 deleted months. The post-COVID level is estimated (by the imputation regression) to be 19% below the pre-COVID path.
Exponential smoothing breaks on the raw data. With the COVID months included, the level smoothing parameter goes to 1 and, on the log scale, AICc even drops the seasonal component.
Regression imputation rescues exponential smoothing. On the imputed series the seasonal models pass the diagnostics, and Damped HW reached a test RMSE of 72.5. The trend assumption (none, linear or damped) is what separates the seasonal models over a two-year horizon.
My own Holt–Winters code reproduces ETS(). The SSE agrees to 0.46% and both put \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) at the boundary, confirming a fixed seasonal pattern and slope.
Using only the post-COVID years (Section 4.5) avoids imputation, but leaves just 27 months. The best exponential smoothing model fitted to that window was Damped HW (test RMSE 75.3), against 72.5 for damped Holt–Winters on the imputed series. Across the three trend forms the post-COVID RMSE ranged from 75.3 to 117.5, so with so little data the result depends heavily on the choice of trend. The damped model was the only one whose accuracy barely changed between the two training windows, which makes it the most robust choice.
Overall, the best model on the test set was Damped HW, the best that also passed the diagnostics was Damped HW, and the best in cross-validation was SARIMA (Project 1). Among the Section 2 models, Damped HW was the most accurate in cross-validation, so the Project 1 SARIMA remains a very strong benchmark: regression and exponential smoothing match it, but only beat it clearly on one of the two evaluations.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
7.2 Issues and limitations

The imputed values are treated as data. Exponential smoothing sees the 25 imputed months as exact observations with no noise. This makes the estimated error variance too small (so the intervals are too narrow) and can pull the smoothing parameters, since the imputed stretch is perfectly smooth. Multiple imputation (adding resampled residuals to the imputed values and averaging over many fits) would address this.
The imputation model is a modelling choice. The linear ramp between the pre- and post-COVID levels is a simple assumption. A different path (for example a faster or slower recovery) would change the imputed level in 2021 and, through the smoothing, the estimated slope.
Choice of intervention shape. The decay, pulses and step were chosen by looking at the data, so there is a risk of over-fitting the shape of the shock to this series. The pulse months were picked by eye.
Profile likelihood standard errors. Treating \(\hat\delta\) as known when computing the other standard errors understates their uncertainty.
Cross-validation shortcuts. The regression’s \(\delta\) and error orders, and the ETS forms, were held fixed across origins, which favours them slightly because they were chosen with the full training set.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
7.3 What I would do differently
I would use multiple imputation for the COVID window so that the exponential smoothing intervals reflect the uncertainty in the imputed values, and estimate \(\delta\) jointly with the other regression parameters by maximising the likelihood directly. A cleaner solution to both problems is a model that can skip the missing months without imputing them and that has the regression and smoothing ideas built in, which is what the state space models in Project 4 provide.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
7.4 Reflection and model development
Project 1 left me with one clear problem: the COVID collapse was the biggest obstacle to forecasting accommodation demand, and the best I could do with SARIMA was to treat those 25 months as missing. That felt unsatisfying, because those months contain real information about how demand behaves under a shock. Section 2 of the course introduced two approaches that handle this very differently, time series regression and exponential smoothing, so I wanted to see whether modelling the shock, rather than deleting it, would give better forecasts or at least a better understanding of what happened.
The project changed shape considerably along the way. My first versions were framed around “modelling the COVID shock” and combined a single ETS model, a regression with intervention terms and a basic structural model fitted with the Kalman filter. As the portfolio came together, I realised this mixed topics from different parts of the course, and that the state space material belonged in Project 4, where it could be developed properly. I refocused this project on regression and exponential smoothing alone, which gave me room to go much deeper into each one. It also let me address a weakness I had listed in my own earlier draft, that everything rested on a single test set, by adding rolling-origin cross-validation.
On the regression side, I deliberately started with the simplest possible model, a static regression with a trend, seasonal dummies and intervention terms. Its adjusted \(R^2\) of 0.965 looked excellent, but the residuals drifted in long runs and the Durbin–Watson statistic was 0.53. That was the moment the lectures’ warning about regression on time series became concrete for me: a good in-sample fit can hide errors that make every standard error and interval unreliable. Letting the errors follow an ARIMA process fixed this, and each remaining decision came from the data. I replaced the deterministic trend with a first difference because the post-COVID level clearly did not follow a straight line. I kept seasonal dummies rather than Fourier terms because the sharp December peak needs many harmonics, which AICc confirmed. And because the decay rate enters the model non-linearly, I chose it by profiling the AICc over a grid. The most subtle lesson was in interpreting the result. With a unit root in the errors, the level shift coefficient is not the gap between the pre- and post-COVID levels, because part of the recovery is carried by the error process. I only understood this properly once the imputation regression gave a very different estimate of that gap.
Exponential smoothing taught me the opposite lesson about COVID. Fitted to the raw data, the level smoothing parameter went straight to 1, and on the log scale the model even dropped the seasonal component altogether. Unlike ARIMA, exponential smoothing cannot skip missing months, so I had to decide what to put in the gap. I chose to impute the window with a regression fitted only to the non-COVID months, which carries the seasonal pattern across the gap with a smooth transition between the two levels. Writing the Holt–Winters recursions myself was the most useful part of this section. It reproduced ETS() almost exactly, and it showed me something I would have missed by only calling the function: the 13 initial states are parameters too, and they dominate the estimation.
The results did not always agree with each other, and working out why was the most valuable part of the project. AICc preferred the undamped Holt–Winters model, but on the test set it was one of the worst, because it extrapolated a fixed downward slope for two full years, while the damped version, which lets the slope fade, was the best model of all. The test set and the cross-validation also disagreed: damped Holt–Winters won on the test set, but the Project 1 SARIMA won in cross-validation. This showed me that in-sample criteria measure one-step fit, while forecasting over two years depends mostly on how the trend is extrapolated, and that a single test set is not enough to rank models.
I also tested an additional idea. Since exponential smoothing already puts most of its weight on recent observations, I wondered whether the imputation was needed at all, or whether I could simply fit the models to the post-COVID years from April 2022. Working through it showed me that the weighting only applies to the level: in my models the seasonal pattern and the slope barely update, so they still come from the start of the series in 2015. Fitting only the last two years was the way to let them reflect current behaviour, at the cost of having just 27 months of data. The results were mixed. The undamped Holt–Winters model improved a great deal, because it no longer extrapolated a slope from 2015, but the no-trend model got worse. The damped model gave almost the same accuracy on both windows, which convinced me more than any single score that damping is the safest choice when the trend is uncertain. The seasonal pattern learned from two years was also very close to the one from the full series, which confirmed again how stable it is. In the end I kept the imputed series as the main approach, because with so little data the outcome depended too much on which trend I happened to choose.
Going forward, the main weakness I would address is that the imputed COVID months are treated as exact data. They contain no noise, which makes the exponential smoothing intervals too narrow; multiple imputation would fix this. More fundamentally, both approaches in this project needed a workaround for the missing months, either intervention terms or imputation. A state space model can skip missing observations directly while keeping the regression and smoothing ideas built in, which is exactly what Project 4 takes up.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: Forecasting South African accommodation demand with ARIMA and SARIMA models
Section and topic: Section 1. Benchmarks, stationarity and differencing, ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA models, model identification and residual diagnostics, forecast evaluation.
Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data.
Question: How much forecast accuracy is gained by moving from simple benchmark methods to ARMA, ARIMA and seasonal ARIMA models for monthly stay unit nights sold in South Africa, and how sensitive is that gain to the way the COVID-19 structural break is handled?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data from Statistics South Africa (Stats SA), Tourist Accommodation statistical release P6410, series B64100 (stay unit nights sold, total industry, thousands), monthly. Analysis window January 2015 to June 2026. Full source details are in Section 2.1.
Methods: In the main analysis the COVID months (March 2020 to March 2022) are treated as missing, so all models are estimated from the pre- and post-COVID data only; fitting the same models with the COVID months kept is reported as a sensitivity check. The transformation and the orders of differencing are chosen from the pre-COVID data using time plots, ACF/PACF plots and unit root tests, with the Guerrero estimate of the Box–Cox parameter reported as a check. A candidate SARIMA model is identified by hand from the ACF and PACF and compared with the model chosen automatically by ARIMA(). Each candidate is checked with residual plots, Ljung–Box tests and, for the final model, its MA roots. The candidates are then compared with four benchmarks (mean, naive, seasonal naive, drift) and simpler ARMA and ARIMA models on a 24-month test set (RMSE, MAE, MAPE, MASE, interval coverage) and by expanding-window rolling-origin cross-validation over horizons of 1 to 12 months.
Target variable: This analysis focuses on stay unit nights sold. This was chosen over income level and occupancy rate because it appears to be the most consistent. Occupancy rate can change when room supply changes and income can be disrupted by inflation or other general increases. Unit nights sold tells a very clear demand picture with minimal factors affecting the quality of the variable over the years.
Key findings: See Section 9.1. In short: with the COVID months left in the data, the seasonal ARIMA models are far worse than the seasonal naive benchmark, because the collapse in April 2020 dominates the estimated variance and distorts the parameters. Treating the COVID window as missing gives a stable SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 “airline” model with well behaved residuals, and that model gives the most accurate forecasts on both the test set and in cross-validation.
What I would do differently: Model the shock explicitly with intervention variables (taken up in Project 3), and compare the expanding window with a sliding window that forgets the pre-COVID years.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

text:
2.2 Reading and reshaping the data
The Stats SA file has one row per series and one column per month, with month columns named MOmmyyyy. The code below reshapes it to long format and builds a tsibble.


Code
raw <- read_excel(data_file)

tourism_long <- raw |>
  filter(H03 %in% c("B64100", "B64101")) |>
  select(H03, H04, starts_with("MO")) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("MO"), names_to = "code", values_to = "nights") |>
  mutate(
    Month    = yearmonth(make_date(as.integer(substr(code, 5, 8)),
                                   as.integer(substr(code, 3, 4)), 1L)),
    nights   = as.numeric(nights),
    industry = if_else(H03 == "B64100", "Total industry", "Hotels")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(nights)) |>
  select(Month, industry, nights)

# Total industry, January 2015 onwards, with a COVID period label
nights_sold <- tourism_long |>
  filter(industry == "Total industry") |>
  select(Month, nights) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter_index("2015 Jan" ~ .) |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    Month <  covid_start ~ "Pre-COVID",
    Month <= covid_end   ~ "COVID window",
    TRUE                 ~ "Post-COVID"
  ))

pre_covid <- nights_sold |> filter(Month < covid_start)

# Stop if the monthly index has implicit gaps
stopifnot(!has_gaps(nights_sold)$.gaps)

  mutate(period = factor(period, levels = c("Pre-COVID", "COVID window", "Post-COVID"))) |>

text:
3.1 Time plot


Code
full_df <- tourism_long |>
  filter(industry == "Total industry") |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(Month))

ggplot(full_df, aes(date, nights)) +
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = as.Date(covid_start), xmax = as.Date(covid_end),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15, fill = "firebrick") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2015-01-01"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue4") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands)")








Figure 1: Monthly stay unit nights sold, total industry, January 2007 to June 2026. The shaded band is the COVID window (March 2020 to March 2022); the dashed line marks the start of the analysis window.





Figure 1 shows three distinct regimes. Before 2020 the series moves around a fairly flat level of about 2,212 thousand nights a month (2019 average) with a strong and regular seasonal pattern. In April 2020 nights sold fell to 57 thousand, 2.7% of April 2019, and the recovery took roughly two years, with setbacks during the later waves. Over the most recent 12 months the average is 1,954 thousand, close to but still below the pre-COVID level. The series is clearly not stationary in mean over the full window, and the variability is much larger during the COVID window than anywhere else.

3.2 Seasonal patterns


Code
nights_sold |>
  filter(period != "COVID window") |>
  fill_gaps() |>
  gg_season(nights, labels = "right") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(y = "Nights sold (thousands)", x = NULL)








Figure 2: Seasonal plot of nights sold by year (pre-COVID and post-COVID years only).







Code
pre_covid |>
  gg_subseries(nights) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(y = "Nights sold (thousands)", x = NULL)








Figure 3: Seasonal subseries plot for the pre-COVID years (2015 to 2019). Blue lines are the monthly means.





Figure 2 and Figure 3 show that the shape of the seasonal pattern is very stable from year to year: a dip in January, a local peak in March (Easter and school holidays), a low in May and June, then a steady rise to the highest values in October to December. The post-COVID years sit lower but follow the same shape. This matters for modelling: a stable seasonal shape suggests a seasonal difference (or a seasonal MA term close to the boundary), and it means that the seasonal naive method is a strong benchmark.

Hotels account for more than half of all nights sold and move in close proportion to the total, in every period (Figure 5). The COVID points simply slide down the same line rather than forming a separate cloud, so the shock hit all accommodation types together. The post-COVID points sit slightly above the pre-COVID cloud, so hotels now take a somewhat larger share of a smaller market, but the relationship is still close to a straight line. text:
3.5 Stationarity and identification (pre-COVID data)
Identification is done on the pre-COVID data only, because the COVID collapse would dominate any ACF calculated over the full series and hide the ordinary dependence structure.


Code
lx  <- log(pre_covid$nights)
d12 <- diff(lx, lag = 12)

kpss_lx  <- unitroot_kpss(lx)
kpss_d12 <- unitroot_kpss(d12)
nsd_lx   <- unname(unitroot_nsdiffs(lx, .period = 12))
nd_lx    <- unname(unitroot_ndiffs(lx))
nd_d12   <- unname(unitroot_ndiffs(d12))

tibble(
  Series           = c("log nights", "seasonally differenced log nights"),
  `KPSS statistic` = c(kpss_lx["kpss_stat"], kpss_d12["kpss_stat"]),
  `KPSS p-value`   = c(kpss_lx["kpss_pvalue"], kpss_d12["kpss_pvalue"]),
  `First differences suggested (ndiffs)` = c(nd_lx, nd_d12),
  `Seasonal differences suggested (nsdiffs)` = c(nsd_lx, NA)
) |>
  kable(digits = 3)   # NA (not applicable) cells shown as a dash via knitr.kable.NA




Table 2: Unit root tests on log nights sold, January 2015 to February 2020.

The seasonal strength test suggests 1 seasonal difference for the log series, and the seasonal difference is taken. The first difference is a judgement call, because here the tests and the plots disagree. The KPSS test does not reject stationarity of the seasonally differenced series, and ndiffs suggests 0 further first differences. The KPSS p-values are interpolated from a table that only runs from 0.01 to 0.1, so a reported value of 0.1 should be read as “at least 0.1”. However, Figure 6 still shows a slowly decaying ACF over the first several lags, the classic sign of a wandering level. With only 62 pre-COVID months the tests have little power to detect a unit root. The time plot also shows that the level after COVID settled below its pre-COVID value, which a model with a fixed mean cannot represent. For these reasons one first difference is taken despite the test result. The fitted non-seasonal MA coefficient is checked later for signs of over-differencing; a value near -1 would point to over-differencing.


Code
pre_covid |>
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(log(nights), 12), plot_type = "partial", lag_max = 36)








Figure 6: Seasonally differenced log nights sold (pre-COVID) with its ACF and PACF.







Code
pre_covid |>
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(difference(log(nights), 12)), plot_type = "partial", lag_max = 36)








Figure 7: Seasonally and first differenced log nights sold (pre-COVID) with its ACF and PACF.





After both differences (Figure 7) the series looks stationary. The ACF has a clear negative spike at lag 1 (r1 = -0.39) and the PACF tails off over the first few lags, which points to a non-seasonal MA(1) term. The lag 12 autocorrelation is small (r12 = 0.11) and well inside the 95% bounds in Figure 7, so the ACF on its own does not show a clear seasonal MA signature. The isolated spike at lag 9 (and the borderline one at lag 13) has no seasonal interpretation; with 36 lags shown, one or two exceedances are expected by chance, so these are not modelled. A seasonal MA(1) term is still included, for two reasons. First, a seasonal difference usually induces negative autocorrelation at the seasonal lag, and a seasonal MA(1) is the standard term for it. Second, the short pre-COVID sample makes the lag 12 estimate imprecise. The term is kept only if its fitted coefficient is clearly non-zero, which is checked in Table 5. The hand identified model is therefore
\[
(1 - L)(1 - L^{12}) \log y_t = (1 + \theta_1 L)(1 + \Theta_1 L^{12})\,\varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{WN}(0, \sigma^2),
\]
the SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 or “airline” model. No constant is included because with d + D = 2 a constant would imply a quadratic trend in the forecasts.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
4.1 Modelling approach
The exploratory analysis (time plot, seasonal plots and STL decomposition) showed proportional seasonal swings, so the series is modelled on the log scale. The Guerrero estimate is reported but not followed, for the reasons given above. One seasonal and one first difference of log nights sold make the series approximately stationary, based on the unit root tests, the ACF and the time plot. The lag 1 spike in the ACF of the differenced series, together with the seasonal difference, points to the SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 model, and the model chosen automatically by ARIMA() is included as an alternative candidate. All models are estimated by maximum likelihood with ARIMA() in fable, in the main analysis and in the sensitivity check.
Each model’s residuals are then checked against the white noise standard with Ljung and Box tests, residual plots, the ACF and a histogram. A model that fails goes back to model identification, and only models that pass are used to forecast. A model that passes must still beat the benchmarks on the test set before it earns its place. In this report, models that fail the residual checks are still forecast on the test set, but only as reference points showing why the checks matter. They are not candidates for the final model.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
4.2 The COVID problem
ARIMA models assume that one set of parameters describes the whole series. The COVID window breaks this in two ways. First, the April 2020 collapse produces residuals many times larger than normal, which inflates \(\hat\sigma^2\) and therefore every prediction interval. Second, the estimation tries to explain the shock and the recovery with the same MA and AR terms that describe normal month-to-month behaviour, which pulls the coefficients away from their usual values. Simply deleting the COVID months is not possible, because an ARIMA model needs equally spaced observations.
Two designs are used. Design B is the main analysis; Design A is a sensitivity check that shows what happens if the break is ignored.

Design B, main analysis (COVID as missing): replace March 2020 to March 2022 by NA. ARIMA() in fable can evaluate the likelihood when some observations are missing: the missing months simply contribute nothing to it. The parameters are therefore estimated only from the pre-COVID and post-COVID months, while the monthly time ordering (which the lag structure of the model depends on) is kept intact. The benchmark methods also cope with missing values (for example, seasonal naive uses the last observed value for each month).
Design A, sensitivity check (COVID kept): fit every model to the observed series, including the COVID months.

The letters are kept from the order in which the designs were first set up; throughout the report, B is the design the conclusions rest on.
This is a deliberately simple treatment of the break. A more structural treatment with intervention variables is left for Project 3.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
4.3 Training and test sets


Code
train_A <- nights_sold |> filter(Month < test_start)
train_B <- train_A |>
  mutate(nights = if_else(period == "COVID window", NA_real_, nights))
test    <- nights_sold |> filter(Month >= test_start)

design_levels <- c("A (sensitivity): COVID kept", "B (main): COVID as missing")

train <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble(train_A) |> mutate(design = design_levels[1]),
  as_tibble(train_B) |> mutate(design = design_levels[2])
) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = design)

# Full observed series with the design key, used for accuracy() so that
# both designs are scored against the same actual values and the MASE
# uses the same scaling for both designs.
nights_keyed <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble(nights_sold) |> mutate(design = design_levels[1]),
  as_tibble(nights_sold) |> mutate(design = design_levels[2])
) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = design)


The models are trained on January 2015 to June 2024 (114 months, of which 25 are set to missing in Design B) and tested on July 2024 to June 2026 (24 months). A two year test set covers two full seasonal cycles, so every calendar month is forecast twice, at short and long horizons.

Why these models. The four benchmarks are the standard set from the notes. Seasonal naive is the one that matters most: because the seasonal shape is so stable (Figure 2), simply repeating last year’s value is a hard target, and any ARIMA model has to beat it to justify its extra parameters. The ARMA and non-seasonal ARIMA models are deliberately misspecified reference points rather than serious candidates. The ARMA has no differencing and no seasonal terms, and the ARIMA handles the level but not the seasonality. Including them shows how much each feature of the data (the wandering level, then the seasonality) contributes to forecast accuracy. The real candidates are the two seasonal models: the hand identified airline model from the ACF and PACF, and the automatic ARIMA() choice as a check on the hand identification.
The differencing orders are fixed from the identification step rather than chosen by unit root tests inside ARIMA(), so that both designs use the same differencing and the comparison isolates the effect of the COVID treatment. Point forecasts from the log scale models are back-transformed with the bias adjustment that fable applies by default, so they are forecasts of the mean rather than the median.

The two designs give very different models from the same data. Under Design A the residual variance of the airline model is 0.1073 on the log scale, against 0.0008 under Design B, about 134 times larger. The coefficients move too (Table 5). Under Design A the seasonal MA coefficient is -1.000. A value at or near -1 means the seasonal MA factor \((1 + \Theta_1 L^{12})\) almost cancels the seasonal difference \((1 - L^{12})\): the model is close to non-invertible and is effectively saying that the seasonal pattern is fixed and should not have been differenced. It also sits on the boundary of the parameter space, where the usual standard errors are unreliable. Under Design B the estimate is -0.499 and the non-seasonal MA coefficient is -0.332 (against 0.280 under Design A). The Design B values are inside the invertible region (Figure 8). The non-seasonal MA coefficient agrees in sign with the negative lag 1 autocorrelation found in the identification step and is well away from -1, so there is no sign that the first difference over-differences the series. The seasonal MA coefficient is about 3.4 standard errors from zero, which confirms that the seasonal MA term is needed even though the lag 12 autocorrelation was weak in the identification step.


Code

  filter(design == design_levels[2]) |>
  select(SARIMA_airline) |>
  gg_arma()








Figure 8: Inverse MA roots of the Design B airline model. All roots lie inside the unit circle, so the model is invertible. The twelve roots near the circle come from the seasonal MA term (modulus about 0.94); the single root near 0.33 comes from the non-seasonal MA term.





Under Design B the automatic search chose ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,2)[12] with AICc -293.3, compared with -288.0 for the hand identified model. Whether the extra flexibility is worth it is answered by the test set below, not by the AICc.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
5.2 Residual diagnostics


Code
aug <- augment(fit) |> filter(.model %in% arima_models)

dof_tbl <- tidy(fit) |>
  filter(.model %in% arima_models, term != "constant") |>
  count(design, .model, name = "dof")

lb_tbl <- aug |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(dof_tbl, by = c("design", ".model")) |>
  group_by(design, .model) |>
  summarise(
    dof     = first(dof),
    lb_stat = Box.test(.innov, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = first(dof))$statistic,
    lb_p    = Box.test(.innov, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = first(dof))$p.value,

    .groups = "drop"
