Figure 10: ACF and histogram of the Design B airline model residuals. The ACF is computed with missing values passed through, so the pre-COVID and post-COVID residuals are both used.





Under Design A the residual plot is dominated by a handful of enormous residuals in 2020 (the largest is 8.9 standard deviations from zero), so the normality assumption behind the prediction intervals fails badly, even though the Ljung and Box test (p = 0.912) does not detect autocorrelation. This is a useful reminder that a white noise test only checks the correlation structure: residuals can be uncorrelated and still be far from the identically distributed errors the model assumes. Under Design B the airline residuals look like white noise (p = 0.140), and the histogram is roughly symmetric. Two spikes in the residual ACF (Figure 10), at lags 9 and 18, just cross the 95% bounds. With 36 lags about two exceedances are expected by chance and the Ljung and Box test does not reject, so the model is accepted; but lag 9 also stood out in the identification step, so it is noted as a limitation. The ARMA model without differencing leaves strong autocorrelation in its residuals under Design B (p = 0.000), which is expected: it has no way to represent the seasonal pattern.
Which models pass the residual checks. Under Design B the models that pass the white noise test are: SARIMA (0,1,1)(0,1,1), SARIMA (auto). The models that fail are: ARIMA, ARMA. A model that fails should be re-identified rather than used to forecast. For the ARMA and non-seasonal ARIMA models, re-identifying means recognising from their residual ACF that the seasonal autocorrelation has not been modelled, which leads straight to the seasonal models. The automatically selected SARIMA passes as well, but only just (p = 0.051, right at the 5% cut-off), so it remains a candidate alongside the hand identified model, with weaker support. Under Design A every model technically passes the Ljung and Box test, but the airline model fails the residual checks in a different way: its residuals are far from identically distributed (the COVID residuals are extreme outliers) and its seasonal MA coefficient sits on the invertibility boundary. Re-identifying the orders under Design A would not fix this, because the problem is the data, not the orders. The fix is to change how the break is handled, which is what Design B does.
Candidates for the final model. Only the models that pass the residual checks under Design B are candidates for forecasting. The test set comparison below then checks the last condition: whether these candidates beat the benchmarks.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.1 Key findings

Seasonality is the dominant and most stable feature of the series. The seasonal shape barely changed even through the COVID years, which is why the seasonal naive method is hard to beat. The non-seasonal ARMA and ARIMA models cannot represent the seasonal pattern and fail the residual diagnostics; the ARMA happened to score reasonably on the test set, but not for reasons that would carry over to other periods.
How the break is handled matters more than which ARIMA model is chosen. With the COVID months kept (Design A), the seasonal ARIMA models were worse than the seasonal naive benchmark on the test set and much worse in cross-validation. The cause is a residual variance inflated by about 134 times, a seasonal MA coefficient pushed to the invertibility boundary (-1.000), and point forecasts pushed upwards by the bias adjustment.
With the COVID window treated as missing (Design B), the hand identified airline model was the only model to pass the residual checks and beat the benchmarks: it passed the diagnostics and performed best, with a test RMSE of 101.6 thousand nights (MAPE 4.25%), white noise residuals and slightly conservative prediction intervals (the 80% intervals covered 92% of test months and the 95% intervals all of them). It also had the lowest cross-validated error at every horizon from 1 to 12 months.
A lower AICc did not guarantee better forecasts. The automatically selected seasonal model had a lower AICc than the hand identified model but higher test RMSE, so the simpler model identified from the ACF and PACF was preferred.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.2 Issues and limitations

Choice of COVID window. The window (March 2020 to March 2022) follows the national state of disaster. The data suggest the recovery continued after April 2022, so some post-COVID months still carry the recovery trend into the training data. A sensitivity check with a window ending in December 2022 would test how much this matters.
Treating the shock as missing discards information. Setting 25 months to missing throws away real data, and the approach would not work for a shock at the very end of a series. An intervention model (a level shift or a ramp with a gradual recovery) would use those months instead of ignoring them; this is the starting point for Project 3.
Transformation. The log was used for interpretability; a Box–Cox transformation with the Guerrero \(\hat\lambda\) could be compared as a check.
Level shift after COVID. Demand has recovered to slightly below its pre-COVID level. The differenced models adapt to this because they forecast from the most recent level, but the mean benchmark does not. Under Design A it only did reasonably well because the COVID months drag the long-run average down close to the recovered level; under Design B, without those months, its average sits well above the test data and it is among the worst methods.
Residual autocorrelation at lag 9. The airline residuals pass the Ljung and Box test, but lag 9 crosses the bounds both before fitting and in the residuals. It has no obvious calendar explanation and adding a lag 9 term would be hard to justify, so it is left unmodelled.
MASE scaling. The MASE denominator uses an in-sample period that contains the COVID collapse, so the MASE values are deflated. RMSE and MAPE were used as the main measures.
Bias adjustment. Back-transforming with the mean (bias adjusted) forecast is the right choice when the forecasts are added up, for example into annual totals, but it makes the forecasts very sensitive to an inflated \(\hat\sigma^2\). This was a large part of the failure of Design A and is easy to miss.
Short post-COVID history. Only about two years of post-COVID data are in the training set, and the test set is two years long, so the conclusions rest on a fairly short stretch of “normal” data.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.3 What I would do differently
I would model the COVID shock directly with intervention variables in a regression with ARIMA errors, so that the 25 months are used rather than discarded. Project 3 takes up this idea on the same series and the same test set, which allows a direct comparison with the SARIMA results from this project. I would also compare a sliding window with the expanding window in the cross-validation, since a sliding window is the natural choice when structural breaks are plausible.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.4 Project reflections and development
When I first started thinking about the best way to approach this problem I was very intrigued by the idea of using financial data. I immediately found some data online and had AI do a mini analysis of the data with SARIMA, ARIMA and the other models present in this project. I quickly found that the analysis would not yield the kind of results I wanted because of the volatility and variation within financial stock data. I therefore pivoted and went back and forth on a couple of different econometric datasets. I had the idea to use the Airbnb dataset that I had worked with earlier in the year during a data analytics course but unfortunately the data was not able to be processed in a time series way. Therefore, using the assistance of AI I was able to track down and pull data from the Stats SA website about tourist accommodation, a dataset that would fit and perform much more consistently with AR, MA, ARIMA and SARIMA models.
Upon looking at the EDA this data showed a clear seasonal pattern with a unique drop in 2020 due to the COVID pandemic as well as clear signs of non-stationarity. This also changed the way I wanted to approach the project because I first wanted to start with fitting an AR and an MA model and then build up to ARMA and then ARIMA and SARIMA. This idea quickly disappeared when the EDA showed clear signs of non-stationarity and variability. I therefore decided to shift the focus of my project onto ARIMA and SARIMA modelling and the process of differencing.
I found that this data was quite similar to a seasonally adjusted electrical equipment dataset that was covered in one of the coding lectures. This is due to the fact that both datasets had a level of non-stationarity and the variability mostly occurred due to a shock at a specific time. For this dataset it was COVID and for the other dataset it was the 2008/2009 crash. In that example the crash caused a sharp drop and a slow recovery that a single ARIMA model struggled to describe, which is exactly the problem COVID created here, so seeing it in the lecture first helped me recognise the issue in my own data.
The biggest thing I learned from this project is how much a single structural break can damage a model that otherwise looks reasonable. When I kept the COVID months in, the airline model still passed the Ljung–Box test, and at first I took that as a sign the model was fine. Only when I looked at the residual plot and the forecasts did I see that a handful of residuals from 2020 had inflated the variance by more than 100 times, pushed the seasonal MA coefficient to -1 and made the forecasts and intervals useless. This taught me that a white noise test only checks whether the residuals are correlated, not whether they are well behaved, so checking a model has to include actually looking at the residuals and not just reading off a p-value.
The part I found most difficult was making decisions when the evidence disagreed. The unit root tests said no first difference was needed while the ACF and the time plot suggested one was, the Guerrero estimate pointed to a different transformation from the log I had chosen, and the automatic model had a better AICc than my hand-identified model but forecast worse on the test set. Earlier in the course I would have just followed whichever test or criterion the software gave me. Working through these cases made me understand that modelling is a set of judgement calls, and that the important thing is to explain why I made each choice and then check it afterwards, for example by confirming that the fitted MA coefficient was not close to -1 and that the seasonal MA term was clearly significant.
I also reworked the project part way through so that the report follows the order in which the modelling decisions are actually made, with the COVID months treated as missing as the main analysis and keeping them only as a sensitivity check. This made the report much easier to follow, because every decision now has a clear place, and it made me see modelling as a loop rather than a straight line: a model that fails the residual check sends you back to identification instead of straight to forecasting.
I used AI throughout this project to help me find the data, debug my code and review my write-up, and these uses are recorded in my AI use log. The review in particular picked up places where my text did not match my own output, such as describing an autocorrelation as negative when it was positive. Going back through each of these against my tables and plots was a useful lesson in checking that every claim in a report is actually supported by the results.
Going forward, the main thing I want to explore is handling the COVID shock directly instead of setting those months to missing, since treating them as missing throws away two years of real data. That is the starting point for Project 3, where I model the shock with intervention variables on the same series and test set so the results can be compared directly with this project.

title: Week 09
text:
Session or topic covered: State Space Models
This week we covered state space models and how they can be used to represent time series data. The main idea is that an observed time series can be broken down into an underlying signal and random noise. The signal is represented by a set of state variables that describe the state of the system at time \(t\). These state variables are often not directly observable, so we only see noisy measurements of the underlying process. Examples include an underlying population level in medicine or ecology, the true demand level in economics, or the level and trend of a time series.
A state space model has two main equations. The observation equation describes how the observed data are generated from the underlying state, and the state equation describes how the state evolves over time. In the general linear form these are
\[
Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t, \qquad \theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t.
\]
Here \(\theta_t\) is the state vector, \(F\) determines how the state variables contribute to the observation, and \(G\) describes how the previous state contributes to the current state. The terms \(v_t\) and \(w_t\) are the observation and state errors, with covariance matrices \(V\) and \(W\), and in linear Gaussian state space models both are assumed to be normally distributed. The state follows a Markov structure, meaning the current state depends on the previous state rather than directly on the entire history of the process.
One of the main things I had to work through this week was the distinction between the state and the observation. At first I thought of the state simply as the true value of the quantity we want to estimate. I now understand that it is more precisely a description of the state of the system at a particular time. It can contain several components, such as the level, slope and seasonal effect, rather than just one underlying value. The state is not necessarily known exactly, and the model uses the observed data to make inferences about it.
I also spent time understanding how the transition matrix \(G\) works. I had been thinking of \(G\) as some kind of estimate of the previous state, but it actually describes how each component of the previous state vector feeds into the current state vector. This became clearer when I worked through the state space form of an AR(2) model. The original model is
\[
y_t = \alpha + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + e_t.
\]
By defining the state vector and transition matrix as
\[
\theta_t = \begin{pmatrix} y_t \\ y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
G = \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & \phi_2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
we can write the model in state space form. The first row of \(G\) reproduces the AR(2) relationship, because it combines \(y_{t-1}\) and \(y_{t-2}\) with weights \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) to give the new \(y_t\). The second row just carries the previous observation forward, so \(y_{t-1}\) moves into the second slot of the new state vector, ready to be used as the lag-2 value at the next step. Working through this showed me that writing a model in state space form is really about choosing a sensible state vector and then building the matrices so that they reproduce the original model.
We also looked at how other familiar models can be put into state space form. For the ARMA(1,1) model, the state vector includes both the deviation of the series from its mean and a term involving the random error, which allows the autoregressive and moving average parts to sit inside the state equation. An important thing I took from the AR(2) and ARMA(1,1) examples is that the state vector does not have to contain only unobserved quantities. In both representations, observed values or quantities built from the errors are included in the state vector too.
Another important part of the week was structural time series models: the local level model, the local linear trend model and the basic structural model. The local level model represents the series as an underlying level plus observation noise, with the level evolving as a random walk. The local linear trend model adds a trend component, so both the level and its rate of change can evolve over time. The basic structural model adds seasonality as well, breaking the observed series into level, trend, seasonal and irregular components. Seeing them in this order helped me, because each model just adds one more component to the state.
The basic structural model was particularly useful for understanding how to build a state vector out of different components of a series. For quarterly data, the state vector contains the current level, the trend, the current seasonal effect and two lagged seasonal effects. The transition matrix carries the level and trend forward and updates the seasonal components. Because the seasonal effects are constrained to sum to zero over a full year, the current seasonal effect can be written in terms of the previous three. If the four quarterly effects must add up to zero, then once I know three of them the fourth is fixed, which is why only two lagged seasonal effects need to be stored alongside the current one. Working through the matrix helped me see how the structure of the model decides the entries of the transition matrix.
A key skill from this week was learning how to work out \(F\) and \(G\) from a given model. \(F\) comes from the observation equation, by identifying which state variables contribute to the observed value and with what coefficients. \(G\) comes from the state equation, by writing each component of the current state vector in terms of the components of the previous state vector, so each row of \(G\) holds the coefficients from the equation for the corresponding state variable. Once I saw it this way, the matrices stopped looking like fixed formulas I had to memorise and started looking like something I could build from the structure of the model.
Overall, this week helped me understand state space models as a general framework for representing a time series as an evolving underlying process plus the observations we see of it. The most challenging part was moving from the general equations to the specific matrix representations, particularly understanding where each row of the transition matrix comes from. Working through the AR(2), ARMA(1,1) and basic structural model examples showed me that the matrices are built from the relationships between the components of the state vector. I now have a clearer understanding of what the state and observation equations are for and how familiar time series models fit into the state space framework. I want to keep practising building state vectors and transition matrices so that I can derive these representations confidently on my own.

title: Week 07
text:
Session or topic covered: Exponential Smoothing
This week I worked through exponential smoothing and focused on understanding how the different models build on each other. I found this topic quite challenging at first because there were a lot of equations, and I struggled to see how the equations progressed from one model to the next. I understood the general idea of giving more weight to recent observations, but I needed to spend more time making the equations intuitive for myself. This is why I added quite a few of my own explanations to my notes, as rewriting the ideas in simpler language helped me understand what the equations were actually doing.
I started with simple exponential smoothing (SES), where we only estimate the level of the series. It helped me to think of the level as our current idea of where the series is, with \(\alpha\) controlling how much we allow the newest observation to change that estimate. A large \(\alpha\) means the level reacts quickly to each new observation, while a small \(\alpha\) means it only moves a little each time. I then saw how Holt’s method extends this by adding a trend, so we are now estimating both where the series is and how it is changing, with \(\beta\) controlling how quickly the trend estimate is updated. The progression made much more sense to me once I thought of it as SES = level, Holt = level + trend, and Holt-Winters = level + trend + seasonality. Each new model adds one more component to the same basic idea. I still found the actual equations difficult, especially keeping track of what each term represented, but I understand the intuition behind them much better now.
The Air Passengers example was particularly useful because it made me think more critically about whether a model can give good predictions while still not being the most appropriate model for the data. Looking at the plot of Holt’s one-step-ahead predictions against the observed passenger numbers, I thought the predictions worked reasonably well because the fitted values followed the observations quite closely. However, I realised that Holt’s method was not really capturing the full structure of the data, because the series has such a clear seasonal pattern and Holt’s method has no seasonal component. The estimated \(\alpha\) was very large, around \(0.9999\), while \(\beta\) was extremely small, around \(0.0001\). Intuitively this makes sense. Because the model cannot represent the seasonality, the level has to react almost completely to every new observation to keep up with the large seasonal swings, while the underlying trend changes much more slowly. So the close fit was really coming from the level chasing the data, not from the model understanding the pattern, which is exactly the gap that Holt-Winters fills by adding a seasonal component.
I also worked through the damped trend, which I found easier to understand intuitively. Rather than allowing the trend to continue at exactly the same rate forever, we gradually reduce its effect as we forecast further into the future. This seemed like a logical extension of Holt’s method, and it helped me understand why there are different versions of the model rather than just one exponential smoothing equation.
One thing I realised I was confused about this week was the difference between the level, the fitted values and the forecasts. I now understand the level as my current smoothed estimate of where the series is. The fitted value is the prediction I made for an observation that has already happened, using only the information I had before seeing it, so it is a one-step-ahead prediction. The forecast is different because it predicts observations I have not seen yet. Thinking about it this way made it much easier for me to read the graphs: the level is my estimate of where I currently am, the fitted values show how well my model predicted the data I already have, and the forecasts are what I use to look into the future.
Overall, my biggest takeaway from this week was understanding the progression of exponential smoothing models rather than memorising the individual equations. I still need to practise the equations themselves and become more comfortable explaining what each part does without having to translate it into my own words first. However, adding my own intuitive explanations helped me move from seeing a collection of complicated equations to understanding why each new model adds another component.

title: Week 05
text:
Session or topic covered: MA, AR, ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA Models
This was the week we got stuck into the linear models: MA, AR, ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA. Once I got comfortable with the notation, I found the models themselves quite easy to understand, because each one builds on the one before it. What I found hard was the maths behind them and keeping track of what each symbol meant. To get past that, I spent a lot of time Googling each model and looking for intuitive explanations of what the equations were actually saying, rather than just memorising them.
The first thing I had to sort out was the difference between an MA model and an AR model, because at first they looked almost the same to me. An MA model is driven by past shocks (errors), not past observations. In an MA(\(q\)) model, today’s value is a weighted sum of the current shock and the previous \(q\) shocks, and \(\theta\) gives the weight on each one. An AR model is driven by past observations: today’s value depends directly on the previous values of the series itself, with \(\phi\) as the weight. The way I think about it now is that an AR model remembers where the series was, while an MA model remembers the recent surprises. Once I had that, a lot of the notation stopped looking intimidating, because I could tell straight away whether a term was a past value or a past shock. I also realised I had been mixing up the plots for the two models. For both, a negative coefficient makes the series flip back and forth between positive and negative, while a positive coefficient makes it smoother. But in an AR model, a larger \(\phi\) means each value is pulled more strongly towards the previous value, whereas in an MA model \(\theta\) only controls how much yesterday’s shock carries into today.
The slide I found hardest this week was the properties of the MA(1) model, so I worked through the derivations myself. The model is
\[
y_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1},
\]
where the shocks \(\varepsilon_t\) are white noise with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\). The mean is \(E(y_t) = \mu + E(\varepsilon_t) + \theta E(\varepsilon_{t-1}) = \mu\), because the shocks have an expected value of zero. The variance is
\[
\text{Var}(y_t) = \text{Var}(\varepsilon_t) + \theta^2\,\text{Var}(\varepsilon_{t-1}) = (1 + \theta^2)\sigma^2,
\]
with no covariance term because the shocks are uncorrelated with each other. For the covariance at lag 1, \(\text{Cov}(y_t, y_{t-1}) = \text{Cov}(\varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1},\ \varepsilon_{t-1} + \theta\varepsilon_{t-2})\), and the only shock that appears in both is \(\varepsilon_{t-1}\), so the covariance is \(\theta\sigma^2\). Dividing the covariance by the variance gives
\[
\rho(1) = \frac{\theta}{1 + \theta^2}.
\]
At lag 2 or more, \(y_t\) and \(y_{t-2}\) share no shocks at all, so the covariance is zero and \(\rho(h) = 0\) for \(h > 1\). This made the idea of short memory much clearer to me. The autocorrelation cuts off after lag 1 because observations two periods apart have no shocks in common, not because of some rule I had to memorise.
To check I understood it, I worked through the example \(y_t = 5 + \varepsilon_t + 0.6\varepsilon_{t-1}\) with \(\sigma^2 = 9\). The mean is 5, the variance is \((1 + 0.36) \times 9 = 12.24\), the covariance at lag 1 is \(0.6 \times 9 = 5.4\), and so \(\rho(1) = 5.4 / 12.24 \approx 0.44\). At first I pictured this as a curve, but the correct way to picture it is a scatter plot of each observation against the one before it. That plot shows a weak positive straight-line relationship with a correlation of about 0.44. If you plot each observation against the one two periods before, there is no relationship at all. Working through this also made me realise I had been confusing the lag with the forecast horizon, because both use the letter \(h\). In the autocorrelation function, \(h\) is the lag, meaning how far apart two observations are. It is not how many steps ahead we are forecasting.
Another thing I had to correct was where the rule that the coefficient must be less than one applies. For an AR(1) model, \(|\phi| < 1\) is what keeps the series stationary. If \(\phi = 1\) it becomes a random walk, and if \(|\phi| > 1\) it explodes. An MA model is always stationary, whatever the coefficients are, because it is just a finite weighted sum of white noise. But MA models have their own condition, called invertibility, and for an MA(1) it also means \(|\theta| < 1\). I didn’t understand why this mattered until I saw that two different values of \(\theta\) can give exactly the same autocorrelation. For example, \(\theta = 0.5\) gives \(\rho(1) = 0.5 / 1.25 = 0.4\), and \(\theta = 2\) gives \(\rho(1) = 2 / 5 = 0.4\). From the data alone we couldn’t tell which model is true, so we always choose the value inside the unit circle. This also keeps the estimation stable, because the model is estimated by maximum likelihood and the unobserved past shocks have to be rebuilt step by step.
The partial autocorrelation function confused me at first. What helped was thinking of it as removing the intermediate links between observations so that only the direct link is left. In an AR(1) model, \(y_t\) is correlated with \(y_{t-2}\), but only because both are linked through \(y_{t-1}\). Once the effect of \(y_{t-1}\) is removed, there is no direct link left, so the PACF cuts off after lag 1. For an MA(1) it is the other way round: the ACF cuts off after lag 1 and the PACF dies away gradually. This gave me a practical way to choose between models. For an AR(\(p\)) the ACF decays gradually and the PACF cuts off after lag \(p\), for an MA(\(q\)) the ACF cuts off after lag \(q\) and the PACF decays gradually, and for an ARMA both decay gradually. Any spike outside the 95% confidence bands is treated as significant. I also learned that this is a guide rather than a strict rule, because sample ACFs are noisy, so the final choice also depends on information criteria and on checking the residuals.
ARMA models made sense once I understood AR and MA separately. They simply allow both past observations and past shocks to affect today’s value. That suits something like electricity demand, which carries on from day to day but also gets hit by shocks, like a cold snap, that fade after a few days. My approach is to start with the simplest model, see whether an MA part is needed, and only then consider differencing.
For non-stationarity, I initially wasn’t sure what the I in ARIMA stood for. It stands for integrated, and it refers to the differencing step we use when a series has no constant mean or variance over a long period. Differencing was one of the things I found most confusing this week, because I wasn’t sure what it was actually for or when I was supposed to do it. At first I thought you just differenced any series that had a trend, and I kept mixing it up with lagging. I now understand that lagging just moves a value to a different time period, while differencing, \(y_t - y_{t-1}\), subtracts the previous value from the current one, so instead of modelling the level of the series, we model how much it changes from one period to the next.
The purpose of differencing is to make a non-stationary series stationary, so that the AR and MA ideas can actually be applied to it. A random walk made this clear to me. Each value is the previous value plus a new random shock, so the series wanders off and never returns to a fixed level. If you difference it, \(y_t - y_{t-1} = \varepsilon_t\), which is just white noise, because the only thing that changes from one period to the next is the new shock. Differencing also removes a straight-line trend. If \(y_t = 5 + 0.4t + \varepsilon_t\), then
\[
y_t - y_{t-1} = 0.4 + \varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1},
\]
so the trend disappears and we’re left with a constant plus noise.
The part I found hardest was knowing when to difference. The signs I now look for are a plot where the series wanders and does not keep returning to a constant level, an ACF that decays very slowly instead of dropping off quickly, and the unit root tests. The ADF test assumes the series has a unit root unless the data shows otherwise, and the KPSS test assumes the series is stationary unless the data shows otherwise, so if ADF fails to reject and KPSS rejects, both are pointing towards differencing. I also learned that differencing is the right fix for a stochastic trend, where the trend comes from random shocks building up over time. It is not always the right fix for a deterministic trend, which follows a fixed line. In that case it is better to fit the trend and subtract it, because differencing a fixed trend leaves \(\varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}\), which introduces a pattern into the errors that wasn’t there before. For seasonality that doesn’t fade, we use a seasonal difference instead, \(y_t - y_{t-m}\), which compares each value to the same season one cycle earlier. With monthly data, that means comparing each month to the same month a year before. If a series has both a trend and seasonality, it may need both kinds of difference.
I also had a question about whether to difference once or twice. The rule I now follow is to difference once, check whether the series looks stationary, and only difference again if it still doesn’t. Almost no series needs more than two differences. The value of \(d\) should be chosen from the plots and unit root tests before fitting, not by comparing AIC values, because differencing once fits the model to \(n - 1\) values and differencing twice fits it to \(n - 2\), so their likelihoods can’t be compared. Differencing too much causes its own problems. If the variance goes up after differencing instead of down, or the lag-1 autocorrelation comes out at about \(-0.5\), that’s a sign I have gone one step too far. The aim is to difference just enough to make the series stationary, and no more.
This also helped me with the transformation confusion I had in Week 4, where I had been mixing up transforming the data to make it normal with transforming it to stabilise the variance. The correct order when preparing a series for ARIMA is to first transform the series (for example with a log or Box-Cox transform) if its variance grows with its level, then difference it if there is a stochastic trend or fit and subtract the trend if it is deterministic, and then use seasonal differencing if there is seasonality that doesn’t fade. Transforming first matters because a stable variance often means less differencing is needed.
The ARIMA(1,1,1) equation confused me when it was written out on the original scale, because the coefficient on \(y_{t-1}\) became \(1 + \phi\) and an extra \(-\phi y_{t-2}\) term appeared. That made it look like there was strong dependence at lag 2. I now understand that these terms only come from rewriting a differenced model in terms of the original values. The most helpful thing was thinking about what each part contributes to a forecast. Take \(c = 1\), \(\phi = 0.6\) and \(\theta = 0.3\), where the last two observations were 120 and 115 and the last error was 2. Then the forecast is
\[
\hat{y} = 1 + 1.6(120) - 0.6(115) + 0.3(2) = 124.6.
\]
Intuitively, this is the last value of 120, plus a constant of 1, plus momentum of 3 (60% of the previous increase of 5), plus 0.6 from feeding back the previous forecast error. Thinking of the forecast as past level, plus past change, plus past error made the equation much easier for me to understand.
The modelling workflow tied everything together. We plot the data, make the series stationary, identify candidate models from the ACF and PACF, estimate them by maximum likelihood, check the residuals, and only forecast if the residuals pass. Otherwise, we go back and try a different model. The way I understand the loop back is that if the residuals still have structure in them, there is information in the data that the model hasn’t captured, and the residuals should look like white noise. The Ljung-Box test checks many lags together instead of one at a time, so it’s less likely to raise a false alarm by chance. A large p-value is what we want, but it isn’t proof that the model is correct. I also learned to use a QQ plot to check whether the residuals are normal, because that affects whether the prediction intervals can be trusted. I realised that cross-validation from Week 3 fits naturally into this process too, as a way of comparing the candidate models on data they haven’t seen.
Finally, I had wondered whether ARIMA is only for trends, and whether the models follow a strict order from AR to MA to ARMA to ARIMA to SARIMA. I now see them as building blocks. ARIMA handles dependence and trend, and SARIMA adds a seasonal part on top of that. It is written as \((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_m\), where the second bracket uses the same ideas but at the seasonal lag \(m\). With monthly data, the seasonal difference is \(y_t - y_{t-12}\), which compares each month to the same month a year earlier. The airline model, SARIMA\((0,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}\), was a good example for me of how a model with no AR terms at all can still work very well on monthly data. In practice, the best approach is to fit a few candidate models and compare which one captures the data best.

title: Week 03
text:
Session or topic covered: Residuals, Train and Test Samples and Validation
I actually really enjoyed the start of this weeks material. I found the concepts generally quite standard for a statistical anlysis and I could start visualizing a bit more clearly how a project or genuine analysis could shape.
My first issues started to appear when I initially didn’t really understand the difference between residuals and forecast errors because both are essentially measuring how wrong the model is. I now understand that the key difference is what data we are measuring the error on. Residuals are the errors on data the model has already seen and used to fit itself, so they are useful for checking the model’s fit and diagnosing problems. Forecast errors are the errors on new data that the model has never seen, so they tell us how well the model actually predicts. This also helped me understand why small residuals don’t necessarily mean the model will forecast well.
One thing I found particularly interesting was the idea of temporal ordering in forecasting. I initially thought that when splitting data into training and validation sets, we could simply choose observations randomly, like we often do in other statistical or machine learning problems. However, with time series, this would allow information from the future to influence the model, which would not reflect how forecasting actually works. The rule that every training observation must come before every validation observation makes intuitive sense because, when we are forecasting the future, we can only use information that was available at that point in time. This also helped me understand temporal leakage as a model that can appear extremely accurate if it accidentally uses future information, but that accuracy is misleading because we would not have access to that information when making a real forecast.
I initially found rolling-origin evaluation quite confusing, but it helped once I thought of it as repeatedly pretending to be at different points in the past. Instead of having one fixed train/test split, we move the forecasting point forward through time, each time using only the data that would have been available at that point to predict what comes next. For example, we could use January–June to predict July, then January–July to predict August, and so on. I used an LLM to visually understand how the validation metjods could work and this immediatley helped to understand it in a bit of a different and intuitive way. We then look at all the forecast errors together. I like the intuition that we are essentially asking, if I had been making forecasts at different points in time, how well would my model have performed? This gives us a more reliable picture of forecasting accuracy than relying on just one train/test split.
Links: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1 · Project 1: ARIMA and SARIMA · Project 3: Regression and Exponential Smoothing

title: Week 01
text:
Session or topic covered: Introduction to Time Series
Coming into the first lesson of the semester, I had a very basic understanding of what time series was. In the first lecture we covered the foundational definitions, such as the ordering of observations, the types of time series we can get, the spacing between observations, and how dependence can be made visible. The most challenging concept for me this week was definitely temporal regularity and the aggregation effect. At first I didn’t understand the idea of aggregation smoothing out high-frequency structure, or how changing the level of aggregation reveals different structure in the series. The wording was quite complicated and confusing, so I did some research until I understood exactly what it meant. When I feel confused about a topic, I usually ask AI to explain the concept not just mathematically or statistically but intuitively, so that I can understand the idea in a simple way and then build it up into a deeper understanding.
I now understand that granularity is about the resolution we look at the data in. As the granularity changes, different patterns become visible, and focusing on a finer level of detail lets us see patterns that are hidden at a coarser level. For example, hourly temperature data shows the fluctuations throughout the day, while daily data only shows the average temperature for each day. The temperature itself doesn’t behave any differently; we are just seeing a different level of detail. That is what the idea that nothing changes about the underlying process, only what we see changes, means to me now.
During class we discussed the difference between prediction and forecasting, which I initially found confusing. After doing some research, I now understand forecasting as a specific type of prediction. Both involve using available information to estimate an unknown quantity, but forecasting specifically focuses on estimating a future value, often by using historical time series data and assuming that patterns observed in the past may continue into the future. Prediction is a broader concept and does not necessarily involve time or historical data.
From the introduction to time series, I think one of the most important conversations we had in class was around goals and planning. The loop from forecasting to goal, to plan, to implementation, to outcome is important for understanding the life cycle of a forecast. It helped me understand how to go about setting a goal and planning how to organise and manage the data, which I think will be very helpful when dealing with major projects.

section: What I learned about using AI
text:
What I learned about using AI
The most useful thing AI did for me was not writing code but helping me find out why something was wrong. The clearest case was Project 2, where my GARCH code agreed with rugarch on the real data, so I believed it was correct. It was only the simulation, where I knew the true answer, that showed the problem, and AI helped me trace it to the optimiser. That taught me that agreement with a package, or a confident explanation from an AI, is not proof. Every method I coded myself is now checked against something independent: a package, a known likelihood or a simulation.
I also learned that AI is only as good as what I ask it. When I asked for general help, the suggestions were generic. When I gave it my own output and asked whether my write-up matched it, it found real errors, but I still had to go back to the tables myself to confirm each one. Finally, I found AI most valuable for intuition when I was stuck on a concept, but the understanding only really came when I worked through the maths or the code myself, which is what the journal records.

title: Week 02
text:
Session or topic covered: Stationarity and Random Walks
Generally I found this week’s work quite intuitive. The weeks are moving fairly slowly, with small amounts of theory covered at a time. When I revised this week’s content, I found the concept of growing uncertainty confusing because I assumed that as we forecast further into the future, the uncertainty would simply continue increasing in the same way for all time series models. I initially struggled to understand why the prediction intervals for a random walk continue to widen indefinitely, while those of a stationary AR(1) model eventually level off.
I now understand that the difference comes from how each process responds to shocks. In a random walk, \(y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\), every shock stays in the series permanently, so the value \(h\) steps ahead is today’s value plus the sum of \(h\) new shocks. Each shock has variance \(\sigma^2\) and they are uncorrelated, so the forecast error variance is
\[
\text{Var}(y_{t+h} - \hat{y}_{t+h}) = h\sigma^2,
\]
which keeps growing in a straight line with no limit. In a stationary AR(1) process, \(y_t = \phi y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\) with \(|\phi| < 1\), the effect of a shock is multiplied by \(\phi\) every period, so old shocks gradually die out and the process returns towards its long-run mean. The forecast error variance is
\[
\text{Var}(y_{t+h} - \hat{y}_{t+h}) = \sigma^2\,\frac{1 - \phi^{2h}}{1 - \phi^2},
\]
and because \(\phi^{2h} \to 0\) as \(h\) grows, this settles at \(\sigma^2 / (1 - \phi^2)\), which is just the variance of the process itself. Putting numbers in made this concrete for me. With \(\sigma^2 = 1\) and \(\phi = 0.8\), the AR(1) forecast variance is 1 at one step ahead and can never go above \(1 / 0.36 \approx 2.78\), so far into the future the best I can do is forecast the mean with the process’s normal spread around it. A random walk with the same \(\sigma^2\) already has a variance of 10 at ten steps ahead, and 100 at a hundred steps.
So although uncertainty initially increases as the forecasting horizon grows, for a stationary process it reaches a finite limit. This helped me understand that forecasting further into the future does not always mean uncertainty grows without bound; it depends on whether the underlying process is stationary or non-stationary. It also made me see why a random walk is such a hard series to forecast far ahead, because its shocks never fade.

title: Week 04
text:
Session or topic covered: Operators, Stationarity and White Noise
This week covered operators, stationarity and white noise, and at first it felt like the most abstract week so far. When I first saw the lag operator I didn’t see the point of it, because writing \(Ly_t = y_{t-1}\) seemed like a complicated way of saying the previous value. It made more sense once I thought of an operator as a shortcut for moving around a time series. \(L\) takes you back one period and the lead operator \(F\) takes you forward one. Many real series, like GDP, inflation and exchange rates, depend on their own recent past, and operators give a clean way to describe that without writing out the value two periods ago every time.
The direction of the shift confused me. Take the series 3, 7, 4, 8, 5 observed at times 1 to 5. Applying \(L\) gives NA, 3, 7, 4, 8. At time 2 the lagged value is 3, which was observed at time 1, and at time 1 there is nothing earlier, so there is a gap. I expected a lag to move things backwards, but the subscript records where the value came from, not where it is displayed, so the series shifts to the right. The lead operator does the opposite and gives 7, 4, 8, 5, NA. I also had to be careful not to read \(L^2 y_t\) as \((y_{t-1})^2\). It means applying the lag twice, so \(L^2 y_t = y_{t-2}\). Lagging is also different from differencing: lagging only moves a value to a new time label, while \((1 - L)y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}\) creates a new series of changes.
For stationarity, what helped me was realising that the values can move around while the rules generating them stay the same. The mean and variance are constant, and the covariance between two observations depends only on how far apart they are, not on when they occur. This made it clear why a series with a trend or seasonality is not stationary, since in both cases the mean depends on when you look. I didn’t see the point of ergodicity at first, but it clicked when I realised we only ever observe one realisation of a process. Ergodicity means that averaging over time along that one long series gives the same answer as averaging across all the series the process could have produced.
Transformations were the most confusing part for me. I thought the reason for transforming a series was to make it normal, but I had mixed two ideas together. A log or Box-Cox transform is mainly there to stabilise the variance when the spread grows with the level, because it shrinks large values more than small ones. Normality is a separate question. Once I separated these, I could match each problem to its fix: a transformation for growing variance, removing a fitted trend when the trend is deterministic, differencing when it is stochastic, seasonal differencing for seasonality that doesn’t fade, and splitting the sample at a structural break. Transforming before differencing also makes sense, since stabilising the variance first often means less differencing is needed.
I didn’t understand why white noise got so much attention until I saw that it is what we want our residuals to look like. If the residuals still show a pattern, the model has missed something, and if they look like white noise, it has captured the linear structure. Weak white noise only requires the observations to be uncorrelated, while strict white noise requires them to be independent and identically distributed. The key for me was that uncorrelated does not mean independent, because correlation only measures linear relationships. For example, if \(x\) is equally likely to be \(-1\), \(0\) or \(1\) and \(y = x^2\), then \(y\) is completely determined by \(x\), yet their correlation is zero, because \(y\) rises whether \(x\) is negative or positive, so there is no straight-line pattern.
Finally, we saw how dependence can be built from white noise using \[
y_t = \tfrac{1}{3}(\varepsilon_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}).
\] Each value is a weighted combination of three nearby shocks. The shocks are unrelated, but \(y_t\) and \(y_{t+1}\) share \(\varepsilon_t\) and \(\varepsilon_{t+1}\), so they are correlated and the result is no longer white noise. This is called filtering. I also saw why this filter is useful for smoothing but not for forecasting, because it uses \(\varepsilon_{t+1}\), a future shock we would never have when making a forecast. A forecasting model can only combine current and past shocks.

title: Week 06
text:
Session or topic covered: Practical Coding: Fitting AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA Models in R
I found Week 6 particularly valuable because it gave us the opportunity to focus on practical coding and apply the concepts we had covered in lectures. Having dedicated time to work through examples in R helped me connect the theoretical material to the actual process of conducting a time series analysis. Implementing the methods myself made the material more intuitive, because I could see how the different stages of an analysis fit together, rather than focusing only on understanding the theory. This was especially useful in preparing for the projects, as it gave me the chance to practise the techniques and become more comfortable with the coding process before applying them to my own data.
It was particularly helpful to work through examples of autoregressive (AR), moving average (MA) and autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models, as well as ARIMA and seasonal ARIMA models. Working with these models in code helped me understand how each approach accounts for a different kind of pattern in time series data. Implementing AR models let me explore how previous observations can help explain current values, while MA models brought in the role of past errors. ARMA models brought these two ideas together, and ARIMA models extended them by adding differencing to deal with non-stationarity.
The biggest thing I learned this week was that model identification is a process rather than a single step. In the practical examples, we examined the data and its ACF and PACF plots, considered which model structures were plausible, compared the candidate models using information criteria such as AICc, and then checked the residuals to see whether the fitted model had actually captured the time-dependent patterns. Working through these steps showed me that time series modelling is not simply about selecting and fitting a model. It involves a sequence of decisions, and each one needs to be justified.
The practical work also made the coding process feel much more manageable. Working through an example step by step meant I could focus on understanding what each function was doing and how its output related to the model, rather than feeling overwhelmed by the whole analysis at once. This helped me develop a more systematic way of working through problems, particularly when interpreting outputs or trying to understand why a particular modelling step was necessary. It reinforced for me that being able to explain the reasoning behind the code matters more than just getting it to run.
Overall, Week 6 helped me consolidate my understanding of the material while building the practical skills I need for the projects. I feel more prepared to approach my project work because I have practised the modelling process and become more familiar with implementing time series methods in R. My main takeaway is that practical experience is essential for building confidence in time series analysis, particularly when applying theoretical concepts to real data. Going forward, I want to keep building my coding skills while making sure I understand and can justify the modelling decisions I make, so that my projects show not only that the methods are implemented correctly but also that I understand why they are appropriate.

title: Week 08
text:
Session or topic covered: Regression: GAMMs, GARMA and VAR Models
Overall, I found the regression week manageable when working through examples, because they helped me connect the theoretical concepts to how they are actually implemented. The more advanced models towards the end of the week were much harder for me. My difficulty was not the mathematical notation itself, but building an intuition for how the models work, when they would be appropriate, and what problem each one was designed to solve. I realised that I could follow the steps in an example without really understanding why the model was set up that way. To deal with this, I spent extra time breaking down the model equations, looking for intuitive explanations, using visual representations, and relating each of the more complex models back to methods I already understood.
Generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) were particularly challenging because I couldn’t see how the different components of the model work together. I wanted to understand how the model uses smooth functions to capture non-linear relationships while also accounting for random effects, and why both are needed in the same model. To work through this, I broke the model down into its pieces and made sure I understood the purpose of each one before thinking about how they combine. What I now understand is that each part fixes a different shortcoming of ordinary linear regression. The smooth functions mean the relationship between a variable and the response doesn’t have to be a straight line, so the data decides the shape of the curve. The random effects are there because observations from the same group or individual are related to each other, so treating them as independent would overstate how much information we have. A GAMM is therefore the right choice over a standard linear regression when the relationship is not linear and the observations come in groups or repeated measures, and it can handle both of those at the same time.
With generalised autoregressive moving average (GARMA) models, my main difficulty was understanding how the regression part interacts with the autoregressive and moving average structure. I was familiar with regression and with modelling dependence over time separately, but I struggled to see how they combine in one model. I focused on breaking down the notation and identifying the role of each component, using what I already knew about regression and ARMA models as a starting point. What I now understand is that the two parts answer different questions. The regression part explains the series using outside information, while the ARMA part picks up the dependence over time that the explanatory variables don’t account for. Treating these as separate problems would leave autocorrelation in the regression errors, which is exactly the kind of leftover pattern that tells us a model has missed something. So a GARMA is useful whenever we have explanatory variables but the series still depends on its own past once those variables are included. Where I still need practice is in selecting and interpreting these models on real data.
I also found vector autoregressive (VAR) models challenging, especially the idea of modelling several time series jointly. At first it was hard to interpret the idea that the current value of each variable can depend on the past values of several variables, rather than only on its own history. I wanted to understand how this differs from fitting separate autoregressive models to each series. What helped was thinking of a VAR as a system of connected equations, one for each variable, where each equation includes lagged values of all the variables in the system. Thinking about electricity demand and electricity generation made this concrete for me: a change in demand today is likely to be followed by a change in generation, and the two series influence each other over time. Separate AR models would each only look at their own past and would miss that link completely. What I now understand is that VAR models are the right tool when the relationships and dynamic interactions between several time series are themselves of interest, not just each series on its own.
Working through these models taught me that understanding a model involves more than recognising its equation or being able to run it in R. I need to understand what problem it is designed to solve, why its extra complexity is justified, and what each of its components means in the context of the data. A good test I now use is whether I can say what would go wrong if I used the simpler model instead: a straight line where the relationship curves, independent errors where observations are grouped or autocorrelated, or separate models where series affect each other. Breaking the models down, connecting them to methods I already understood, and using practical examples helped me build this intuition. Going forward, I want to become more confident in identifying when these advanced models are appropriate, interpreting their results, and explaining why I would choose one modelling approach over another.

title: Week 10
text:
Session or topic covered: Kalman Filter
This week was all about the Kalman filter. I worked through the lecture slides and the second half of the state space chapter, and the parts I found hardest were the three updating equations, why the intervals are called prediction intervals, and the difference between filtering and smoothing.
The idea itself is simple once you see it. The Kalman filter estimates a hidden state over time by combining what the model predicts the state should be with what we actually observe. Neither is perfect: the prediction carries uncertainty and the observation carries noise, so the filter weighs the two by how much each can be trusted. A phone’s live location works this way. The GPS reading jumps around by a few metres, but your true position moves smoothly, so combining where you probably are (based on where you were a moment ago) with the noisy reading gives a better estimate than either alone.
What made it click for me was thinking about it in Bayesian terms. At each time step, the prediction from the previous step is the prior, the new observation gives the likelihood, and combining them gives the posterior, which then becomes the prior for the next step:
\[
\pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \propto \pi(y_t \mid \theta_t)\, \pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}).
\]
Because everything is normal, the posterior stays normal, so the filter only ever has to keep track of a mean and a variance.
The equations with \(F\), \(G\), \(W\) and \(V\) felt abstract until I worked them out for the local level model,
\[
y_t = \theta_t + v_t, \quad v_t \sim N(0, V), \qquad \theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \quad w_t \sim N(0, W),
\]
where \(F = G = 1\) and everything is a single number.
First, predict the state:
\[
a_t = m_{t-1}, \qquad R_t = C_{t-1} + W.
\]
My best guess for today’s level is yesterday’s estimate, but I’m less certain about it because the level could have moved, which is why the state noise \(W\) gets added to the variance.
Second, predict the observation:
\[
f_t = a_t, \qquad Q_t = R_t + V.
\]
The predicted observation is just the predicted state, but its variance is bigger because it includes uncertainty about the state plus the observation noise \(V\).
Third, update once \(y_t\) comes in. The forecast error and the Kalman gain are
\[
e_t = y_t - f_t, \qquad K_t = \frac{R_t}{R_t + V},
\]
and \(K_t\) always sits between 0 and 1. The update can be rewritten as
\[
m_t = a_t + K_t e_t = (1 - K_t)\, a_t + K_t\, y_t,
\]
and this was the most useful thing I worked out all week. The new estimate is just a weighted average of my prediction and the observation. If the observations are very noisy (large \(V\)), \(K_t\) is close to 0 and I mostly trust my prediction. If the state moves around a lot (large \(W\), so large \(R_t\)), \(K_t\) is close to 1 and I mostly trust the new observation. The variance update
\[
C_t = (1 - K_t)\, R_t
\]
shows that observing something always shrinks the uncertainty.
Missing values then made sense straight away. If \(y_t\) is missing there’s no new information, so \(K_t = 0\), giving \(m_t = a_t\) and \(C_t = R_t\). The posterior equals the prior and the uncertainty keeps growing through \(W\). In the Nile example with 1910 to 1915 removed, the filtered level goes flat and the bands widen over exactly those years.
The prediction interval question confused me for a while. The interval
\[
f_t \pm 1.96\sqrt{Q_t}
\]
describes where the next observation will land, so it includes both the uncertainty about the state and the observation noise. That’s what makes it a prediction interval. A confidence interval would be about the state itself and would use \(C_t\) instead.
I also kept mixing up filtering and smoothing. Filtering estimates the state at time \(t\) using only data up to \(t\), so it reacts to every new observation and jumps around. Smoothing runs backwards once all the data is in and estimates where the state was at time \(t\) using everything, including later observations, which is why the smoothed Nile level is so much less jumpy.
Finally, the likelihood fell into place. Each one-step-ahead prediction satisfies \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(f_t, Q_t)\), so the likelihood is just a product of these normals:
\[
\ell(\phi) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{n} \log Q_t - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{(y_t - f_t)^2}{Q_t}.
\]
That’s what lets \(V\) and \(W\) be estimated by maximum likelihood instead of assumed known, although the surface can be flat or have several peaks, so it’s worth trying different starting values. Next I want to write the filter myself from scratch, check it against dlm on simulated data and the Nile series, and then add the smoother and likelihood so I can estimate the variances on my own.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: Volatility of the South African rand with ARCH and GARCH models
Section and topic: Section 1. Conditional variance models: stylised facts of returns, testing for ARCH effects, ARCH, GARCH and asymmetric GARCH models, volatility forecasting.
Type of project: Implementation (own maximum likelihood code for GARCH(1,1), checked against rugarch and by a small simulation study) and model comparison on real-world data. The Value-at-Risk backtest is an idea not covered in the lectures.
Question: Do daily USD/ZAR exchange rate returns show volatility clustering, and which conditional variance model gives the most reliable one-day-ahead risk forecasts?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data: the South African rand to US dollar spot exchange rate (FRED series DEXSFUS, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System), daily, January 2010 to September 2026. Full source details are in Section 2.1.
Methods: Exploratory analysis of the stylised facts; Ljung and Box and ARCH LM tests; identification, estimation and residual checks for both the mean and the variance equation; ARCH(1), GARCH(1,1) with normal and Student t errors, and GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student t errors; my own implementation of the GARCH(1,1) likelihood; a rolling out-of-sample evaluation of 1000 one-day-ahead forecasts, scored by Value-at-Risk backtests (Kupiec and Christoffersen tests), quantile loss and QLIKE, against historical simulation and constant variance benchmarks.
Key findings: The returns show all the stylised facts: almost no autocorrelation in the returns themselves, strong autocorrelation in squared returns, and fat tails. ARCH(1) fails the residual diagnostics, while the GARCH(1,1) models capture the clustering with a very persistent variance. Student t errors fit better than normal errors, and depreciation shocks raise volatility more than appreciation shocks. Out of sample, the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model gives the best forecasts by quantile loss and QLIKE, but all the GARCH models are too conservative in the lower tail because they assume a symmetric distribution while the returns are positively skewed; historical simulation has the best coverage. Details are in Section 9.1.
What I would do differently: Use a longer test period so that the 1% VaR tests have more power, and add a skewed Student t distribution so that the GARCH VaR can capture the asymmetry between rand depreciation and appreciation.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
section: 2.2 Reading the data and computing returns
text:
2.2 Reading the data and computing returns
The code downloads the series the first time the document is rendered and saves it as usdzar_fred.csv. If the download fails (for example without an internet connection), download the CSV manually from the FRED page above and save it in the same folder as this file under that name.


Code
if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  fred_url <- paste0("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=DEXSFUS",
                     "&cosd=", start_date, "&coed=", end_date)
  download.file(fred_url, data_file, mode = "wb")
}

fx_raw <- read.csv(data_file, na.strings = c(".", ""))
names(fx_raw) <- c("date", "rate")

fx <- fx_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), rate = as.numeric(rate)) |>
  filter(!is.na(rate), date >= start_date, date <= end_date) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(r = 100 * (log(rate) - lag(log(rate)))) |>
  filter(!is.na(r)) |>
  mutate(day = row_number())

# tsibble indexed by trading day (the calendar dates are irregular
# because of weekends and US public holidays)
fx_ts <- fx |> as_tsibble(index = day)

r <- fx$r
n <- length(r)


Days on which FRED records no rate (US public holidays) are dropped, so returns are measured from one trading day to the next. The return is defined as
\[
r_t = 100 \times (\log P_t - \log P_{t-1}),
\]
where \(P_t\) is the number of rand per US dollar. A positive return means the rand weakened against the dollar. The analysis uses 4,188 daily returns from 5 January 2010 to 30 September 2026.
I work with log returns rather than plain differences of the rate, \(P_t - P_{t-1}\), for three reasons. First, log returns are scale-free: the rand moved from about R7.31 to R16.42 per dollar over the sample, so a 10-cent move is a 1.4% change at the start but only 0.6% at the end, and plain differences would treat these as the same shock. Second, because the size of rand moves grows with the level of the rate, plain differences show a variance that rises over time because of the trend in the level rather than volatility clustering (Figure 1), which would contaminate the variance equation. Third, multiplied by 100, a log return is approximately the percentage change, and log returns add across days, so a multi-day return is the sum of the daily ones.


Code
p_diff <- ggplot(fx |> mutate(d = rate - lag(rate)), aes(date, d)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily change (rand)")

p_logr <- ggplot(fx, aes(date, r)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily log return (%)")

p_diff + p_logr








Figure 1: Left: plain daily differences of the rate (rand). Right: daily log returns (%). The plain differences fan out as the rate rises; the log returns do not.

The rand weakened from about 7.31 to 16.42 per dollar over the period, which shows up as a small positive mean return of 0.0194% a day. This is tiny next to the daily standard deviation of 0.939%, which is the first stylised fact: over one day the mean is close to zero and nearly all the action is in the variance. The annualised volatility is 14.9%. The return series in Figure 2 shows the second stylised fact very clearly: volatility clustering. Large moves come in bursts, most obviously around the two marked events, separated by long calm stretches. The largest single move in the sample is -6.26% on 17 March 2016.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
3.2 Distribution of returns


Code
p_hist <- ggplot(fx, aes(r)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 80,
                 fill = "steelblue4", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean(r), sd = sd(r)),
                colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Daily return (%)", y = "Density")

p_qq <- ggplot(fx, aes(sample = r)) +
  stat_qq(size = 0.5, colour = "steelblue4") +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Normal quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles")

p_hist + p_qq








Figure 3: Left: histogram of daily returns with the normal density that has the same mean and variance. Right: normal QQ plot.





The excess kurtosis of 1.88 and the S-shaped QQ plot in Figure 3 show fat tails: there are many more very small and very large returns than a normal distribution allows. The Jarque and Bera statistic is 651.4 (p < 0.001), so normality is rejected decisively. Part of this is a direct consequence of volatility clustering: a mixture of calm days with a small variance and turbulent days with a large variance has fatter tails than any single normal distribution. Whether returns are still fat-tailed after allowing for a changing variance is a separate question that the Student t models answer below.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
section: 3.3 Dependence in returns and in squared returns
text:
3.3 Dependence in returns and in squared returns


Code
p1 <- fx_ts |> ACF(r, lag_max = 50) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Returns")
p2 <- fx_ts |> ACF(r^2, lag_max = 50) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Squared returns")
p3 <- fx_ts |> ACF(abs(r), lag_max = 50) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Absolute returns")
p1 / p2 / p3








Figure 4: ACF of returns, squared returns and absolute returns, up to 50 trading days.





Figure 4 is the key plot of the project. The returns themselves have almost no autocorrelation: the largest absolute autocorrelation in the first 20 lags is only 0.042. The squared and absolute returns, in contrast, have positive autocorrelations that are significant at nearly every lag shown and decay very slowly. This is the signature of volatility clustering: the direction of tomorrow’s move is close to unpredictable, but its size depends strongly on recent sizes. The Ljung and Box test on 20 lags gives Q = 31.6 (p 0.048) for the returns and Q = 417.2 (p < 0.001) for the squared returns. The test on the returns is only just significant at the 5% level. With more than 4,000 observations even autocorrelations of about 0.04 can be detected, and correlations that small are of no practical use for forecasting the direction of the rand. After standardising by the GARCH volatility no autocorrelation remains (Table 5), so the mean equation is kept as a constant.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
5.1 Modelling approach for returns
The modelling follows the same approach as Project 1, applied to both equations of the model. The rate is modelled on the log scale, so that changes are proportional to the level (Figure 1), and log returns are the first difference of the log exchange rate. The returns fluctuate around a constant mean, so no further differencing is needed. For the mean equation the ACF of the returns is close to zero at all lags, so a constant mean, ARMA(0,0), is used. For the variance equation the slowly decaying ACF of squared returns suggests that a low order ARCH model will not be enough and that GARCH(1,1) is the natural candidate, since it is an ARCH(\(\infty\)) model with geometrically decaying weights. The models are estimated by maximum likelihood with rugarch, and with my own code for GARCH(1,1) (Section 6).
The standardised residuals \(\hat z_t = \hat\varepsilon_t / \hat\sigma_t\) should then show no autocorrelation (mean equation adequate) and their squares should show no autocorrelation (variance equation adequate). A model that fails goes back to identification, and only models that pass are used to forecast. A model that passes must still beat the benchmarks out of sample (Section 7).

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
5.2 Candidate models
All models have a constant mean, \(r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t\) with \(\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t\), and differ in the variance equation and in the distribution of \(z_t\):

Standardised Student t with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom


GJR-GARCH(1,1) t
\(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + (\alpha + \gamma I_{t-1}) \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2\), with \(I_{t-1} = 1\) if \(\varepsilon_{t-1} < 0\)
Standardised Student t






The GJR model allows good and bad news to affect volatility differently. For a share price the usual finding is that falls (negative returns) raise volatility more than rises. For USD/ZAR the interpretation is reversed: a negative return is a strengthening of the rand, so \(\gamma > 0\) would mean that rand appreciation raises volatility more, and \(\gamma < 0\) that rand depreciation raises volatility more.


Code
make_spec <- function(model = "sGARCH", order = c(1, 1), dist = "norm") {
  ugarchspec(
    variance.model     = list(model = model, garchOrder = order),
    mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
    distribution.model = dist
  )
}

specs <- list(
  "ARCH(1) normal"    = make_spec(order = c(1, 0)),
  "GARCH(1,1) normal" = make_spec(),
  "GARCH(1,1) t"      = make_spec(dist = "std"),
  "GJR-GARCH(1,1) t"  = make_spec(model = "gjrGARCH", dist = "std")
)
dists <- c("norm", "norm", "std", "std")
names(dists) <- names(specs)

fits <- lapply(specs, function(sp) ugarchfit(spec = sp, data = r, solver = "hybrid"))

Interpreting the GARCH(1,1) t fit. The ARCH coefficient \(\hat\alpha\) = 0.045 measures how strongly volatility reacts to yesterday’s shock, and \(\hat\beta\) = 0.942 measures how much of yesterday’s volatility carries over. Their sum, the persistence, is 0.9874, very close to 1. A volatility shock therefore dies out slowly, with a half-life of about 55 trading days. The implied long-run (unconditional) standard deviation is 0.945% a day, or 15.0% a year, and forecasts of volatility revert towards this level.
Normal or Student t errors? Even after allowing for a changing variance, the estimated degrees of freedom are \(\hat\nu\) = 11.0. That is not extreme, but it is well short of the normal limit (\(\nu \to \infty\)): a Student t distribution with this many degrees of freedom has excess kurtosis \(6/(\nu - 4)\) = 0.86, close to the excess kurtosis of the t model’s standardised residuals in Table 5. The log likelihood improves by 34.1 when moving from normal to t errors for the same variance equation, for just one extra parameter, so the standardised returns are still fat-tailed. This matters for risk: a normal model will understate the probability of extreme days.
Asymmetry. The GJR term is \(\hat\gamma\) = -0.051 (p < 0.001). It is negative and significant, so shocks that weaken the rand (positive returns) raise volatility more than shocks that strengthen it. This is the reverse of the leverage effect in share prices, and is typical of emerging market currencies, where sudden depreciations are associated with stress and capital outflows. By BIC the preferred model is the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model.

                 "GARCH(1,1) t" = 2, "GJR-GARCH(1,1) t" = 3)

diag_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
  z <- as.numeric(residuals(fits[[m]], standardize = TRUE))
  lbz  <- Box.test(z,   lag = 20, type = "Ljung-Box")
  lbz2 <- Box.test(z^2, lag = 20, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = n_garch_par[[m]])
  alm  <- arch_lm(z, q = 12)
  tibble(Model = m,
         `LB z (p)` = lbz$p.value,
         `LB z^2 (p)` = lbz2$p.value,
         `ARCH LM on z (p)` = unname(alm["p.value"]),
         `Excess kurtosis of z` = mean((z - mean(z))^4) / var(z)^2 - 3)
}))

  mutate(Passes = if_else(`LB z^2 (p)` > 0.05 & `ARCH LM on z (p)` > 0.05,
                          "Yes", "No"))

The two Ljung and Box tests have different jobs, as the notes stress: autocorrelation left in \(\hat z_t\) would send me back to the mean equation, while autocorrelation left in \(\hat z_t^2\) sends me back to the variance equation.
For ARCH(1) the test on \(\hat z_t^2\) gives p < 0.001 and the ARCH LM test on \(\hat z_t\) gives p < 0.001. A single lag of the squared shock cannot reproduce the slow decay seen in the ACF of squared returns, so ARCH(1) fails the residual checks. I therefore went back to identification and moved to GARCH(1,1), which adds the lagged variance and so gives the model a long memory with only one extra parameter. ARCH(1) is kept in the comparison only as a reference point; it is not used for forecasting.
All three GARCH(1,1) models pass: no significant autocorrelation remains in the squared standardised residuals, so the variance equation is adequate and the models can be used to forecast. The test on \(\hat z_t\) itself gives p-values of 0.112, 0.289, 0.280, 0.268 across the four models, so the constant mean is adequate.

The conditional standard deviation band in Figure 5 widens in the turbulent periods and narrows in calm periods, which a constant variance model cannot do. The QQ plots in Figure 6 show that the normal model’s residuals still have heavy tails, while the residuals of the t model lie much closer to the line, confirming the choice of the Student t distribution. The t model’s residuals still bend slightly above the line in the lower tail: the largest strengthening days are less extreme than a symmetric t distribution expects. This is a first sign of the skewness that turns out to matter in the backtest.
