text:
6.1 A small simulation check
Agreement with a package shows that two implementations agree, not that either is right. As a second check, I simulated 100 series of the same length as the data from a GARCH(1,1) with known parameters (set equal to the rugarch estimates) and refitted each one with my code.


Code
sim_garch11 <- function(n, mu, omega, alpha, beta, burn = 500) {
  N <- n + burn
  z <- rnorm(N); e <- s2 <- numeric(N)
  s2[1] <- omega / (1 - alpha - beta)
  e[1]  <- sqrt(s2[1]) * z[1]
  for (t in 2:N) {
    s2[t] <- omega + alpha * e[t - 1]^2 + beta * s2[t - 1]
    e[t]  <- sqrt(s2[t]) * z[t]
  }
  mu + e[(burn + 1):N]
}

true_par <- rg[, 1]
names(true_par) <- c("mu", "omega", "alpha", "beta")

# re-run after adding fnscale to fit_garch11()
set.seed(42)
n_sim <- 100
sim_est <- t(replicate(n_sim, {
  y <- sim_garch11(n, true_par["mu"], true_par["omega"], true_par["alpha"], true_par["beta"])
  fit_garch11(y, se = FALSE)$estimate   # standard errors not needed here
}))

The first time I ran this check, the results did not match the theory: in almost half of the replications my code returned \(\hat\alpha = 0\) and \(\hat\beta = 1\), a constant variance model, even though every series was simulated with clear GARCH effects. The problem was the optimiser, not the likelihood. R’s BFGS method takes a first step proportional to the gradient, and with a negative log likelihood of about 5,500 the gradient is large, so the first step could jump far into a flat region where \(\alpha \approx 0\), and the optimiser stopped there. Dividing the objective by the sample size (fnscale in optim()) keeps the steps at a sensible size. With this change 0 of the 100 replications end at that corner, the estimates are centred on the true values with small bias, and the spread of the estimates across replications is of the same size as the Hessian based standard errors. The real-data fit was not affected, since it matches rugarch, but it could have been. A check against a package alone would not have found this, which is the reason for running a simulation.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
7.1 Design
In-sample fit does not answer the research question, which is about forecasts. The last 1000 trading days (from 30 September 2022 to 30 September 2026) are used as a test period. For each day in the test period, every model produces a one-day-ahead forecast of the mean and standard deviation using only data up to the previous day. The GARCH models are re-estimated every 25 trading days on an expanding window, which keeps the evaluation free of temporal leakage.
From each forecast distribution I compute the VaR at four levels: the 1% and 5% quantiles (losses for someone holding dollars when the rand strengthens) and the 95% and 99% quantiles (losses for someone who needs dollars, such as an importer, when the rand weakens). For Student t models,
\[
\text{VaR}_{p,t} = \hat\mu_{t|t-1} + \hat\sigma_{t|t-1} \, t_{\nu}^{-1}(p) \sqrt{(\nu - 2)/\nu},
\]
where the last factor rescales the t distribution to unit variance.
Two benchmarks without a GARCH variance are included, in the spirit of the benchmark methods in the notes:

Historical simulation (HS): the VaR is the empirical quantile of the previous 250 returns.
Rolling normal: a normal distribution with the mean and variance of the previous 250 returns.

The ARCH(1) model failed the residual diagnostics, so it is not part of the forecast comparison.


Code
roll_models <- c("GARCH(1,1) normal", "GARCH(1,1) t", "GJR-GARCH(1,1) t")

rolls <- lapply(specs[roll_models], function(sp) {
  rl <- ugarchroll(sp, data = r, n.ahead = 1, forecast.length = n_test,
                   refit.every = refit_every, refit.window = "recursive",
                   solver = "hybrid", calculate.VaR = FALSE)
  if (convergence(rl) != 0) rl <- resume(rl, solver = "gosolnp")
  rl
})




Code
levels_p  <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99)
test_idx  <- (n - n_test + 1):n
realised  <- r[test_idx]

var_quantile <- function(mu, sigma, p, dist, shape = NULL) {
  if (dist == "norm") mu + sigma * qnorm(p) else mu + sigma * qstd_unit(p, shape)
}

# GARCH model forecasts
fc_list <- lapply(roll_models, function(m) {
  d <- as.data.frame(rolls[[m]], which = "density")
  out <- tibble(model = m, t = seq_len(n_test), mu = d$Mu, sigma = d$Sigma,
                realised = realised)
  for (p in levels_p) {
    out[[paste0("q", p)]] <- var_quantile(d$Mu, d$Sigma, p, dists[[m]], d$Shape)
  }
  out
})

# Benchmarks
bench_hs <- tibble(model = "Historical simulation", t = seq_len(n_test),
                   realised = realised)
bench_rn <- tibble(model = "Rolling normal", t = seq_len(n_test),
                   realised = realised)
past <- lapply(test_idx, function(i) r[(i - hs_window):(i - 1)])
bench_rn$mu    <- sapply(past, mean)
bench_rn$sigma <- sapply(past, sd)
bench_hs$mu    <- bench_rn$mu
bench_hs$sigma <- bench_rn$sigma
for (p in levels_p) {
  bench_hs[[paste0("q", p)]] <- sapply(past, quantile, probs = p, names = FALSE)
  bench_rn[[paste0("q", p)]] <- bench_rn$mu + bench_rn$sigma * qnorm(p)
}

fc_all <- bind_rows(fc_list, list(bench_hs, bench_rn)) |>
  mutate(date = fx$date[test_idx][t])

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
7.2 Backtest tests
For each model and level, a hit is a day on which the realised return falls beyond the VaR (below it for the 1% and 5% levels, above it for the 95% and 99% levels). Under a correct model the hits are independent Bernoulli(\(p^*\)) variables, where \(p^* = p\) for the lower tail and \(p^* = 1 - p\) for the upper tail. I implemented two standard likelihood ratio tests.

Kupiec unconditional coverage test: is the hit rate equal to \(p^*\)? With \(x\) hits in \(T\) days and \(\hat\pi = x / T\), \(LR_{uc} = -2 \left[ (T - x)\log(1 - p^*) + x \log p^* - (T - x)\log(1 - \hat\pi) - x \log \hat\pi \right] \sim \chi^2_1 .\)
Christoffersen conditional coverage test: adds a test of independence, comparing a first-order Markov chain for the hits with an independent sequence, so that clustered hits are detected. \(LR_{cc} = LR_{uc} + LR_{ind} \sim \chi^2_2\).



Code
kupiec_test <- function(hits, p) {
  n <- length(hits); x <- sum(hits); phat <- x / n
  ll0 <- (n - x) * log(1 - p) + x * log(p)
  ll1 <- if (x == 0 || x == n) 0 else (n - x) * log(1 - phat) + x * log(phat)
  lr  <- -2 * (ll0 - ll1)
  c(hits = x, expected = n * p, LR_uc = lr, p_uc = pchisq(lr, 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

christoffersen_test <- function(hits, p) {
  h0 <- hits[-length(hits)]; h1 <- hits[-1]
  n00 <- sum(h0 == 0 & h1 == 0); n01 <- sum(h0 == 0 & h1 == 1)
  n10 <- sum(h0 == 1 & h1 == 0); n11 <- sum(h0 == 1 & h1 == 1)
  pi01 <- n01 / (n00 + n01)
  pi11 <- if ((n10 + n11) > 0) n11 / (n10 + n11) else 0
  pi1  <- (n01 + n11) / (n00 + n01 + n10 + n11)
  xlogy <- function(x, y) ifelse(x == 0, 0, x * log(y))
  ll_ind <- xlogy(n00, 1 - pi01) + xlogy(n01, pi01) +
            xlogy(n10, 1 - pi11) + xlogy(n11, pi11)
  ll_dep <- xlogy(n00 + n10, 1 - pi1) + xlogy(n01 + n11, pi1)
  lr_ind <- -2 * (ll_dep - ll_ind)
  lr_cc  <- kupiec_test(hits, p)[["LR_uc"]] + lr_ind
  c(p_ind = pchisq(lr_ind, 1, lower.tail = FALSE),
    p_cc  = pchisq(lr_cc, 2, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

# quantile (tick) loss: the proper scoring rule for a p quantile
tick_loss <- function(y, q, p) mean((p - (y < q)) * (y - q))

    d <- fc_all[fc_all$model == model, ]

    y <- d$realised

    hits <- if (p < 0.5) as.integer(y < q) else as.integer(y > q)
    k <- kupiec_test(hits, p_star)
    ch <- christoffersen_test(hits, p_star)
    tibble(Hits = k[["hits"]], Expected = k[["expected"]],
           `Kupiec p` = k[["p_uc"]], `Christoffersen p` = ch[["p_cc"]],

text:
7.3 Variance forecast accuracy
The VaR tests look at the tails. To compare the variance forecasts as a whole I use the QLIKE loss, \(L_t = \log \hat\sigma_{t|t-1}^2 + (r_t - \hat\mu_{t|t-1})^2 / \hat\sigma_{t|t-1}^2\), with the squared return as a noisy proxy for the true variance. QLIKE is robust to that noise in the sense that it ranks forecasts correctly in expectation, and it penalises under-prediction of variance more heavily than over-prediction, which is the right asymmetry for risk management.

  group_by(Model = model) |>
  summarise(QLIKE = mean(log(sigma^2) + (realised - mu)^2 / sigma^2), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(QLIKE)

  geom_line(data = filter(plot_df, model == "GARCH(1,1) t"),
            aes(y = realised), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q0.01, colour = model), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q0.99, colour = model), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = hits_df, aes(y = realised), colour = "black", size = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("GARCH(1,1) t" = "firebrick",
                                 "Historical simulation" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Return (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 7: Test period returns with the 1% and 99% one-day VaR from the GARCH(1,1) t model (red) and historical simulation (blue). Points mark returns beyond the GARCH 1% or 99% VaR.





Coverage. Out of the four levels, the number of rejections (Kupiec or Christoffersen test at 5%) is 1 for GARCH(1,1) normal, 3 for GARCH(1,1) t, 2 for GJR-GARCH(1,1) t, 0 for historical simulation and 2 for the rolling normal benchmark. On this count the crudest method, historical simulation, is the best calibrated.
The pattern behind the GARCH rejections is more informative than the counts. They are almost all in the lower tail, and they come from too few hits rather than too many: at the 5% level all three GARCH models are exceeded only 29 times against 50 expected. In the upper tail, where the rand weakens, the GARCH models are close to the expected numbers at both levels. So the GARCH VaR is too conservative on days when the rand strengthens and about right on days when it weakens. The reason is that every model here uses a symmetric distribution for \(z_t\), while the returns are positively skewed: the skewness is 0.20 over the test period and 0.22 over the full sample, so large weakening moves are more common than strengthening moves of the same size. A symmetric distribution has to share its tail probability equally between the two sides, which overstates the lower tail. Historical simulation uses the empirical quantiles directly, so it picks up the skewness automatically.
Normal or t out of sample. At the 1% level, where a correct model should be exceeded about 10 times, the GARCH(1,1) normal model is exceeded 7 times in the lower tail and 10 times in the upper tail, against 4 and 9 for the GARCH(1,1) t model. Neither model is exceeded too often. The heavier tails of the t distribution push its 1% VaR further out, which in the already over-covered lower tail makes it more conservative (rejected by the Kupiec test, p 0.030). The clear in-sample advantage of t errors therefore does not show up as better coverage in this test period, although it does show up in the loss functions below.
Clustering of exceedances. The benchmarks react slowly to a change in volatility, because a window of 250 days gives a return from a year ago the same weight as yesterday’s. Their VaR therefore moves in slow steps (Figure 7), staying too wide for months after volatility falls and too narrow after it jumps. In this test period the cost of that slowness was small. The test period was calmer than the training period (daily standard deviation 0.83% against 0.97%), with no volatility jump on the scale of 2016 or 2020, and the Christoffersen test does not reject historical simulation at any level. The rolling normal benchmark is rejected at two levels: at 5%, like the GARCH models, it has too few hits, and at 99% its normal tails are too thin (18 hits against 10 expected). The GARCH(1,1) t model is rejected by the Christoffersen test at the 95% level (p 0.034) even though its hit count is almost exactly right, so some of its upper-tail hits came in pairs. The GARCH VaR bands widen and narrow within days, which is the behaviour that matters when volatility does change quickly.
Ranking. Averaged over the four levels, the lowest quantile loss is achieved by the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model, and the lowest QLIKE by the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model. Both are proper scoring rules, so they reward forecasts that are close to the truth across the whole period, not just a correct hit count. The differences between the three GARCH models are small and were not tested formally, so the ranking among them is indicative; the gap between the GARCH models and the rolling normal benchmark on QLIKE is much larger.
Answer to the research question. The returns clearly show volatility clustering, and no single model wins on every criterion. The GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model gives the best one-day-ahead risk forecasts overall: it has the lowest quantile loss and QLIKE, it captures the asymmetry between depreciation and appreciation, and its VaR is well calibrated in the upper tail, which is the tail that matters to someone exposed to a weaker rand. Its weakness is the lower tail, where its symmetric error distribution makes the VaR too conservative, and there the distribution-free historical simulation is better calibrated. A GARCH model with a skewed error distribution would be the natural way to combine the strengths of both.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.1 Key findings

The rand shows all the stylised facts of financial returns: almost no autocorrelation in returns, strong and slowly decaying autocorrelation in squared returns, and fat tails (excess kurtosis 1.9). The ARCH LM test confirms a time-varying variance (p < 0.001).
The residual checks rejected ARCH(1) because ARCH structure remained in its standardised residuals, which led to GARCH(1,1).
Volatility is highly persistent: \(\hat\alpha + \hat\beta\) = 0.9874, a half-life of about 55 trading days.
Student t errors are clearly better than normal errors (\(\hat\nu\) = 11.0), so even after removing volatility clustering, extreme days are more common than a normal distribution implies.
Asymmetry: \(\hat\gamma\) = -0.051 (p < 0.001). There is significant asymmetry in how depreciation and appreciation shocks affect volatility.
Out of sample, the preferred model by quantile loss is GJR-GARCH(1,1) t and by QLIKE GJR-GARCH(1,1) t. But all the GARCH models are too conservative in the lower tail (29 hits at 5% against 50 expected), because they assume a symmetric distribution while the returns are positively skewed. Historical simulation is the only method with no rejected VaR tests. In the upper tail, which matters to someone exposed to a weaker rand, the GARCH hit counts are close to the expected numbers, and the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model passes both tests at both upper levels.
The simulation check found an optimiser problem in my own GARCH code: R’s BFGS stopped at the degenerate corner \(\alpha = 0\), \(\beta = 1\) in almost half of the replications until the objective was rescaled.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.2 Issues and limitations

Power of the tests. With 1000 test days, a correct 1% VaR is expected to be exceeded only 10 times, so the Kupiec test has little power to separate a 1% model from, say, a 1.5% model. A model that “passes” is not proven correct.
Tests with a large sample. The residual tests in-sample use more than 4000 observations, so even very small departures from white noise can be significant. I combined the formal tests with the plots and the out-of-sample results rather than relying on p-values alone.
Very high persistence. A persistence close to 1 can be a sign of structural breaks in the level of volatility (for example a calmer period after 2020) rather than true long memory, as discussed in the notes. A model with a regime change in volatility, such as a hidden Markov model, would be a natural alternative.
Data choices. FRED noon rates in New York miss moves that happen during South African trading hours after the New York fix, and dropping US holidays makes some returns cover two days. Neither should affect the conclusions much, but a Johannesburg close series would be a useful check.
Refitting every 25 days rather than daily saves time but means the parameters lag slightly behind; the volatility itself is still updated every day.
Symmetric error distributions. All the models assume that, given the volatility, a strengthening and a weakening of the same size are equally likely. The backtest shows that this is the main weakness of the GARCH VaR for the rand.
Size of the loss differences. The QLIKE and quantile loss differences between the three GARCH models are small and were not tested formally (for example with a Diebold and Mariano test).
VaR is only one risk measure. It says nothing about how large losses are once the VaR is exceeded. Expected shortfall would be the natural extension.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.3 What I would do differently
I would add a skewed Student t distribution (available in rugarch) so that the GARCH VaR can reflect the positive skewness found in the backtest, use a longer test period so that the 1% tests have more power, and add expected shortfall to the backtest. A further comparison would be a hidden Markov model that lets volatility switch between a small number of regimes, using the same returns and the same backtest.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.4 Reflection and model development
Going into this project, I knew that ARCH and GARCH models are built to model volatility directly. They don’t try to predict which way a series moves; they predict how much it moves. I felt that currencies were the place to test that, because exchange rates are famously volatile and close to unpredictable in direction. The rand in particular has been going through a very interesting period. It weakened to R19.82 per dollar in April 2025, its weakest level in my sample, then strengthened steadily to around R15.80 by January 2026. Over the same two years the conflict involving Iran escalated, and when war broke out between the United States and Iran at the end of February 2026, the rand went from months of calm to moving by 2 to 3% in a day. That is exactly the kind of behaviour GARCH models are designed for, and because these events fall inside my test period, I could see how the models handled a real shock rather than only a historical one. It also connected back to Project 1, where my first idea had been to use financial data until its volatility made it a poor fit for ARIMA models. This project let me return to that idea with the right tools, but taking it in a more macroeconomic direction than a purely financial one.
The model was not chosen in one step; each decision came from something I saw in the data. The first was to work with log returns rather than the exchange rate itself. The rate trends from about R7 to almost R20 over the sample, so the level is not stationary, and plain daily changes in rand grow as the level rises. Log returns fix both problems, following the same transform-then-difference logic as Project 1. Next I looked at the ACF, expecting it to tell me which ARMA terms to use. However, the ACF of the returns was flat, so there was nothing for AR or MA terms to pick up and the mean equation became just a constant. Since the returns themselves showed no structure, I followed the approach in our class notes and looked at the squared returns, which act as a measure of the size of each day’s shock. That is where the real signal appeared: the autocorrelations were positive and still significant after 50 trading days. The direction of tomorrow’s move cannot be predicted, but its size can, and the ARCH LM test confirmed that the variance is not constant.
From there I built up the variance model step by step. I started with the simplest option, ARCH(1), but it failed the residual checks because ARCH structure was still left over. The slowly decaying ACF of the squared returns showed why: an ARCH model would need dozens of lags to capture that long memory, while GARCH(1,1) achieves it with one extra parameter, because the lagged variance carries all earlier shocks forward. The residuals still showed heavy tails, so I replaced the normal distribution with a Student t. And because the most violent episodes in the data, in 2015, 2020 and 2026, were all times when the rand weakened, I added the GJR term so that depreciation and appreciation could affect volatility differently. It turned out to be significant: shocks that weaken the rand raise volatility far more than shocks that strengthen it. Since my question was about forecasting risk, I did not stop at in-sample fit, and instead judged the models in a rolling one-day-ahead Value-at-Risk backtest against two simple benchmarks.
The project went through several phases, each driven by a decision about what would make the analysis more reliable or easier to follow. My early drafts focused on getting the full analysis working as a stand-alone report: the models, my own GARCH code, the simulation check and the backtest. As the analysis settled, my focus shifted from getting results to justifying them, starting with an explicit argument for using log returns, since that was the first modelling decision and everything else built on it. The biggest change came when I stepped back and critically reviewed the whole project, which led to the coding and modelling improvements that made the final version far more reliable.
The most important of these was a problem I almost missed. My GARCH code matched rugarch exactly on the real data, so I assumed it was correct, but the simulation check showed otherwise: in almost half of the simulated series my code returned a constant-variance model, even though every series had clear GARCH effects. I really struggled to identify where the issue was and used an LLM to help investigate it. The cause turned out to be the optimiser. With such a large log likelihood, R’s BFGS took a first step so big that it landed in a flat region and stopped. Rescaling the objective fixed it, and the estimates then sat right on the true values. Getting the fix to show up taught me a second lesson: because the simulation was cached, R would have kept showing the old results until I forced that chunk to run again. Both problems showed me that code can look right without being right, and that matching a package only shows that two programs agree on one dataset. The simulation, where I knew the true answer, was what exposed the problem.
The backtest taught me to look at the pattern behind a result rather than just the headline. Historical simulation, the simplest method, was the only one with no rejected tests, and every GARCH rejection came from too few hits in the lower tail. The explanation was that the rand’s returns are positively skewed, but all my models assume a symmetric distribution, so they overstate the risk of large strengthening moves. That ended up being one of the most interesting findings of the project. It also showed me that different evaluation measures answer different questions: the loss functions said GJR-GARCH with t errors gave the best forecasts overall, while the coverage tests said historical simulation was better calibrated, and both were true. Finally, tidying up outdated references and aligning the modelling approach with Project 1 made the whole report more consistent and easier to trust.
Going forward, the natural next step is a GARCH model with a skewed Student t distribution, which would keep GARCH’s ability to react to shocks within days while fixing the lower tail. I would also like to look more closely at the weeks of the US–Iran war inside the test period, to see how each model coped while the shock was happening, and to add expected shortfall, since VaR says nothing about how large losses are on the days it is exceeded.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: State space models for South African accommodation demand
Section and topic: Section 2. Linear Gaussian state space models (dynamic linear models): the Kalman filter, maximum likelihood through the prediction error decomposition, the Kalman smoother, forecasting, structural time series models and missing observations.
Type of project: Implementation from first principles on real-world data, with a simulation study and a model comparison.
Question: What do filtering, the likelihood, smoothing and prediction tell us about monthly accommodation demand in South Africa when the 25 COVID-19 months are treated as missing? How does the filter track demand through the gap, how well do the data pin down the model, how much demand was lost to COVID-19, and do the forecasts beat the Project 1 SARIMA and the Project 3 exponential smoothing models?
Data: Statistics South Africa, Tourist Accommodation release P6410, series B64100 (stay unit nights sold, thousands), monthly, January 2015 to June 2026 (Section 2).
Methods: My own Kalman filter, likelihood, Kalman smoother and forecasts, written in the notation and structure of the course notes and checked against dlm (the package used in the notes) and against the exact log likelihood of the Project 1 SARIMA. Beyond the notes, I derive the smoothed covariances between months (for an honest band on total lost demand) and auxiliary residuals that test for breaks, and I use a boundary-corrected likelihood ratio test for the seasonal variance. Four structural models are estimated by maximum likelihood and compared by AIC, likelihood ratio tests, profile likelihoods and residual diagnostics. A simulation study checks the lost-demand estimate, and the forecasts are evaluated on the Projects 1 and 3 test set and by rolling-origin cross-validation.
Key findings:

My filter reproduces the Project 1 SARIMA log likelihood exactly (147.1098) and agrees with dlm’s filter and smoother.
Demand behaves like a random-walk level (monthly SD about 2%) plus a slowly evolving seasonal pattern. A fixed seasonal pattern is rejected (p = 0.002), and there is almost no month-specific noise.
When data resumed in April 2022, demand was 31% below what the filter expected. The filter re-learned the level within a few months without being told anything about COVID-19.
About 22.4 million stay unit nights (48% of expected demand) were lost between March 2020 and March 2022 (95% band 19.3 to 25.5 million).
The best state space model (damped trend + AR(1)) has a test RMSE of 89.9 thousand nights. That beats seasonal naive (132.6) and the Project 1 SARIMA (101.6), but not the Project 3 damped Holt–Winters model (72.5).

What I would do differently: Use the exact diffuse initialisation, add the Project 3 intervention terms and an Easter regressor to the state space model, and let the variances differ before and after COVID-19.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 3.1 The model and what each part means
text:
3.1 The model and what each part means
Write \(y_t = \log(\text{nights sold}_t)\). The simplest model that matches Figure 1 is a local level plus seasonal model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \mu_t + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_t, & \varepsilon_t &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon), \\
\mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \xi_t, & \xi_t &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_\xi), \\
\gamma_t &= -\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{11} \gamma_{t-j} + \omega_t, & \omega_t &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_\omega).
\end{aligned}
\]
In words:

\(\mu_t\) is the underlying level of demand: log nights sold with the calendar effect removed. A level shock \(\xi_t\) is a permanent change in demand, such as a new air route, a visa rule or the post-COVID reset.
\(\gamma_t\) is the seasonal effect of the calendar month (December high, winter months low). The twelve effects sum to roughly zero over a year, and the shock \(\omega_t\) lets the pattern change slowly, for example if school holidays move or the mix of business and leisure travel changes.
\(\varepsilon_t\) is month-specific noise that does not persist, such as a large conference.

The three variances decide how the filter interprets a surprise: is a month with unexpectedly high sales a sign that demand has moved up for good (level), that the seasonal pattern has changed (seasonal), or a one-off (irregular)? Estimating them is the job of the likelihood.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
3.2 State space form
I use the notation of the course notes (and of dlm, Petris et al., 2009). A dynamic linear model is
\[
Y_t = F \theta_t + v_t, \quad v_t \sim N(0, V), \qquad
\theta_t = G \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \quad w_t \sim N(0, W), \qquad
\theta_0 \sim N(m_0, C_0).
\]
For the model above the state vector holds the level and the current and previous ten seasonal effects, \(\theta_t = (\mu_t, \gamma_t, \gamma_{t-1}, \dots, \gamma_{t-10})^\top\), so it has \(p = 12\) elements, and
\[
F = (1, 1, 0, \dots, 0), \quad
G = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & G_\gamma \end{pmatrix}, \quad
G_\gamma = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1 & \cdots & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
V = \sigma^2_\varepsilon, \quad W = \text{diag}(\sigma^2_\xi, \sigma^2_\omega, 0, \dots, 0).
\]
\(F\) is a row vector, as in dlm. This is the model in the notes’ Cape Town temperature example, dlmModSeas(frequency = 12) + dlmModPoly(1), except that there the seasonal states come first and the level last.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
3.3 Four candidate structural models
All four models share the seasonal component above. They differ in the trend and in whether a short-run AR(1) component \(c_t\) is added:



Table 2: The four structural models. All have the seasonal component of the level + seasonal model.

In each case \(y_t = \mu_t + \gamma_t\, (+\, c_t) + \varepsilon_t\). The slope \(\nu_t\) is the monthly growth rate of demand. The damped trend model is the state space counterpart of the damped Holt–Winters method that did best in Project 3, and the level + seasonal model corresponds to ETS(A,N,A). The AR(1) component allows deviations from the trend that last a few months, such as a slow recovery after a shock. Each model only changes \(F\), \(G\) and \(W\); the code that filters, smooths and forecasts never changes.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
3.4 Filtering, likelihood, smoothing and prediction
Filter. Following the notes, suppose that at the end of month \(t-1\) we have \(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(m_{t-1}, C_{t-1})\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{predict the state:} & a_t &= G m_{t-1}, & R_t &= G C_{t-1} G^\top + W, \\
&\text{predict } y_t: & f_t &= F a_t, & Q_t &= F R_t F^\top + V, \\
&\text{update:} & m_t &= a_t + K_t e_t, & C_t &= R_t - K_t F R_t,
\end{aligned}
\]
with forecast error \(e_t = y_t - f_t\) and Kalman gain \(K_t = R_t F^\top Q_t^{-1}\). \(e_t\) is the surprise in month \(t\), \(Q_t\) its variance, and \(K_t\) says how the surprise is shared out between the level and the seasonal effects. If month \(t\) is missing (a COVID month) it carries no information, so the posterior equals the prior: \(K_t = 0\), \(m_t = a_t\) and \(C_t = R_t\). The filter carries its last view of demand forward and becomes less certain every month, because \(W\) is added to \(R_t\) in each step. In the code I compute \(C_t\) in the equivalent Joseph form \((I - K_t F) R_t (I - K_t F)^\top + K_t V K_t^\top\). It is algebraically the same as the notes’ formula, but stays a valid variance matrix when \(V\) is close to zero, which it turns out to be here.
Likelihood. As in the notes, the log likelihood is the sum of the one-step predictive densities \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(f_t, Q_t)\),
\[
\ell(\psi) = -\tfrac{1}{2} \textstyle\sum_{t} \left( \log 2\pi + \log Q_t + e_t^2 / Q_t \right),
\]
summed over the observed months only: the COVID months contribute nothing. The initial level and seasonal effects are unknown, so, as the notes suggest, I set \(m_0 = 0\) and \(C_0\) very large (\(10^7 I\)). I then leave the first \(d = 13\) forecast errors out of the likelihood, since they only serve to learn the starting values (the large-variance approximation to the exact diffuse filter, Durbin and Koopman, 2012, Chapter 5). The notes warn that this likelihood can be flat with several local maxima, so every model is fitted from several starting values.
Smoother. The Kalman smoother in the notes starts at \(s_n = m_n\), \(S_n = C_n\) and works backwards:
\[
s_t = m_t + J_t (s_{t+1} - a_{t+1}), \qquad S_t = C_t - J_t (R_{t+1} - S_{t+1}) J_t^\top, \qquad J_t = C_t G^\top R_{t+1}^{-1},
\]
so that \(\theta_t \mid y_{1:n} \sim N(s_t, S_t)\). Missing months need no special treatment, since there \(m_t = a_t\) and \(C_t = R_t\) already.
Two things beyond the notes. The matrices \(J_t\) give more than \(s_t\) and \(S_t\), and I need two extra results from them:

Covariances between months. \(\text{Cov}(\theta_s, \theta_t \mid y_{1:n}) = J_s J_{s+1} \cdots J_{t-1} S_t\) for \(s < t\). This is needed for the uncertainty of a total over several months, such as the demand lost over the COVID window. Adding up the monthly intervals would wrongly treat the months as perfectly correlated.
Smoothed shocks. The smoothed state shock is \(\hat w_t = s_t - G s_{t-1}\), with \(\text{Var}(w_t \mid y_{1:n}) = S_t + G S_{t-1} G^\top - S_t J_{t-1}^\top G^\top - G J_{t-1} S_t\). Since \(\text{Var}(\hat w_t) = W - \text{Var}(w_t \mid y_{1:n})\), the standardised level and seasonal shocks are auxiliary residuals: \(t\)-statistics for a break in the level or the seasonal pattern in month \(t\) (Harvey and Koopman, 1992; Durbin and Koopman, 2012, Section 2.12).

Prediction. As in the notes’ KF() example, forecasts come from running the filter on the series with \(h\) missing values attached at the end: \(f_t\) and \(Q_t\) for those months are the forecast mean and variance.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.1 The filter, likelihood, smoother and forecasts

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.2 Building the four models and fitting them
text:
4.2 Building the four models and fitting them
Variances are estimated on the log scale, as in the notes’ lik.fun (dV = exp(x[1]), dW = exp(x[2])), so they stay positive.


Code
# Parameter vector for each model (seas = FALSE fixes the seasonal variance at zero)
param_names <- function(trend, ar, seas = TRUE) {
  c("eps", "level", if (trend != "ll") "slope", if (seas) "seas",
    if (trend == "damped") "phi", if (ar) c("ar_var", "rho"))
}

unpack <- function(theta, trend, ar, seas = TRUE) {
  nm <- param_names(trend, ar, seas)
  p  <- as.list(exp(theta)); names(p) <- nm
  if (trend == "damped") p$phi <- 0.98 * plogis(theta[nm == "phi"])   # phi in (0, 0.98)
  if (ar)                p$rho <- tanh(theta[nm == "rho"])             # rho in (-1, 1)
  if (trend == "ll")     p$slope <- NA
  if (!seas)             p$seas <- 0
  p
}

# Model matrices; trend: "llt" (local linear trend), "ll" (local level), "damped"
structural_mod <- function(p, trend, ar) {
  n_tr <- if (trend == "ll") 1 else 2
  m  <- n_tr + 11 + ar
  GG <- matrix(0, m, m); FF <- matrix(0, 1, m)
  GG[1, 1] <- 1; FF[1] <- 1                                 # level
  if (n_tr == 2) {                                          # slope
    GG[1, 2] <- 1
    GG[2, 2] <- if (trend == "damped") p$phi else 1
  }
  s1 <- n_tr + 1                                            # seasonal block (11 states)
  GG[s1, s1:(s1 + 10)] <- -1
  GG[(s1 + 1):(s1 + 10), s1:(s1 + 9)] <- diag(10)
  FF[s1] <- 1
  if (ar) { GG[m, m] <- p$rho; FF[m] <- 1 }                 # AR(1) component
  w <- numeric(m)
  w[1] <- p$level; if (n_tr == 2) w[2] <- p$slope; w[s1] <- p$seas; if (ar) w[m] <- p$ar_var
  C0 <- diag(1e7, m)                                        # m0 = 0, C0 large (notes)
  if (ar) C0[m, m] <- p$ar_var / (1 - p$rho^2)              # stationary prior for c_t
  list(FF = FF, GG = GG, V = p$eps, W = diag(w, m), m0 = rep(0, m), C0 = C0, s1 = s1)
}

d_diffuse <- 13   # same number of dropped forecast errors for every model, so AIC is comparable

ssm_negll <- function(theta, y, trend, ar, seas = TRUE, d = d_diffuse) {
  -KF_loglik(KF(y, structural_mod(unpack(theta, trend, ar, seas), trend, ar)), d)
}

# Maximum likelihood from several starting values (the notes warn of flat peaks)
fit_structural <- function(y, trend, ar, seas = TRUE, start = NULL, d = d_diffuse, polish = TRUE) {
  nm  <- param_names(trend, ar, seas)
  th0 <- c(eps = log(1e-3), level = log(1e-3), slope = log(1e-5), seas = log(1e-5),
           phi = qlogis(0.9 / 0.98), ar_var = log(1e-3), rho = atanh(0.5))[nm]
  starts <- if (is.null(start)) list(th0, th0 + 0.5, th0 - 1) else list(start)
  best <- NULL
  for (s in starts) {
    o <- optim(s, ssm_negll, y = y, trend = trend, ar = ar, seas = seas, d = d,
               method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 500))
    if (polish)                                   # Nelder-Mead polish; skipped in cross-validation
      o <- optim(o$par, ssm_negll, y = y, trend = trend, ar = ar, seas = seas, d = d,
                 method = "Nelder-Mead", control = list(maxit = 4000))
    if (is.null(best) || o$value < best$value) best <- o
  }
  p   <- unpack(best$par, trend, ar, seas)
  mod <- structural_mod(p, trend, ar)
  list(theta = best$par, p = p, mod = mod, kf = KF(y, mod), loglik = -best$value,
       k = length(nm), trend = trend, ar = ar, seas = seas,
       converged = best$convergence == 0)
}

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.3 Check 1: against dlm, the package used in the notes
text:
4.3 Check 1: against dlm, the package used in the notes
Before interpreting anything, I check that my code computes the right quantities on this series, missing months included. The first check fits the level + seasonal model exactly as in the notes: the model is built with dlmModSeas() + dlmModPoly(), and dlmMLE() is run from three starting values.
dlmMLE() keeps all 89 observed months in the likelihood. So for this check only, I also maximise my likelihood with nothing dropped (\(d = 0\)). Then, at dlm’s estimates, I compare my filtered and smoothed states with dlmFilter() and dlmSmooth().


Code
build_ll <- function(x) {
  dlmModSeas(frequency = 12, dV = exp(x[1]), dW = c(exp(x[3]), rep(0, 10))) +
    dlmModPoly(1, dV = 0, dW = exp(x[2]))
}
dlm_starts <- list(log(c(1e-3, 1e-3, 1e-5)), log(c(1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-4)), log(c(1e-2, 1e-2, 1e-3)))
dlm_fits   <- lapply(dlm_starts, function(s) dlmMLE(y_tour, parm = s, build = build_ll))
dlm_values <- sapply(dlm_fits, `[[`, "value")
dlm_fit    <- dlm_fits[[which.min(dlm_values)]]
dlm_var    <- exp(dlm_fit$par)                         # irregular, level, seasonal

my_full <- fit_structural(y_tour, "ll", FALSE, d = 0)  # my ML, same likelihood as dlm




Code
# my filter and smoother at dlm's estimates; dlm puts the 11 seasonal states first
p_dlm   <- list(eps = dlm_var[1], level = dlm_var[2], seas = dlm_var[3], slope = NA)
mod_dlm <- structural_mod(p_dlm, "ll", FALSE)
kf_dlm  <- KF(y_tour, mod_dlm)
ks_dlm  <- KS(kf_dlm, mod_dlm)
perm    <- c(12, 1:11)                                  # my state j is dlm's state perm[j]
d_filt  <- dlmFilter(y_tour, build_ll(dlm_fit$par))
d_smth  <- dlmSmooth(d_filt)
after   <- (d_diffuse + 1):n_tr                          # months after the diffuse start
diff_filt   <- max(abs(dropFirst(d_filt$m)[after, perm] - kf_dlm$mt[after, ]))
diff_smooth <- max(abs(dropFirst(d_smth$s)[after, perm] - ks_dlm$st[after, ]))
S_dlm       <- dlmSvd2var(d_smth$U.S, d_smth$D.S)
diff_svar   <- max(sapply(after, function(t) abs(S_dlm[[t + 1]][12, 12] - ks_dlm$St[1, 1, t])))
# dlmLL() is the negative log likelihood without the constant (n/2) log(2 pi)
n_obs   <- sum(!is.na(y_tour))
my_nll_at_dlm <- -KF_loglik(kf_dlm, 0) - 0.5 * n_obs * log(2 * pi)
dlm_nll       <- dlmLL(y_tour, build_ll(dlm_fit$par))

tibble(
  ` ` = c("Irregular variance", "Level variance", "Seasonal variance", "Log likelihood"),
  `dlmMLE()` = c(sci(dlm_var, 2), fmt(-dlm_fit$value - 0.5 * n_obs * log(2 * pi), 3)),
  `My filter, my ML estimates` = c(sci(c(my_full$p$eps, my_full$p$level, my_full$p$seas), 2),
                                   fmt(my_full$loglik, 3))
) |> kable()

The two agree (Table 3). The level and seasonal variances match to two significant figures, and the maximised log likelihoods differ by 3.5e-05. The irregular variance is close to zero in both, but its exact value differs, because the likelihood is flat near zero (Section 5.3).
The three dlmMLE() starting values reach objective values of -120.70, -120.70, -120.70, with convergence codes 0, 0, 0. All three converge to the same maximum, as the notes recommend checking. At dlm’s estimates, from month 14 onwards:

My filtered states differ from dlmFilter() by at most 2.2e-08.
My smoothed states differ from dlmSmooth() by at most 2.3e-08.
The smoothed level variances differ by at most 3.3e-11.
My log likelihood matches dlmLL() to 7.3e-07.

In the first 13 months the individual level and seasonal states are not yet identified: their prior variance is \(10^7\), so their values are arbitrary to many decimal places in both programs. Only their sum, the forecast, is meaningful, which is why those months are left out of the likelihood.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.4 Check 2: reproducing the Project 1 SARIMA likelihood
text:
4.4 Check 2: reproducing the Project 1 SARIMA likelihood
Project 1’s SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 (the “airline” model) was fitted to the same log series with the same months missing. R evaluates its likelihood with a Kalman filter. stats::makeARIMA() writes the ARIMA model in state space form, giving \(G\), \(F\), \(W\) and the first predictive distribution of the 14 differencing and MA states. If my filter is correct, running it on those matrices must give exactly the log likelihood that arima() reports. I also maximise the likelihood myself, using my filter, to see whether I get the same estimates.


Code
y_ts <- ts(y_tour, start = c(2015, 1), frequency = 12)
fit_airline <- arima(y_ts, order = c(0, 1, 1),
                     seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12), method = "ML")

airline_mod <- function(ma, sma, s2) {
  theta <- c(ma, rep(0, 10), sma, ma * sma)               # (1 + theta B)(1 + Theta B^12)
  Delta <- c(1, rep(0, 10), 1, -1)                         # (1 - B)(1 - B^12)
  mk <- makeARIMA(numeric(0), theta, Delta, kappa = 1e6)
  list(FF = matrix(mk$Z, 1), GG = mk$T, V = 0, W = mk$V * s2,   # mk$V is the state noise
       m0 = mk$a, C0 = NULL, a1 = mk$a, R1 = mk$Pn * s2, s2 = s2)
}
# arima() leaves out the diffuse forecast errors (Q_t / sigma^2 >= 10^4) from the likelihood
airline_ll <- function(mod, y = as.numeric(y_ts)) {
  kf <- KF(y, mod, a1 = mod$a1, R1 = mod$R1); ok <- which(!is.na(kf$et))
  ok <- ok[kf$Qt[ok] / mod$s2 < 1e4]
  list(ll = -0.5 * sum(log(2 * pi) + log(kf$Qt[ok]) + kf$et[ok]^2 / kf$Qt[ok]), n = length(ok))
}

cf <- coef(fit_airline)
ll_at_arima <- airline_ll(airline_mod(cf["ma1"], cf["sma1"], fit_airline$sigma2))

# My own ML estimates (MA parameters through tanh so they stay invertible)
my_airline <- optim(c(atanh(-0.3), atanh(-0.5), log(1e-3)), function(p)
  -airline_ll(airline_mod(tanh(p[1]), tanh(p[2]), exp(p[3])))$ll, method = "BFGS")
my_ma <- tanh(my_airline$par[1:2]); my_s2a <- exp(my_airline$par[3])




Code
tibble(
  ` ` = c("MA(1) coefficient", "Seasonal MA(1) coefficient", "Innovation variance",
          "Log likelihood", "Months in the likelihood"),
  `arima()` = c(fmt(cf["ma1"], 4), fmt(cf["sma1"], 4), sci(fit_airline$sigma2, 3),
                fmt(fit_airline$loglik, 4), as.character(fit_airline$nobs)),
  `My filter at arima()'s estimates` = c("", "", "", fmt(ll_at_arima$ll, 4), as.character(ll_at_arima$n)),
  `My filter, my ML estimates` = c(fmt(my_ma[1], 4), fmt(my_ma[2], 4), sci(my_s2a, 3),
                                   fmt(-my_airline$value, 4), "")
) |> kable()

What the estimates say about accommodation demand (Table 5):

There is almost no month-specific noise. The irregular variance is essentially zero in every model, so the filter treats nearly every surprise as either a permanent change in demand or a change in the seasonal pattern. On the log scale, demand behaves like a random-walk level plus a slowly evolving seasonal pattern.
The level moves; the growth rate does not. In the level + seasonal model the level variance is 4.5e-04, a monthly standard deviation of 2.1% in underlying demand. In the BSM the slope variance is 1.3e-11, so the growth rate is effectively a fixed drift.
The seasonal pattern changes slowly. The seasonal variance is about 0.19 times the level variance: each month’s seasonal effect drifts by roughly 0.9% a month. It is almost the same in all four models (8.5e-05 to 9.6e-05), whatever the trend.
Damping and AR(1). The damped trend model estimates \(\phi\) = 0.904. The AR(1) component raises the log likelihood by only 0.10 for two extra parameters. It also changes what the components mean: its level variance falls to 1.6e-06 (from 3.6e-04), because the AR(1) term (rho = 0.70) takes over the month-to-month movement that the level carries in the other models. In that model the ‘level’ is close to a smooth damped trend, and the AR(1) term is the wandering part of demand.
Model selection. The lowest AIC belongs to the Level + seasonal model, which I use for the filtering and smoothing analysis below. The AIC values span only a few units, so the data do not strongly distinguish between the trend specifications: with the growth rate barely moving, adding a slope buys almost nothing in one-step fit. Its effect shows up in long-horizon forecasts instead (Section 9).

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 5.2 Does the seasonal pattern really change?
text:
5.2 Does the seasonal pattern really change?
The seasonal variance is small, and Project 3 concluded that the seasonal pattern hardly changes: there, every seasonal ETS model put the seasonal smoothing parameter \(\gamma\) at its lower bound. So I test it directly. I refit the selected model with the seasonal variance fixed at zero, which is the constant-seasonal model in the notes’ dlmModSeas(..., dW = 0) example, and compare the two by a likelihood ratio test. Zero is on the boundary of the parameter space, so the null distribution of the statistic is a 50:50 mixture of a point mass at zero and \(\chi^2_1\), and the \(p\)-value is half the usual one.


Code
fit_fixed_seas <- fit_structural(y_tour, sel$trend, sel$ar, seas = FALSE)
lr_seas <- 2 * (sel$loglik - fit_fixed_seas$loglik)
p_seas  <- 0.5 * pchisq(lr_seas, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

# ETS(A,*,A) on the pre-COVID months: how gamma depends on the trend
pre_df <- train |> filter(Month < covid_start)
ets_trend <- pre_df |>
  model(`ETS(A,N,A)`  = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
        `ETS(A,A,A)`  = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
        `ETS(A,Ad,A)` = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A"))) |>
  tidy() |>
  filter(term %in% c("alpha", "gamma")) |>
  select(Model = .model, term, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = estimate)
eg <- function(m, col) ets_trend[[col]][ets_trend$Model == m]


The data reject a fixed seasonal pattern: the likelihood ratio statistic is 8.49 (p = 0.002). So the state space model needs a seasonal pattern that moves, while Project 3’s ETS models did not. Refitting ETS to the pre-COVID months shows where the difference comes from:

Without a trend, ETS(A,N,A) gives \(\gamma\) = 0.76 and \(\alpha\) = 0.24.
With a trend, \(\gamma\) drops to 1.2e-04 (ETS(A,A,A)) or 1.1e-04 (ETS(A,Ad,A)).

The ETS seasonal smoothing parameter is fragile: it depends on which other component absorbs the surprises. In the state space model, the seasonal variance is almost the same in all four trend specifications (Table 5), so the evolving seasonal pattern does not depend on the trend.
What exactly the seasonal shocks capture is another matter. With the irregular variance at zero, every one-off month (a moved Easter, a big conference) has to be absorbed by either the level or the seasonal component. Part of the seasonal variance may therefore be month-specific noise that the model cannot place anywhere else. The auxiliary residuals in Section 7.3 check whether such months stand out.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 5.3 Profile likelihoods: how well do the data pin down the variances?
text:
5.3 Profile likelihoods: how well do the data pin down the variances?
The individual variances control the filter’s behaviour, so it matters how precisely they are estimated. For the selected model I compute the profile log likelihood of each variance: fix it on a grid and maximise over the other two. A 95% confidence interval is the set of values whose profile is within \(\chi^2_{1, 0.95}/2 = 1.92\) of the maximum, which, unlike a Wald interval, works on the boundary. The grids reach down to \(10^{-8}\), effectively zero, so an interval can only stop at the end of a grid if the variance cannot be told apart from zero.


Code
nm_sel <- param_names(sel$trend, sel$ar)
profile_par <- function(which_par, grid) {
  free <- setdiff(seq_along(nm_sel), which_par)
  start <- sel$theta[free]
  sapply(grid, function(val) {
    f <- function(th) { full <- numeric(length(nm_sel)); full[free] <- th
                        full[which_par] <- log(val)
                        ssm_negll(full, y_tour, sel$trend, sel$ar) }
    o <- optim(start, f, method = "Nelder-Mead", control = list(maxit = 2000))
    start <<- o$par
    -o$value
  })
}
grids <- list(Irregular = exp(seq(log(1e-8), log(4e-4),   length.out = 30)),
              Level     = exp(seq(log(1e-4), log(1.5e-3), length.out = 30)),
              Seasonal  = exp(seq(log(1e-8), log(4e-4),   length.out = 40)))
par_index <- c(Irregular = which(nm_sel == "eps"), Level = which(nm_sel == "level"),
               Seasonal = which(nm_sel == "seas"))
prof <- bind_rows(lapply(names(grids), function(nm)
  tibble(par = nm, value = grids[[nm]], pll = profile_par(par_index[[nm]], grids[[nm]]))))




Code
prof_rel <- prof |> mutate(rel = pll - sel$loglik)
ggplot(prof_rel, aes(value, rel)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue4") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_scientific()) +
  facet_wrap(vars(par), scales = "free_x") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-8, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Variance (log scale)", y = "Profile log likelihood")

prof_ci <- prof_rel |>
  group_by(par) |>
  summarise(lo = min(value[rel >= -1.92]), hi = max(value[rel >= -1.92]),
            lo_edge = lo == min(value), hi_edge = hi == max(value), .groups = "drop")
pci <- function(p, col) prof_ci[[col]][prof_ci$par == p]
ci_text <- function(p) {
  if (pci(p, "lo_edge")) paste0("from zero up to ", sci(pci(p, "hi")))
  else paste0("from ", sci(pci(p, "lo")), " to ", sci(pci(p, "hi")))
}








Figure 2: Profile log likelihoods of the three variances of the selected model, relative to the maximum. Values above the dashed line (−1.92) form the 95% profile confidence interval. Horizontal axes on the log scale.





The three variances behave very differently (Figure 2):

Level variance: well determined. Its 95% profile interval runs from 2.8e-04 to 7.1e-04, so the monthly standard deviation of underlying demand is between 1.7% and 2.7%. The data are informative about how fast demand moves.
Seasonal variance: less well determined. Its interval runs from 2.0e-05 to 1.8e-04. Zero is excluded, in line with the likelihood ratio test, but the rate at which the seasonal pattern changes is known only to within a factor of about 9.
Irregular variance: on the boundary. Its interval runs from zero up to 1.9e-04. The data cannot distinguish “no month-specific noise” from “a little”, but they rule out a large irregular component. This is why the estimate is essentially zero, why dlm and I find different tiny values for it (Table 3), and why a Wald interval based on the curvature at the maximum would be meaningless here.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
5.4 Diagnostics


Code
r_sel  <- std_resid(sel_kf, d_diffuse)
n_r    <- sum(!is.na(r_sel))
acf_r  <- acf(na.omit(r_sel), lag.max = 36, plot = FALSE)
pacf_r <- pacf(na.omit(r_sel), lag.max = 36, plot = FALSE)
corr_plot <- function(lag, val, ylab) {
  ggplot(tibble(lag = lag, val = val), aes(lag, val)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(n_r), linetype = "dashed", colour = "steelblue") +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0)) +
    labs(x = "Lag (months)", y = ylab)
}
p1 <- ggplot(tibble(Month = as.Date(train$Month), r = r_sel), aes(Month, r)) +
  covid_rect() + geom_hline(yintercept = c(-2, 2), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Std. error")
p2 <- corr_plot(acf_r$lag[-1], acf_r$acf[-1], "ACF")
p3 <- corr_plot(pacf_r$lag, pacf_r$acf, "PACF")
p4 <- ggplot(tibble(r = r_sel), aes(r)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Std. error", y = "Count")
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + plot_layout(nrow = 2)

sw_p    <- shapiro.test(na.omit(r_sel))$p.value
sw_p_nr <- shapiro.test(na.omit(r_sel[-i_restart]))$p.value
r_pre   <- sd(r_sel[train$period == "Pre-COVID"], na.rm = TRUE)
r_post  <- sd(r_sel[train$period == "Post-COVID"][-1], na.rm = TRUE)








Figure 3: Standardised one-step forecast errors of the selected model, laid out as in the notes’ residual plots: over time, ACF, PACF and histogram.





As in the earlier projects, I only forecast from models whose standardised forecast errors look like white noise. All four models pass the Ljung and Box test at the 5% level (Table 5), and for the selected model there is no remaining autocorrelation at the seasonal lags (Figure 3), so the evolving seasonal component captures the calendar pattern.
The Shapiro–Wilk test gives p = 0.048 with all months and p = 0.161 without the restart month: the departure from normality is entirely due to April 2022. The standard deviation of the standardised errors is 0.85 before COVID and 1.06 after the restart. That suggests demand has been more volatile since the pandemic than a single set of variances assumes.


Code
# Influence of the restart month: refit with April 2022 also treated as missing
y_nr <- y_tour; y_nr[i_restart] <- NA
fit_nr <- fit_structural(y_nr, sel$trend, sel$ar, start = sel$theta)


The restart month. 2022 Apr is by far the least likely month: it contributes -4.38 to the log likelihood, against about 2.3 for a typical month, and its standardised error of -3.36 is the outlier in Figure 3. The filter had carried its February 2020 view of demand forward for 25 months, and demand on restart was far below it. This one month has some pull on the estimates. With April 2022 also treated as missing, the level variance becomes 3.5e-04 (from 4.5e-04) and the seasonal variance 7.8e-05 (from 8.5e-05), because the level no longer has to absorb the post-COVID reset in one step. Apart from the restart, no single month dominates the likelihood, so the estimates are not driven by a few outliers.

section: 6.1 Learning the starting values, and losing certainty in the gap
text:

  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SD of predicted level")








Figure 4: Standard deviation of the filter’s estimate of underlying demand (the level of log nights sold, so roughly a percentage), given the data up to the previous month, from February 2016 once the diffuse start has been absorbed. It settles to a steady state, grows through the COVID gap and collapses again after the restart.





With \(C_0 = 10^7 I\) the filter starts out knowing nothing. Once it has seen each calendar month once, in February 2016, its uncertainty about the level has collapsed to 3.1%. It then settles into a steady state in which the standard deviation of the level estimate is about 2.6%: the information gained each month just balances the new level shock.
During the 25 missing months nothing is learned and \(R_t\) grows linearly (each month adds \(\sigma^2_\xi\) to the level variance, plus the seasonal uncertainty). By March 2022 the filter’s uncertainty about the level has risen to 10.9%, 4.3 times its pre-COVID value (Figure 4).

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
6.2 The restart in April 2022


Code
filt |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("2019 Jan"), Month <= yearmonth("2023 Dec")) |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month))) +
  covid_rect(log_y = TRUE) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = exp(pred_y - 1.96 * pred_sd), ymax = exp(pred_y + 1.96 * pred_sd)),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = exp(pred_y)), colour = "steelblue4") +
  geom_point(aes(y = exp(y)), size = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands, log scale)")








Figure 5: One-step-ahead predictions from the filter (blue, with 95% interval) and observed log nights sold (black), 2019 to 2023. Inside the gap the blue line is the filter’s prediction carried forward from February 2020; the first observed month after the gap is far below it.





On the eve of the restart the filter predicted 2,137 thousand nights for April 2022 (95% interval 1,716 to 2,662). In fact 1,466 thousand were sold, 31% below the prediction (Figure 5). The interval is wide because of the gap, and still did not cover the outcome: from the model’s point of view, the post-COVID reset was a level shock larger than any it had seen.
What happens next shows the gain at work. Because the uncertainty about the level was large, the gain in April 2022 gave 95% of the surprise to the level (against 66% in the steady state), so the filter moved its view of demand down almost all the way in a single month. Within a few months the gain and the level uncertainty were back to their pre-COVID steady state (Figure 4), and the one-step predictions were tracking the data again (Figure 5). The filter needed no information about when or how COVID ended; the missing-data step (\(K_t = 0\)) and the gain did all the work.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 6.3 The steady-state gain is exponential smoothing
text:
6.3 The steady-state gain is exponential smoothing


Code
fit_pre <- fit_structural(log(pre_df$nights), sel$trend, sel$ar)
K_pre   <- fit_pre$kf$Kt[nrow(pre_df), ]


Once the gain has settled to a constant \(\bar K\), the update is \(m_t = a_t + \bar K e_t\): a fixed share of each surprise goes to the level and a fixed share to the current month’s seasonal effect. That is the error-correction form of additive Holt–Winters, ETS(A,N,A) (\(\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha e_t\), \(s_t = s_{t-12} + \gamma e_t\)), with \(\alpha\) the level share and \(\gamma\) (roughly) the seasonal share.
For the selected model, the steady-state gain gives 66% of each surprise to the level and 34% to that calendar month’s seasonal effect. These add to 100% because there is no irregular component to absorb any of the surprise.
Fitted to the pre-COVID months only (ETS cannot handle the gap), the state space model’s steady-state gain is 0.41 for the level and 0.57 for the seasonal effect. ETS(A,N,A) on the same months gives \(\alpha\) = 0.24 and \(\gamma\) = 0.76. The split differs, but in both cases the two shares add to about one: a surprise in accommodation demand is almost never treated as a one-off.
The split also depends on the period. On the pre-COVID months the seasonal effect gets the larger share (57%), but on the full training data the level does (66%). Including the post-COVID months raises the level variance from 1.1e-04 to 4.5e-04, because the level has to absorb the reset and the more volatile recovery, and a larger level variance moves the steady-state gain towards the level. The gain is not a fixed property of the series, which is one more sign that a single set of variances for the whole decade is a simplification.
The two methods split it differently partly because ETS estimates \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) directly, with the initial states as free parameters, while the state space model derives the gain from the variances. Partly it is the fragility of \(\gamma\) shown in Section 5.2. This is the link between Projects 3 and 4: the smoothing parameters of exponential smoothing are a steady-state Kalman gain, determined by the signal-to-noise ratios.

lev <- tibble(Month = train$Month, filtered = filt$level_filt, smoothed = ks_sel$st[, 1],

Figure 6: Underlying demand (the level, back-transformed to thousands of nights per month with the seasonal effect removed): filtered in real time (dashed) and smoothed with hindsight (solid, with 95% interval).





The filtered level (Figure 6) is noisier than the smoothed level because it reacts to each month’s surprise with no chance to see whether the next month confirms it. Outside the gap, the typical revision between the real-time and the hindsight estimate is about 1.3% of demand (the standard deviation of the difference on the log scale). Inside the gap no data arrive, so the filtered level stays flat at its February 2020 value, while the smoother bridges the pre- and post-COVID levels. The gap between the two lines there is the difference between the two counterfactuals in Section 7.1.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 7.1 The counterfactual and the demand lost
text:
7.1 The counterfactual and the demand lost


Code
FF_sel      <- sel$mod$FF
signal_mean <- as.numeric(ks_sel$st %*% t(FF_sel))           # level + seasonal (+ AR)
signal_se   <- sqrt(vapply(seq_len(n_tr), function(t) as.numeric(FF_sel %*% ks_sel$St[, , t] %*% t(FF_sel)), 0))

comp <- tibble(Month = train$Month, observed = log(train$nights),
               level = ks_sel$st[, 1], season = ks_sel$st[, s1_sel],
               signal = signal_mean, se = signal_se, period = train$period)

# Demand lost over the gap: total counterfactual minus total actual. The total is a
# sum of correlated log-normals, E(e^X_t) = exp(mu_t + Sig_tt / 2) and
# Cov(e^X_s, e^X_t) = E(e^X_s) E(e^X_t) (exp(Sig_st) - 1); the band is mean +- 1.96 sd.
lost_from <- function(mu, Sig, actual) {
  Ex     <- exp(mu + diag(Sig) / 2)
  total  <- sum(Ex)
  sd_tot <- sqrt(sum(outer(Ex, Ex) * (exp(Sig) - 1)))
  tibble(lost = total - sum(actual),
         lo = total - 1.96 * sd_tot - sum(actual), hi = total + 1.96 * sd_tot - sum(actual),
         share = (total - sum(actual)) / total, total = total, sd_total = sd_tot)
}
actual_gap  <- train$nights[gap]
Sig_smooth  <- smooth_signal_cov(ks_sel, FF_sel, gap)
Sig_filter  <- filter_signal_cov(sel_kf, sel$mod, gap)        # February 2020 view only
lost_smooth <- lost_from(signal_mean[gap], Sig_smooth, actual_gap)
lost_filter <- lost_from(filt$pred_y[gap], Sig_filter, actual_gap)
# for comparison: the band from adding up the monthly limits (perfect correlation)
naive_hw <- sum(exp(signal_mean[gap] + 1.96 * signal_se[gap]) - exp(signal_mean[gap] - 1.96 * signal_se[gap])) / 2

  select(Month, Level = level, Seasonal = season) |>
  pivot_longer(-Month) |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month), value)) +

Code
comp |>
  mutate(pred_filter = filt$pred_y, sd_filter = filt$pred_sd) |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("2019 Jan"), Month <= yearmonth("2022 Dec")) |>
  mutate(in_gap = period == "COVID window",
         cf = if_else(in_gap, exp(signal + se^2 / 2), NA_real_),
         lo = if_else(in_gap, exp(signal - 1.96 * se), NA_real_),
         hi = if_else(in_gap, exp(signal + 1.96 * se), NA_real_),
         ff = if_else(in_gap, exp(pred_filter + sd_filter^2 / 2), NA_real_)) |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cf), colour = "steelblue4", linewidth = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ff), colour = "darkorange", linetype = "dashed", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = exp(observed)), colour = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands)")








Figure 8: Observed nights sold (black) during the COVID window, against two estimates of demand without COVID-19: the smoother (blue, with monthly 95% interval), which uses the data on both sides of the gap, and the filter’s forecast made in February 2020 (orange dashed), which uses only the data before it.





The smoothed level (Figure 7) falls gently before 2020 and is lower after the gap than before it; inside the gap the smoother bridges the two. The amplitude of the seasonal pattern is stable over the decade, but the individual monthly effects drift a little, as the likelihood ratio test in Section 5.2 requires.
Because the COVID months were not used to estimate anything, the smoothed signal in the window is a model-based estimate of what demand would have been without the pandemic (Figure 8). Comparing it with what was actually sold, the model estimates that about 22.4 million stay unit nights were lost between March 2020 and March 2022 (95% band 19.3 to 25.5 million). That is 48% of the demand expected over those 25 months.
The band uses the smoothed covariances between the 25 months. Adding up the monthly intervals instead would treat the months as perfectly correlated and give a half-width of 4.4 million nights, against 3.1 million here. The months are strongly but not perfectly correlated: they share the same bridged level, but each has its own seasonal uncertainty.
Filtering and smoothing give two different counterfactuals:

The filter’s forecast from February 2020 asks “what did we expect before the pandemic?”. It puts the loss at 31.0 million nights (95% band 23.9 to 38.1 million) and attributes all of the drop to COVID-19.
The smoother asks “given where demand ended up, what path is most likely?”. Because demand after the gap was lower than before it, its counterfactual drifts down through the window, and the estimated loss is smaller. It attributes part of the drop to a lasting change in demand that, under the model, would have happened anyway.

Which is “right” depends on whether the lower post-COVID level reflects a change that was under way regardless (the smoother’s reading) or a scar left by the pandemic (closer to the filter’s). The data cannot settle this, so I report the smoother’s figure as the main estimate and the filter’s as an upper reference.

  mutate(name = recode(name, level_aux = "Level shock", seas_aux = "Seasonal shock")) |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month), value)) +
  covid_rect() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-2, 2), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue4", width = 25, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(name), ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Auxiliary residual")








Figure 9: Standardised smoothed level shocks (top) and seasonal shocks (bottom). A value outside ±2 (dashed) suggests a break in the level, or a change in the seasonal pattern, in that month.





The smoothed shocks \(\hat w_t = s_t - G s_{t-1}\) estimate each month’s level and seasonal shock with hindsight. Standardised, they act as \(t\)-tests for breaks (Figure 9). The largest level shock is in 2022 May (2.71), the change in the level from April to May 2022: demand on restart was depressed even relative to the new post-COVID level, and the level rose again as the recovery got going, followed by 2023 Apr (2.34) and 2022 Nov (-1.79). The largest seasonal shock is in 2018 May (-2.81).
The months beyond ±2 are 2018 Jan, 2018 May, 2018 Jun, 2019 May, 2019 Sept, 2022 May, 2023 Mar, 2023 Apr. They are spread over the calendar rather than concentrated in the holiday months.
With 74 months tested, about 4 values beyond ±2 are expected by chance in each panel. There are 2 for the level and 6 for the seasonal shocks. For the level this is no more than chance, so apart from the post-COVID reset there is no strong evidence of further breaks in demand. The seasonal shocks are within what chance would give. Together with the likelihood ratio test in Section 5.2, this says the seasonal pattern drifts gradually rather than breaking: the seasonal variance is needed, but no single month’s shock stands out.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
9.1 Forecasts on the test set
The state space forecasts are produced by KF_forecast() on the log scale and back-transformed with the bias adjustment \(\exp(f + Q/2)\). For comparison, the seasonal naive benchmark, the Project 1 SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 (COVID as missing) and the best Project 3 model, damped Holt–Winters on the regression-imputed series, are refitted here with the same code as in those projects.


Code
# Project 3 imputation of the COVID window (regression on the non-COVID months)
impute_covid <- function(df) {
  n_win <- month_num(covid_end) - month_num(covid_start) + 2
  df <- df |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(t = row_number(), mon = factor(month(as.Date(Month))),
           in_win = Month >= covid_start & Month <= covid_end,
           ramp = pmin(pmax((month_num(Month) - month_num(covid_start) + 1) / n_win, 0), 1),
           y_obs = if_else(in_win, NA_real_, log(nights)))
  fit <- lm(y_obs ~ t + mon + ramp, data = df)
  df |>
    mutate(nights_imp = if_else(in_win, exp(predict(fit, newdata = df)), nights)) |>
    select(Month, nights, nights_imp, period)
}

ref_forecasts <- function(d, h) {
  dB <- d |> mutate(nights = if_else(period == "COVID window", NA_real_, nights))
  dI <- impute_covid(d) |> as_tsibble(index = Month)
  summ <- function(fc) {
    dist <- fc[[fabletools::distribution_var(fc)]]
    tibble(.model = fc$.model, Month = fc$Month, mean = fc$.mean,
           lo95 = quantile(dist, 0.025), hi95 = quantile(dist, 0.975))
  }
  bind_rows(
    summ(forecast(d  |> model(`Seasonal naive` = SNAIVE(nights)), h = h)),
    summ(forecast(dB |> model(`SARIMA (Project 1)` =
                                ARIMA(log(nights) ~ 0 + pdq(0, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 1, 1))), h = h)),
    summ(forecast(dI |> model(`Damped HW (Project 3)` =
                                ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A"))),
                  h = h))
  )
}

ssm_forecasts <- function(fits, y, months) {
  bind_rows(lapply(names(fits), function(nm) {
    fc <- KF_forecast(y, fits[[nm]]$mod, length(months))
    tibble(.model = nm, Month = months,
           mean = exp(fc$mean + fc$var / 2),
           lo95 = exp(fc$mean - 1.96 * sqrt(fc$var)),
           hi95 = exp(fc$mean + 1.96 * sqrt(fc$var)))
  }))
}

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
9.2 Rolling-origin cross-validation
As in Projects 1 and 3, I repeat the comparison over 13 origins from June 2024 to June 2025, forecasting 1 to 12 months ahead. At each origin every model is re-estimated; to save time, the state space models start BFGS from their training-set estimates and skip the Nelder–Mead polish. All four state space models are included, so that cross-validation can confirm or overturn the test-set ranking.


Code
cv_models <- names(specs)
cv_origins <- 13; cv_h <- 12

cv_fc <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(cv_origins), function(i) {
  cat("CV origin", i, "of", cv_origins, "\n", file = stderr())   # progress in the terminal
  d <- nights_sold |> filter(Month < test_start + (i - 1))
  months <- max(d$Month) + 1:cv_h
  y_d <- log(d$nights); y_d[d$period == "COVID window"] <- NA
  fits_i <- lapply(setNames(cv_models, cv_models), function(nm)
    fit_structural(y_d, specs[[nm]]$trend, specs[[nm]]$ar,
                   start = ssm_fits[[nm]]$theta, polish = FALSE))
  bind_rows(ref_forecasts(d, cv_h), ssm_forecasts(fits_i, y_d, months)) |>
    group_by(.model) |> mutate(h = row_number(), origin = i) |> ungroup()
})) |>
  left_join(as_tibble(nights_sold) |> select(Month, actual = nights), by = "Month") |>
  filter(!is.na(actual))

cv_overall <- cv_fc |>
  group_by(Model = .model) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - mean)^2)),
            MAE  = mean(abs(actual - mean)),
            MAPE = 100 * mean(abs(actual - mean) / actual),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(RMSE)

cv_by_h <- cv_fc |>
  group_by(.model, h) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - mean)^2)), .groups = "drop")




Code
cv_overall |> kable(digits = c(0, 1, 1, 2, 0))
cvr <- function(m) cv_overall$RMSE[cv_overall$Model == m]

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
9.3 Results
Test set. The best state space model on the test set is Damped trend + AR(1) (RMSE 89.9, Table 8). For comparison, seasonal naive has 132.6, the Project 1 SARIMA 101.6 and the Project 3 damped Holt–Winters model 72.5. The lowest RMSE overall belongs to Damped HW (Project 3).
The trend specification decides the ranking. The BSM, whose almost fixed slope comes from the pre-COVID decline, has an RMSE of 156.2, worse than the seasonal naive benchmark. Letting the trend die out (damped trend, RMSE 94.0) or removing it (level + seasonal, RMSE 105.9) helps a great deal (Figure 11). The best model on the test set, Damped trend + AR(1), is not the one AIC selected (Level + seasonal, RMSE 105.9): the AIC differences were small, and one-step fit in the training data is a weak guide to which trend will extrapolate best. All four state space models under-forecast (positive bias): demand grew faster in 2024 to 2026 than the models’ level and trend imply.
The 95% intervals of the state space models cover every test month, but that says more about their width than their quality. The mean width is 627 thousand nights for the best model (545 for the SARIMA), about 7 times its RMSE. With a random-walk level and no irregular noise, all the forecast uncertainty is uncertainty about where the level will drift, and it grows steadily with the horizon. With only 24 test months, full coverage of intervals this wide is expected and not very informative; the simulation’s coverage figures are the better check that the intervals are calibrated.
Cross-validation. Over 13 origins the best model is SARIMA (Project 1) (RMSE 83.5), and the best state space model is Damped trend + AR(1) (RMSE 86.6; Table 9, Figure 12). The other state space models have BSM (113.0), Level + seasonal (92.4), Damped trend (88.4). For reference, the Project 3 damped Holt-Winters model has 89.5 and seasonal naive 112.2. Cross-validation confirms Damped trend + AR(1) as the best state space model. The airline SARIMA and the level + seasonal model have almost the same likelihood (Section 10.1), so it is not surprising that their forecasts are close.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 10.1 The structural model and the Project 1 SARIMA
text:
10.1 The structural model and the Project 1 SARIMA
The SARIMA check (Table 4) gives a bonus. The airline model’s likelihood uses the same 76 months as the structural models’ (both drop 13 diffuse months from the 89 observed), so the two are on the same footing:

The airline model has three parameters and a log likelihood of 147.11 (AIC -288.2).
The Level + seasonal model, with three variances, has 147.46 (AIC -288.9).

The fits are almost identical, which is no coincidence. Once differenced by \((1-B)(1-B^{12})\), the basic structural model is an MA(13) process whose autocorrelations are close to those of the airline model (Harvey, 1989), and the level + seasonal model is the special case with no slope. Project 1’s SARIMA and this project’s structural model are two descriptions of nearly the same process. The structural model’s advantage is that its components have a meaning.

The state space approach is the only one in the portfolio that treats the COVID months as missing and says something about them (Table 10):
