This project also showed that Project 1’s SARIMA is itself evaluated by a Kalman filter on the same missing-data series, and that its likelihood is almost the same as the structural model’s. It also showed that Project 3’s conclusion of a fixed seasonal pattern depended on the trend in the ETS model. In forecasting terms, the best structural model sits between the Project 1 SARIMA and the Project 3 damped Holt-Winters model on the test set. The results across all three projects point the same way: once the break is handled sensibly, the remaining differences come from how each model extrapolates the trend.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
11.1 Key findings

My implementation is correct on this series. It agrees with dlm’s filter and smoother on the accommodation data with the COVID months missing (largest smoothed-state difference 2.3e-08), and it reproduces the exact log likelihood of the Project 1 airline SARIMA (147.1098 against 147.1098 from arima()).
Likelihood. The Level + seasonal model has the lowest AIC, but the four structural models and the airline SARIMA are within a few log likelihood units of each other. The level variance is well determined (monthly SD of underlying demand 1.7% to 2.7%), a fixed seasonal pattern is rejected (p = 0.002), the irregular variance sits on the boundary at zero, and April 2022 is by far the least likely month.
Filtering. Nearly every surprise in accommodation demand is treated as lasting: the steady-state gain gives 66% to the level and 34% to the seasonal pattern, the state space version of exponential smoothing’s \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\). Through the gap, the filter’s uncertainty about demand grew 4.3-fold. On restart, demand was 31% below the filter’s prediction, and the filter re-learned the level within a few months without being told anything about COVID.
Smoothing. About 22.4 million stay unit nights (48% of expected demand; 95% band 19.3 to 25.5 million) were lost between March 2020 and March 2022, against 31.0 million if the February 2020 forecast is used as the counterfactual. Across the four models the estimate varies by 0.4 million nights. In simulations from the fitted model, the smoothed counterfactual is within about 6% of the truth in 90% of cases, and its band covers the truth in 93% of them.
Prediction. On the test set the best state space model is Damped trend + AR(1) (RMSE 89.9, against 101.6 for the SARIMA and 72.5 for damped Holt–Winters), and the BSM with its fixed slope is the worst (RMSE 156.2). In cross-validation the best state space model is Damped trend + AR(1).

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
11.2 Issues and limitations

The counterfactual depends on the model. Inside the gap the smoother interpolates with a random-walk level, so the no-COVID path is close to a straight line between the pre- and post-COVID levels. The filter-versus-smoother comparison shows that the estimate of demand lost hinges on whether the lower post-COVID level is treated as something that would have happened anyway.
One set of variances for the whole decade. The forecast errors are more spread out after COVID than before, so the post-COVID period may need larger variances; the restart month alone has a large influence on the level variance.
Moving holidays and the zero irregular variance. Easter and school holidays move between March and April, and with no irregular component the model has to read any one-off month as a level or seasonal shock. The auxiliary residuals do not point clearly at the holiday months, so how much of the seasonal variance is month-specific noise remains open; an Easter regressor would settle it.
Approximate diffuse initialisation and boundary estimates. Using \(C_0 = 10^7 I\) and dropping 13 forecast errors uses up more than a year of data. With the irregular variance on the boundary, AIC and likelihood ratio comparisons behave non-standardly (I used the boundary-corrected test for the seasonal variance).
Intervals treat the variances as known. The simulation suggests this costs little for the smoothing and forecast intervals here, but it rests on the model being right.
Same test window throughout. All projects use one test window and a short cross-validation period, both in the post-COVID recovery, which favours models that do not extrapolate the pre-2020 decline.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
11.3 What I would do differently
I would implement the exact diffuse Kalman filter instead of a large \(C_0\). I would also add the Project 3 intervention terms and an Easter regressor as regression effects inside the state space model. That way the COVID months could be used rather than skipped, and the moving holiday would no longer be read as a shock, which would also show how much of the seasonal variance is really Easter. I would let the variances differ before and after COVID.
Finally, the notes end with a Bayesian state space model in Stan. Fitting this model that way, with priors that keep the irregular variance off the boundary, would carry the parameter uncertainty into the lost-demand estimate.

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 1: The forecasting process (15)
Context: producing sales forecasts for several products of a large biscuit manufacturer.
1. Problem definition. The aim is to forecast future sales for the company’s range of biscuits so that it can make strategic and operational decisions about how, when and where to sell and produce. This means pinning down exactly what is forecast: which products (individual biscuit lines or product families), at what level (national, regional or by retailer), in what units, how far ahead and how often (e.g. weekly forecasts for production scheduling, monthly forecasts a year ahead for ingredient purchasing and budgeting). This is done by talking to the people who will use the forecasts (production, procurement, sales and marketing, finance).
2. Data collection. For each product, collect a record of how many units were sold each period (e.g. monthly), building up a historical time series that can be used to forecast future sales. Also collect information on factors that help explain sales: prices, promotions, advertising campaigns, product launches and competitor activity, along with calendar effects such as public holidays, school holidays and weekends. Knowledge from the sales team about one-off events (stock-outs, factory shutdowns, a large once-off order) is also recorded so the data can be interpreted correctly.
3. Data analysis. This is the exploratory stage, done before any model is fitted. Plot each series and look for trend, seasonality (e.g. peaks before Christmas and Easter), cycles, outliers and structural breaks; check whether a transformation (e.g. logs) or differencing is needed; examine the ACF/PACF; and look at how sales relate to drivers such as promotions, in order to understand consumer demand at different times of the year. The arrow back from model selection shows the process is iterative: what is learnt when fitting a model can send us back to look at the data again.
4. Model selection and fitting. Based on the patterns found in the data analysis (and the ACF and PACF, which show the autocorrelation structure), choose candidate models, e.g. exponential smoothing (such as Holt–Winters for trending, seasonal products), ARIMA/seasonal ARIMA, state space models, or regression models with promotion and price effects, and estimate their parameters on the historical data.
5. Model validation. Assess how accurate each model’s forecasts are. Split the data so that a hold-out (test) set is kept back, and compare forecasts with the actual values using metrics such as RMSE, MAE and MAPE, using validation approaches such as rolling-origin (time series cross-validation) or sliding windows. Residuals should also be checked to make sure they look like white noise. The best-performing model is chosen.
6. Forecasting model deployment. Put the forecasts into practical use, since the whole point of forecasting is to support decisions. The chosen model is built into the company’s planning systems and produces forecasts (with prediction intervals) on a regular schedule, which are used for decisions such as production planning, which products to invest in or refine, and advertising strategies targeted at the products and times of year where sales are strongest.
7. Monitoring forecasting model performance. Continuously compare forecasts with actual sales as they come in and track the forecast errors over time, to detect bias or deterioration, for instance when consumer preferences change or a competitor changes strategy. This monitoring could be automated (e.g. an automated system or AI agent that is fed new data, updates the forecasts and flags when errors drift or market changes occur). When performance deteriorates, the model is re-estimated or the process returns to an earlier stage.

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 2: Expected time patterns (8)
(a) Monthly sales of computer hard drives at a local store (10 years). Over the 10 years I would expect a trend: sales would initially increase steadily as computers became more common and people bought hard drives to keep their computers going for longer, but then trend downwards as technology develops and newer products (e.g. solid-state drives and cloud storage) replace them. There would also be seasonality within each year, e.g. at the beginning of the year when school and university go back, and around Black Friday and the festive season. (Because the data are monthly, within-month effects such as payday are not visible.)
(b) Hourly pulse rate of a person for one week. A strong daily (24-hour) seasonal pattern: pulse rate is elevated during the day while the person is moving around and active, and drops to a resting level while they sleep at night. If the person exercises every day, there will also be a regular daily spike in heart rate at that time. Little or no trend would be expected over a single week.
(c) Daily sales at a fast-food store for six months. A weekly seasonal pattern, with increased demand and sales over weekends (Friday nights to Sunday), plus increases around public holidays (and possibly month-end/payday). Six months is quite a short period, so long-term trends would be hard to see.
(d) Weekly electricity consumption for your local area (10 years). A strong annual seasonal pattern: in South Africa consumption is highest in winter (heating, longer nights) with a possible smaller summer peak from air-conditioning, and dips over the December holidays when businesses and industry shut down. There would also be a trend reflecting population growth and development, possibly offset in recent years by load-shedding, higher tariffs and rooftop solar.

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 3: Matching series to ACFs (12)
The key idea is: a trend makes neighbouring values (even ones far apart) similar, so the ACF starts very high and decays slowly while staying positive; seasonality/cycles make the ACF oscillate, with peaks at lags equal to the period; and a series with neither has small autocorrelations that die out quickly.

Matching each series to its ACF







Time series
ACF
Reason




1. Daily morning temperature of a cow
B
No seasonality or strong trend, just a slight downward drift and irregular variation. The ACF has small-to-moderate positive values that die out without any regular oscillation, consistent with a weakly persistent, non-seasonal series.


2. Accidental deaths in USA (monthly)
A
Clear monthly seasonality with period 12 and no trend. ACF A has a large positive spike at lag 12 and strong negative values around lag 6 (half a seasonal cycle), the pattern of a period-12 seasonal series.


3. International airline passengers
D
Strong upward trend plus seasonality. The trend produces very large positive autocorrelations that decay slowly (ACF D starts near 0.9 and stays high); the seasonality shows as a small bump around lag 12.


4. Annual mink trappings (Canada)
C
An annual series with a regular population cycle of roughly 10 years. ACF C oscillates with peaks near lags 10 and 20 and troughs near lags 5 and 15, matching a ~10-year cycle.

Figure 2: Monthly sales of the souvenir shop, January 1987 – December 1993.









Show code

Figure 3: Seasonal plot: each line is one year.









Trend: sales increase strongly over time, consistent with the shop expanding its premises, products and staff. The growth accelerates in 1992–1993.
Seasonality: a very strong annual pattern. Sales build up through November and peak sharply every December (Christmas tourists), then drop back in January. A smaller secondary peak occurs each March from 1988 onward (the surf festival). There is no March peak in 1987 because the festival only started in 1988.
Changing variance: the size of the seasonal fluctuations grows with the level of the series (the December peaks become enormous), so the seasonality is multiplicative rather than additive.
Unusual features: sales in 1990–1991 stalled: December 1990 (30114) was below December 1989 (34061), and January and March 1991 were lower than a year earlier, breaking the upward trend (possibly an economic downturn or poor tourist season). There are also some months that deviate from the usual seasonal shape, e.g. the unusually high March 1990 and the very sharp jump in December 1992 and 1993.



(b) Why take logarithms? (2)
The variance of the series increases with its level: the seasonal swings are proportional to the level (multiplicative seasonality). Most models (and linear regression) assume constant variance and additive components. Taking logarithms stabilises the variance and turns multiplicative effects into additive ones (\(\log(T \times S \times E) = \log T + \log S + \log E\)), and turns exponential growth into a linear trend (Figure 4).

kable(pred_raw, digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = " "),
      col.names = c("Year", "Predicted total sales", "Lower 95% PI", "Upper 95% PI"))

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 6: IBM daily closing prices (4)

Time plot: the series does not fluctuate around a constant mean. It wanders up from about 450 to 600, then falls sharply to about 300–400, with long local “trends”. There is no level to which it reverts, which is typical of a random walk.
ACF: the autocorrelations start close to 1 and decay extremely slowly (still about 0.8 at lag 25). For a stationary series the ACF should drop to zero quickly; a slowly decaying ACF is the classic sign of non-stationarity.
PACF: there is a single very large spike at lag 1 of almost exactly 1, with all other partial autocorrelations negligible. This indicates \(Y_t \approx Y_{t-1} + e_t\), i.e. an AR(1) with \(\phi_1 \approx 1\), i.e. a unit root.

Together these show the series is non-stationary and should be differenced (first differences \(Y_t - Y_{t-1}\), i.e. the daily price changes, are likely to be stationary).

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 7: Strikes in the USA, 1951–1980 (16)


Show code
strikes_raw <- read_excel(data_file, sheet = 3, .name_repair = "minimal")
strikes <- ts(c(strikes_raw[[2]], strikes_raw[[5]]), start = 1951)



(a) Why ARIMA(0,1,1)? (3)

Original seriesFirst differences




Show code
ggtsdisplay(strikes, main = "Number of strikes", xlab = "Year")








Figure 6: Strikes series: time plot, ACF and PACF.









Show code
ggtsdisplay(diff(strikes), main = "Differenced number of strikes", xlab = "Year")








Figure 7: First differences of the strikes series: time plot, ACF and PACF.









The original series (Figure 6) wanders: it falls from about 5 000 in the early 1950s to about 3 400 in the early 1960s, then rises to around 6 000 in the 1970s, without reverting to a fixed mean. The ACF decays slowly (0.73 at lag 1 and still positive for several lags), and the PACF has one large spike at lag 1. The series is non-stationary, so it should be differenced once (\(d = 1\)).
The differenced series (Figure 7) fluctuates around a constant mean of about zero with roughly constant variance, so it appears stationary. Its ACF has a single negative spike at lag 1 (-0.34, close to the \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n} \approx \pm 0.37\) bound) and is negligible thereafter (the ACF “cuts off” after lag 1), while the PACF decays. This is the signature of an MA(1) process for the differences (\(q = 1\), \(p = 0\)).

Hence ARIMA(0,1,1) is appropriate. (No constant is included since the differences have mean approximately zero, so there is no persistent trend in the series.)


(b) Backshift operator form (2)
With \(B Y_t = Y_{t-1}\), the ARIMA(0,1,1) model is \[(1 - B)\,Y_t = (1 + \theta_1 B)\, e_t \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Y_t = Y_{t-1} + e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1},\] where \(e_t\) is white noise.






Tip



R uses the “\(+\theta\)” sign convention; some textbooks write \((1 - \theta_1 B)e_t\), in which case the sign of the estimate is reversed.




(c) Fit the model and examine the residuals (5)


Show code
fit_strikes <- Arima(strikes, order = c(0, 1, 1))
fit_strikes


Series: strikes 
ARIMA(0,1,1) 

Coefficients:
          ma1
      -0.3094
s.e.   0.1515

sigma^2 = 330817:  log likelihood = -224.98
AIC=453.95   AICc=454.41   BIC=456.69


Show code
theta <- coef(fit_strikes)["ma1"]


The fitted model is \[(1 - B)\,Y_t = (1 -0.3094\,B)\,e_t, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = 330 817.\]


Show code
lb <- checkresiduals(fit_strikes, lag = 10)



    Ljung-Box test

data:  Residuals from ARIMA(0,1,1)
Q* = 4.2581, df = 9, p-value = 0.8936

Model df: 1.   Total lags used: 10








Figure 8: Residual diagnostics for the ARIMA(0,1,1) model.






The time plot of residuals shows no pattern and fluctuates around zero with roughly constant variance.
All residual autocorrelations lie within the significance bounds, so no autocorrelation remains.
The histogram is roughly symmetric and consistent with normality (given only 29 residuals).
The Ljung–Box test gives \(Q^* = 4.258\) on 9 df, p-value \(= 0.894\), so we do not reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are white noise.

The model is therefore satisfactory: the residuals behave like white noise, so the model has captured the structure in the data (Figure 8).


(d) Forecasts three steps ahead by hand (4)
From \(Y_t = Y_{t-1} + e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1}\), the forecasts made at origin \(n = 1980\) are \[\hat{Y}_{n+1} = Y_n + \hat\theta_1\, e_n, \qquad \hat{Y}_{n+h} = \hat{Y}_{n+h-1} \;\;(h \ge 2),\] because future errors have expectation zero. So all three forecasts are equal.


Show code
y_n <- tail(strikes, 1)
e_n <- tail(residuals(fit_strikes), 1)
f1 <- y_n + theta * e_n


With \(Y_{1980} = 3885\), the last residual \(e_{1980} = -880.24\), and \(\hat\theta_1 = -0.3094\): \[\hat{Y}_{1981} = 3885 + (-0.3094)(-880.24) = 4157.33,\] \[\hat{Y}_{1982} = \hat{Y}_{1983} = 4157.33.\]
Checking with R:


Show code
fc_strikes <- forecast(fit_strikes, h = 3)
fc_strikes


     Point Forecast    Lo 80    Hi 80    Lo 95    Hi 95
1981       4157.329 3420.224 4894.435 3030.024 5284.635
1982       4157.329 3261.525 5053.134 2787.314 5527.345
1983       4157.329 3126.986 5187.673 2581.555 5733.104


The R forecasts (4157.33 for each of 1981–1983) agree with the hand calculation.


(e) Plot with forecasts and prediction intervals (2)


Show code
autoplot(fc_strikes) + labs(x = "Year", y = "Number of strikes")








Figure 9: Strikes series with ARIMA(0,1,1) forecasts for 1981–1983 and 80%/95% prediction intervals.





The prediction intervals widen with the forecast horizon (Figure 9), since for a non-stationary (integrated) model the forecast-error variance keeps growing: \(\text{Var} = \sigma^2[1 + (h-1)(1+\theta_1)^2]\).

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 8: Bituminous coal production (10)

(a) What sort of ARIMA model? (3)
The model \(Y_t = c + \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \phi_3 Y_{t-3} + \phi_4 Y_{t-4} + e_t\) is an autoregressive model of order 4 on the undifferenced series with no moving-average terms: an ARIMA(4,0,0), i.e. AR(4), with \(p = 4\), \(d = 0\), \(q = 0\).


(b) Why was this model chosen? (1)
The time plot fluctuates around a fairly constant mean (roughly 300–630 million tons, no persistent trend) and the ACF dies down quickly, so the series appears stationary and no differencing is needed (\(d=0\)). The ACF decays in a damped, sine-wave-like fashion (typical of an AR process), while the PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 4 and cuts off after lag 4, which identifies an AR(4) model.


(c) Forecasts for 1969–1971 (6)


Show code
c0  <- 146.1
phi <- c(0.891, -0.257, 0.392, -0.333)
coal <- c(`1964` = 467, `1965` = 512, `1966` = 534, `1967` = 552, `1968` = 545)

Y <- coal
for (h in 1:3) {
  n <- length(Y)
  Y <- c(Y, c0 + sum(phi * Y[n:(n - 3)]))   # uses Y_{t-1}, ..., Y_{t-4}
}
coal_fc <- tail(Y, 3)


Future errors are set to zero and forecasts are substituted for unknown future values:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{Y}_{1969} &= 146.1 + 0.891(545) - 0.257(552) + 0.392(534) - 0.333(512) = 528.66 \\
\hat{Y}_{1970} &= 146.1 + 0.891(528.66) - 0.257(545) + 0.392(552) - 0.333(534) = 515.64 \\
\hat{Y}_{1971} &= 146.1 + 0.891(515.64) - 0.257(528.66) + 0.392(545) - 0.333(552) = 499.49
\end{aligned}
\]


Show code
kable(data.frame(Year = 1969:1971, `Forecast (million tons)` = round(coal_fc, 2),
                 check.names = FALSE))




Table 6: AR(4) forecasts of bituminous coal production.






Year
Forecast (million tons)




1969
528.66


1970
515.64


1971
499.49








The forecasts decline gradually from the 1968 level, moving back towards the long-run mean of the series, \(\mu = c/(1 - \sum\phi_i) = 475.9\) million tons, as expected for a stationary AR model (Table 6).

title: Spectral Analysis: Finding the Seasons in Nottingham’s Weather
text: Spectral analysis breaks a time series up into waves of different lengths and tells us which wave is the strongest, much like a music equaliser shows which notes are loudest in a song.

title: Spectral Analysis: Finding the Seasons in Nottingham’s Weather
text:
1. Dataset
nottem (comes with R): average monthly air temperature in Nottingham, England, in °F, from 1920 to 1939 (240 months).

title: Spectral Analysis: Finding the Seasons in Nottingham’s Weather
text:
2. What I expected
Summer is warm and winter is cold every year, so I expected one big bar at a period of 12 months and very little anywhere else. I also expected the wave to peak in July and bottom out in January, and that the cycle would not change over the 20 years.
Preparing the series. A trend would pile up at the lowest frequencies and could hide the real peak, so a trending series should be detrended or differenced first. Over the 20 years, nottem rises only about 1.5°F, which is tiny next to the seasonal swing, so I left it as it is (detrend = FALSE).
Watch the units (the ts() catch). nottem is stored as a ts with frequency = 12, so spec.pgram(nottem) measures frequency in cycles per year, and the seasonal peak shows up at 1. I pass as.numeric(x) instead, which gives cycles per month, so the peak shows up at 1/12 and 1/frequency is the period in months.


Code
x <- nottem
t <- 1:length(x)

P <- spec.pgram(as.numeric(x), taper = 0, detrend = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
top <- order(P$spec, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
knitr::kable(data.frame(period_months = round(1 / P$freq[top], 1),
                        share_of_variation = paste0(round(100 * P$spec[top] / sum(P$spec), 1), "%")),
             caption = "The three tallest bars in the periodogram")



The three tallest bars in the periodogram


period_months
share_of_variation




12
91.2%


6
1.5%


20
0.5%





The tallest bar is at 12 months and holds 91% of all the variation. The next one (6 months) holds only 1.5%. So the dominant period is 12 months, as expected.


Code
r <- acf(x, lag.max = 36, plot = FALSE)$acf
round(c(lag6 = r[7], lag12 = r[13], lag24 = r[25], lag36 = r[37]), 2)


 lag6 lag12 lag24 lag36 
-0.88  0.88  0.87  0.81 


Link to the ACF. The ACF tells the same story in the time domain. It is about −0.88 at lag 6 (summer vs winter) and about +0.88, +0.87 and +0.81 at lags 12, 24 and 36. The periodogram sums all of that up as one number: a 12-month period.

title: Spectral Analysis: Finding the Seasons in Nottingham’s Weather
text:
3. Fitting the harmonic


Code
fit <- lm(x ~ cos(2 * pi * t / 12) + sin(2 * pi * t / 12))
b <- coef(fit)
amp       <- sqrt(b[2]^2 + b[3]^2)
peak_mon  <- (atan2(b[3], b[2]) / (2 * pi) * 12) %% 12   # t = 1 is January
round(c(mean = unname(b[1]), amplitude = unname(amp), peak_month = unname(peak_mon), R2 = summary(fit)$r.squared), 2)


      mean  amplitude peak_month         R2 
     49.04      11.56       7.23       0.91 


The fitted wave has a mean of 49°F and goes 11.6°F above and below it. It peaks at month 7.2 (late July) and bottoms out in late January. This one wave explains 91% of the variation, the same 91% the periodogram showed.


Code
# does the cycle change? dominant period in each decade
sapply(list(`1920s` = window(x, end = c(1929, 12)), `1930s` = window(x, start = 1930)),
       function(w) { p <- spec.pgram(as.numeric(w), taper = 0, detrend = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
                     1 / p$freq[which.max(p$spec)] })


1920s 1930s 
   12    12 


Does the cycle change? The dominant period is 12 months in 1920–29 and again in 1930–39, so here the wave stays the same.

title: Spectral Analysis: Finding the Seasons in Nottingham’s Weather
text:
4. Separating signal and noise


Code
signal <- ts(fitted(fit), start = 1920, frequency = 12)
noise  <- ts(resid(fit),  start = 1920, frequency = 12)
round(c(sd_signal = sd(signal), sd_noise = sd(noise)), 2)


sd_signal  sd_noise 
     8.19      2.53 


Signal = the fitted 12-month wave. Noise = actual − wave, which is the “this month was warmer or colder than usual” part. The noise is about a third as variable as the signal.

title: Spectral Analysis: Finding the Seasons in Nottingham’s Weather
text:
5. Three plots


Code
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))

# (a) periodogram
plot(1 / P$freq, P$spec, type = "h", lwd = 2, log = "x", xlab = "Period (months, log scale)",
     ylab = "Periodogram", main = "(a) One wave dominates: 12 months")

# (b) data, signal, and a forecast checked against held-out data
train <- window(x, end = c(1937, 12)); tt <- 1:length(train)
fit_tr <- lm(train ~ cos(2 * pi * tt / 12) + sin(2 * pi * tt / 12))
fc <- ts(predict(fit_tr, newdata = data.frame(tt = 217:240)), start = 1938, frequency = 12)
rmse <- c(wave = sqrt(mean((window(x, start = 1938) - fc)^2)),
          mean_only = sqrt(mean((window(x, start = 1938) - mean(train))^2)))
plot(x, col = "grey50", xlab = "Year", ylab = "Temperature (deg F)", main = "(b) Data, 12-month wave and 1938-39 forecast")
lines(window(signal, end = c(1937, 12)), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
lines(fc, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("bottomleft", c("data", "signal", "forecast (fit on 1920-37)"),
       col = c("grey50", "steelblue", "darkorange"), lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = c(1, 2, 2),
       bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, cex = 0.9)

# (c) noise
plot(noise, xlab = "Year", ylab = "deg F", main = "(c) Noise: warmer or colder than a typical month")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

title: Spectral Analysis: Finding the Seasons in Nottingham’s Weather
text:
6. Interpretation

Dominant period: 12 months. The periodogram has one tall bar, which is the seasons. The 6-month bar is small and only adjusts the shape: December to February all sit at about 39–40°F, so winter has a flat bottom, while a single sine wave dips to a sharp low of about 37.5°F.
Signal vs noise. A single wave explains 91% of the variation. The other 9% is month-to-month weather luck, like a cold March or a hot August (plot c).
Forecasting. Because the period stays fixed, forecasting is simple: carry the wave forward. Fitted on 1920–37 and used to predict 1938–39, it is off by about 2.2°F on average. Predicting the overall mean every month is off by 7.8°F.
When would it go wrong? If the cycle length drifted (e.g. the sunspot cycle, which moves between about 9 and 14 years), the bar would spread over several neighbouring periods and a fixed wave would slowly fall out of step.

title: State Space Models and Kalman Filter
text:
Topics covered: Writing models in state-space form, the Kalman filter written from first principles, the likelihood from the prediction error decomposition, missing observations and forecasting, regression as a state-space model, and the second differences of the linear growth model.
Data: data simulated from the models in Questions 1–3, and usconsumption (quarterly % changes in US personal consumption and personal disposable income, 1970–2010) from the fpp package (Question 4). Packages: dlm, fpp, knitr.
Code
library(dlm)
library(fpp)
library(knitr)

# Colours and helper used in the text
cols <- c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3")
f2 <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)

title: State Space Models and Kalman Filter
text:
Worked exercises

Question 1: Simulation and Kalman filter

1.1 Simulating the data
I used the simulation loop from the notes, but with \(\theta_0 \sim N(0, 1)\) and the time-varying \(F_t\) and \(G_t\). I simulated 105 values so that I’d have \(F_t\) for the 5 forecast steps, and the true \(y_{101}, \dots, y_{105}\) to compare against.


Code
## simulate data
set.seed(21)
N <- 105
W = 1
V = 2

GG <- 0.5 * sin(pi / 2 * (2 * (1:(N + 1)) + 1))   # one extra for predicting theta[N+1]
all.equal(GG, (-1)^(1:(N + 1)) / 2)


[1] TRUE


Code
FF <- round(rnorm(N, mean = 1, sd = 0.2), 1)

theta <- numeric(N)
y <- numeric(N)
theta0 <- rnorm(1, 0, 1)

theta[1] <- rnorm(1, GG[1] * theta0, sqrt(W))
y[1] <- rnorm(1, FF[1] * theta[1], sqrt(V))

for (i in 2:N) {
 theta[i] <- rnorm(1, GG[i] * theta[i-1], sqrt(W))
 y[i] <- rnorm(1, FF[i] * theta[i], sqrt(V))
}

y.true <- y[101:105]    # kept back to check the forecasts
theta <- theta[1:100]
y <- y[1:100]




Code
plot.ts(y, las = 1)
lines(theta, col = "red")








Figure 1: Simulated observations (black) and the true state (red).





\(G_t\) flips between \(-0.5\) and \(0.5\), so \(\theta_t\) keeps switching sign and doesn’t wander far from 0. Most of what we see in \(y_t\) is observation noise, since \(V = 2\) is bigger than the variance of the state.


1.2 Kalman filter and parameter estimation
This is the KF() function from the notes with three changes: FF and GG are now vectors indexed by time, the first prediction uses GG[1] %*% m0 instead of just m0, and it adds up the log-likelihood for every non-missing \(y_t\).


Code
KF <- function(FF, GG, m0, C0, W, V, y) {
  N <- length(y)
  at <- numeric(N + 1)
  Rt <- numeric(N + 1)
  ft <- numeric(N)
  Qt <- numeric(N)
  mt <- numeric(N)
  Ct <- numeric(N)
  et <- numeric(N)
  ll <- 0

  ## predict theta
  at[1] <- GG[1] %*% m0
  Rt[1] <- GG[1] %*% C0 %*% GG[1] + W

  for (i in 1:N) {

    ## predict y
    ft[i] = FF[i] %*% at[i]
    Qt[i] = FF[i] %*% Rt[i] %*% FF[i] + V

    ## posterior
    if (is.na(y[i])) {
      et[i] = 0
      Kt = 0
    } else {
      Kt = Rt[i] %*% FF[i] %*% solve(Qt[i])
      et[i] <- y[i] - ft[i]
      ll <- ll - 0.5 * (log(Qt[i]) + et[i]^2 / Qt[i])
    }

    mt[i] = at[i] + Kt %*% et[i]
    Ct[i] = Rt[i] - Kt %*% FF[i] %*% Rt[i]

    ## predict theta
    at[i+1] <- GG[i+1] %*% mt[i]
    Rt[i+1] <- GG[i+1] %*% Ct[i] %*% GG[i+1] + W
  }

  return(list(at = at, Rt = Rt, ft = ft, Qt = Qt, mt = mt, Ct = Ct, et = et, ll = ll))
}


optim() needs the parameters as the first argument, and I put both variances on the log scale so they stay positive.


Code
## initial distribution
m0 <- 0
C0 <- 1

neg.ll <- function(parm, y) {
  -KF(FF = FF, GG = GG, m0 = m0, C0 = C0, W = exp(parm[2]), V = exp(parm[1]), y = y)$ll
}

# maximize the likelihood
fit <- optim(par = c(0, 0), fn = neg.ll, y = y, hessian = TRUE)
fit$convergence


[1] 0


Code
exp(fit$par)       # V, W


[1] 2.1601855 0.4808079


Code
# try other starting values, since the likelihood can have local maxima
sapply(list(c(-2, 2), c(2, -2), c(1, 1)), function(s) exp(optim(s, neg.ll, y = y)$par))


          [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
[1,] 2.1594147 2.1608147 2.1600297
[2,] 0.4810052 0.4803779 0.4804032


Code
# approximate 95% intervals, from the Hessian on the log scale
se <- sqrt(diag(solve(fit$hessian)))
exp(cbind(lower = fit$par - 1.96 * se, upper = fit$par + 1.96 * se))


          lower    upper
[1,] 1.24226894 3.756353
[2,] 0.07802035 2.963025




Code
# check against dlm, with F_t and G_t passed in through X
lik.fun <- function(x) {
  dlm(FF = 1, V = exp(x[1]), GG = 1, W = exp(x[2]), m0 = m0, C0 = C0,
      JFF = 1, JGG = 2, X = cbind(FF[1:100], GG[1:100]))   # X needs one row per observation
}
fit.dlm <- dlmMLE(y, parm = c(0, 0), build = lik.fun)
rbind(mine = exp(fit$par), dlm = exp(fit.dlm$par))


         [,1]      [,2]
mine 2.160185 0.4808079
dlm  2.160301 0.4804511


My Kalman filter gives \(\hat V\) = 2.16 and \(\hat W\) = 0.48 (true values 2 and 1), and dlmMLE() gives the same estimates, so the filter is doing the right thing. The other starting values end up in the same place. \(\hat V\) is close to the truth, but \(\hat W\) is only about half of it. Its interval is very wide (roughly 0.08 to 3), so with 100 points and \(V\) twice as big as \(W\), the data don’t say much about the state variance.


1.3 Forecasting up to h = 5
Same trick as the notes: add 5 NAs to the end of \(y\) and run the filter again with the estimated variances.


Code
V.hat <- exp(fit$par[1])
W.hat <- exp(fit$par[2])

y1 <- c(y, rep(NA, times = 5))
y.kf <- KF(FF = FF, GG = GG, m0 = m0, C0 = C0, W = W.hat, V = V.hat, y = y1)

fc <- cbind(forecast = y.kf$ft[101:105],
            lower = y.kf$ft[101:105] - 1.96 * sqrt(y.kf$Qt[101:105]),
            upper = y.kf$ft[101:105] + 1.96 * sqrt(y.kf$Qt[101:105]),
            true = y.true)
kable(fc, digits = 2)





forecast
lower

The forecasts go to 0 straight away, because \(|G_t| = 0.5\) halves the state’s mean every step. The interval width settles at about \(\pm 1.96\sqrt{F_t^2\,\text{Var}(\theta) + V}\), so the model is basically forecasting the long-run mean. Three of the 5 true values fall inside the intervals; \(y_{103}\) and \(y_{104}\) are above them. That’s partly bad luck with this one simulated path, and partly because \(\hat W\) is too small, which makes the intervals too narrow.


1.4 Plotting the fitted and filtered values


Code
all <- cbind(y1,
             c(theta, rep(NA, 5)),
             y.kf$mt,
             y.kf$ft,
             y.kf$ft - 1.96 * sqrt(y.kf$Qt),
             y.kf$ft + 1.96 * sqrt(y.kf$Qt))

plot.ts(all, plot.type = "single", col = c("black", "red", "blue", cols[2], "grey", "grey"),
        lwd = 2, las = 1, ylab = "y", ylim = c(-4, 6.5))
abline(v = 100, lty = 3)
legend("topleft", ncol = 3, lwd = 2, lty = 1, col = c("black", "red", "blue", cols[2], "grey"),
       legend = c("observed", "true", "filtered", "1-step predictions", "95% prediction limits"),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)








Figure 2: Simulated data (black) with the true state (red), filtered state (blue), one-step predictions (orange) and 95% prediction limits (grey). The dotted line marks the start of the forecasts.





The filtered values follow the true state more closely than the one-step predictions do. Because \(G_t\) keeps changing sign, last period’s state says little about this period’s, so \(f_t\) stays close to 0. The update step is what gets the state right, once \(y_t\) is seen.


1.5 Residuals
I used the standardised one-step prediction errors, \(e_t / \sqrt{Q_t}\), which should be white noise with variance 1 if the model is right.


Code
res <- y.kf$et[1:100] / sqrt(y.kf$Qt[1:100])

par(mfrow = c(1, 4))
plot.ts(res, las = 1)
acf(res, main = "")
pacf(res, main = "")
hist(res, main = "", las = 1, xlab = "residual")








Figure 3: Standardised residuals from my Kalman filter: time plot, ACF, PACF and histogram.







Code
c(mean = mean(res), sd = sd(res),
  ljung.box.p = Box.test(res, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)


        mean           sd  ljung.box.p 
-0.007467021  1.004531236  0.671572718 


The residuals have mean close to 0 and standard deviation close to 1, there are no significant spikes in the ACF, and the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.672. The histogram looks roughly normal. So the model has picked up all of the structure, which is expected since it’s the model the data were simulated from.


1.6 Discussion
Writing my own filter showed me where \(F_t\) and \(G_t\) come in. \(G_t\) is used to move the state forward from \(t-1\) to \(t\), so when predicting \(\theta_{t+1}\) inside the loop I needed GG[i+1], not GG[i]. \(F_t\) is used at time \(t\) to map the state to \(y_t\). \(\hat V\) was close to the truth, \(\hat W\) was too small but very uncertain, and my filter gave the same estimates as dlm. The forecasts are not very useful here, since \(|G_t| < 1\) makes the state die out after a couple of steps. The filtered values are much better than the one-step predictions, because the state is hard to predict but easy to estimate once \(y_t\) is seen.



Question 2: AR(2) observed with noise

a) State-space form
Following the AR(2) example in the notes, I put \(\theta_t = (x_t, x_{t-1})'\) in the state vector. Here \(\phi_1 = 0\) and \(\phi_2 = -0.9\):
\[
\theta_t = \begin{pmatrix} x_t \\ x_{t-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -0.9 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_{t-1} \\ x_{t-2} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} w_t \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad W = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_w^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\]
\[
y_t = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \theta_t + v_t, \qquad V = \sigma_v^2
\]
The second row of \(W\) is 0 because \(x_{t-1}\) is just copied over, so there’s no noise there. The starting state is \(\theta_0 = (x_0, x_{-1})' \sim N\big(0, \text{diag}(\sigma_0^2, \sigma_1^2)\big)\).


b) Values of σ₀² and σ₁² for stationarity
\(y_t = x_t + v_t\), and \(v_t\) is white noise independent of \(x_t\), so \(y_t\) is stationary if \(x_t\) is. \(x_t\) is a stationary AR(2) (the roots of \(1 + 0.9B^2\) are outside the unit circle), so it’s enough to start it from its stationary distribution.
For the variance, take variances on both sides of \(x_t = -0.9x_{t-2} + w_t\):
\[
\gamma(0) = 0.81\gamma(0) + \sigma_w^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \gamma(0) = \frac{\sigma_w^2}{1 - 0.81} = \frac{\sigma_w^2}{0.19}
\]
For the lag-1 covariance, multiply by \(x_{t-1}\) and take expectations: \(\gamma(1) = -0.9\gamma(1)\), so \(\gamma(1) = 0\). This means \(x_0\) and \(x_{-1}\) are uncorrelated in the stationary distribution, which agrees with the question saying they’re independent. So
\[
\sigma_0^2 = \sigma_1^2 = \frac{\sigma_w^2}{0.19} \approx 5.26\,\sigma_w^2
\]


c) Simulating with σ_w = 1 and σ_v = 1
I used the simulation loop from the notes. x[1] and x[2] hold \(x_{-1}\) and \(x_0\), and the 100 observations start at x[3].


Code
## simulate data
set.seed(21)
N <- 100
sw <- 1
sv <- 1
s0 <- sqrt(sw^2 / 0.19)    # sigma_0 = sigma_1

x <- numeric(N + 2)
x[1] <- rnorm(1, 0, s0)    # x_{-1}
x[2] <- rnorm(1, 0, s0)    # x_0

for (i in 3:(N + 2)) {
 x[i] <- rnorm(1, -0.9 * x[i-2], sw)
}

x <- x[-c(1:2)]
y <- x + rnorm(N, 0, sv)




Code
plot.ts(y, las = 1, ylab = "")
lines(x, col = "red")
legend("topright", col = c("black", "red"), lty = 1, legend = c("y", "x"), bty = "n")








Figure 4: Simulated system process x_t (red) and observations y_t (black), with σ_v = 1.







Code
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
acf(x, main = "x")
pacf(x, main = "x")
acf(y, main = "y")
pacf(y, main = "y")








Figure 5: Sample ACF and PACF of x_t (top) and y_t (bottom), with σ_v = 1.





\(x_t\) swings up and down every two periods: a high value is followed two steps later by a low one, because of the \(-0.9\). With \(\sigma_v = 1\), \(y_t\) looks almost the same, since the variance of \(x_t\) (about 5.26) is much bigger than the noise.
The ACF of \(x_t\) is zero at odd lags and alternates in sign at even lags (\(-0.9\), \(0.81\), \(\dots\)), dying out slowly. The PACF has one big spike at lag 2 and nothing after it, which is what we’d expect for an AR(2) with \(\phi_1 = 0\). For \(y_t\) the pattern is the same, but every autocorrelation is shrunk by about \(5.26 / 6.26 \approx 0.84\), and the PACF has small extra spikes after lag 2. That’s because an AR(2) plus white noise is really an ARMA(2,2), so its PACF doesn’t cut off exactly.


d) Repeating with σ_v = 10

x <- numeric(N + 2)
x[1] <- rnorm(1, 0, s0)
x[2] <- rnorm(1, 0, s0)

 x[i] <- rnorm(1, -0.9 * x[i-2], sw)

Code

pacf(x, main = "x")
acf(y, main = "y")
pacf(y, main = "y")








Figure 7: Sample ACF and PACF of x_t (top) and y_t (bottom), with σ_v = 10.





Now the noise variance (100) is about 19 times the variance of \(x_t\), so \(y_t\) just looks like white noise and the cycle in \(x_t\) is hidden. In theory the autocorrelations of \(y_t\) are shrunk by \(5.26 / 105.26 \approx 0.05\), so the lag-2 value is only about \(-0.045\). That’s well inside the confidence bands, so with 100 observations the ACF and PACF of \(y_t\) show nothing (the one borderline spike at lag 7 is just chance). This is exactly when a state-space model is useful: the AR(2) structure is still there, but we can only get at it by modelling the noise separately.



Question 3: Second differences of the linear growth model
The linear growth model from the notes is
\[
Y_t = \mu_t + v_t, \qquad \mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad \beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + \gamma_t
\]
with \(v_t \sim N(0, V)\), \(w_t \sim N(0, \sigma_w^2)\) and \(\gamma_t \sim N(0, \sigma_\gamma^2)\), all independent.
Taking the first difference:
\[
\nabla Y_t = (\mu_t - \mu_{t-1}) + (v_t - v_{t-1}) = \beta_{t-1} + w_t + v_t - v_{t-1}
\]
and then the second difference, using \(\beta_{t-1} - \beta_{t-2} = \gamma_{t-1}\):
\[
\nabla^2 Y_t = \gamma_{t-1} + w_t - w_{t-1} + v_t - 2v_{t-1} + v_{t-2}
\]
So \(\nabla^2 Y_t\) is a sum of white noise terms going back at most 2 periods. It has mean 0, and its autocovariances \(c_k\) don’t depend on \(t\):
\[
c_0 = \sigma_\gamma^2 + 2\sigma_w^2 + 6V, \qquad c_1 = -\sigma_w^2 - 4V, \qquad c_2 = V, \qquad c_k = 0 \text{ for } k > 2
\]
So \(\nabla^2 Y_t\) is stationary, and its autocorrelation function cuts off after lag 2, which is the same as an MA(2) model.
To check this, I simulated a long series using the values from the notes’ linear growth example (observation SD 20, level SD 5, slope SD 1), and compared the sample ACF of the second differences with the theory.


Code
## simulate data
set.seed(21)
N <- 10000
V <- 20^2
sw2 <- 5^2
sg2 <- 1^2

mu <- numeric(N)
beta <- numeric(N)
Y <- numeric(N)

for (i in 2:N) {
 beta[i] <- rnorm(1, beta[i-1], sqrt(sg2))
 mu[i] <- rnorm(1, mu[i-1] + beta[i-1], sqrt(sw2))
 Y[i] <- rnorm(1, mu[i], sqrt(V))
}

d2Y <- diff(Y, differences = 2)




Code

rho <- c(1, (-sw2 - 4 * V) / c0, V / c0, rep(0, 8))

acf(d2Y, lag.max = 10, main = "")
points(0:10, rho, col = "red", pch = 4, cex = 1.5)

Question 4: Regression coefficients with a Kalman filter

a) Plot and linear regression


Code

z <- usconsumption[, 2]

plot(usconsumption, las = 1, main = "")








Figure 9: Quarterly % changes in US personal consumption and income.







Code

summary(fit.lm)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ z)

Residuals:

-2.3681 -0.3237  0.0266  0.3436  1.5581 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  0.52062    0.06231   8.356 2.79e-14 ***
z            0.31866    0.05226   6.098 7.61e-09 ***

b) Kalman filter for the regression model
Now the state is \(\theta_t = (a_t, b_t)'\), so \(F_t = (1, z_t)\), \(G = I_2\) and \(W = 0\). The steps are exactly the same as KF(), but \(a_t\) and \(m_t\) are now 2-vectors (rows of a matrix) and \(R_t\) and \(C_t\) are \(2 \times 2\) matrices (stored in a list).


Code
KF.reg <- function(z, m0, C0, W, V, y) {
  N <- length(y)
  GG <- diag(2)
  at <- matrix(0, N + 1, 2)
  Rt <- vector("list", N + 1)
  ft <- numeric(N)
  Qt <- numeric(N)
  mt <- matrix(0, N, 2)
  Ct <- vector("list", N)
  et <- numeric(N)
  ll <- 0

  ## predict theta
  at[1, ] <- GG %*% m0
  Rt[[1]] <- GG %*% C0 %*% t(GG) + W

  for (i in 1:N) {
    FF <- matrix(c(1, z[i]), nrow = 1)

    ## predict y
    ft[i] = FF %*% at[i, ]
    Qt[i] = FF %*% Rt[[i]] %*% t(FF) + V

    ## posterior
    if (is.na(y[i])) {
      et[i] = 0
      Kt = matrix(0, 2, 1)
    } else {
      Kt = Rt[[i]] %*% t(FF) %*% solve(Qt[i])
      et[i] <- y[i] - ft[i]
      ll <- ll - 0.5 * (log(Qt[i]) + et[i]^2 / Qt[i])
    }

    mt[i, ] = at[i, ] + Kt %*% et[i]
    Ct[[i]] = Rt[[i]] - Kt %*% FF %*% Rt[[i]]

    ## predict theta
    at[i+1, ] <- GG %*% mt[i, ]
    Rt[[i+1]] <- GG %*% Ct[[i]] %*% t(GG) + W
  }

  return(list(at = at, Rt = Rt, ft = ft, Qt = Qt, mt = mt, Ct = Ct, et = et, ll = ll))
}




c) Estimating a and b
I used \(m_0 = (0, 0)\) and a very large \(C_0\) (a vague prior), as the notes suggest. Then \(\hat x_{T|T}\) is the last row of \(m_t\).


Code
m0 <- c(0, 0)
C0 <- diag(1e7, 2)
W <- matrix(0, 2, 2)

reg.kf  <- KF.reg(z, m0 = m0, C0 = C0, W = W, V = 1,   y = y)
reg.kf2 <- KF.reg(z, m0 = m0, C0 = C0, W = W, V = 100, y = y)

n <- length(y)
rbind(sigma2.1 = reg.kf$mt[n, ], sigma2.100 = reg.kf2$mt[n, ])


                [,1]      [,2]
sigma2.1   0.5206165 0.3186605
sigma2.100 0.5206165 0.3186605


\(\sigma^2\) makes no difference to the estimates because, with \(W = 0\) and a vague prior, every \(R_t\) and \(Q_t\) is just \(\sigma^2\) times something that doesn’t depend on \(\sigma^2\). So the gain \(K_t = R_t F_t' Q_t^{-1}\) cancels the \(\sigma^2\) out, and \(m_t\) is the same for any value. Only \(C_t\) (the uncertainty) scales with \(\sigma^2\).


d) Comparing with lm


Code
rbind(kalman = reg.kf$mt[n, ], lm = coef(fit.lm))


       (Intercept)         z
kalman   0.5206165 0.3186605
lm       0.5206165 0.3186605


They’re the same: \(\hat a\) = 0.5206 and \(\hat b\) = 0.3187. With a vague prior and no state noise, the Kalman filter is just recursive least squares.


e) and f) Parameter estimates over time
The rows of mt are \(\hat x_{1|1}, \hat x_{2|2}, \dots, \hat x_{T|T}\). Each one is the OLS estimate using only the data up to that quarter. I dropped the first two, since we need at least two points to fit a line.


Code
mt <- ts(reg.kf$mt, start = start(y), frequency = 4)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(window(mt[, 1], start = time(y)[3]), las = 1, ylab = "a", col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = coef(fit.lm)[1], lty = 2)
plot(window(mt[, 2], start = time(y)[3]), las = 1, ylab = "b", col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = coef(fit.lm)[2], lty = 2)








Figure 10: Recursive estimates of the intercept a (left) and slope b (right). The dashed lines are the final estimates from lm.





The estimates jump around a lot in the first few years, which is just because there are so few points. After that they settle, but they still drift: 0.40 for \(b\) after 10 years and 0.32 at the end, with a clear drop around 2001. Recursive estimates should flatten out over time if the true coefficients are constant, since each new point has less and less weight. Because they’re still moving late in the sample, a model with time-varying parameters (a non-zero \(W\)) might fit better. To decide properly, I’d compare the likelihoods of the two models.


g) Estimating σ²
\(\sigma^2\) is the observation variance \(V\), so it can be estimated in the same way as in Question 1: put the likelihood from the filter into optim(). I left out the first two prediction errors, because they come from the vague prior and their \(Q_t\) is huge.


Code
neg.ll.reg <- function(parm, y) {
  out <- KF.reg(z, m0 = m0, C0 = C0, W = W, V = exp(parm[1]), y = y)
  0.5 * sum(log(out$Qt[-(1:2)]) + out$et[-(1:2)]^2 / out$Qt[-(1:2)])
}

fit.s2 <- optim(par = 0, fn = neg.ll.reg, y = y, method = "BFGS")

c(kalman = exp(fit.s2$par),
  RSS.over.n.minus.2 = sum(resid(fit.lm)^2) / (n - 2),
  RSS.over.n = sum(resid(fit.lm)^2) / n)


            kalman RSS.over.n.minus.2         RSS.over.n 
         0.3936959          0.3936922          0.3888911 


My estimate is 0.3937. It matches \(\text{RSS}/(n-2)\), the usual unbiased estimate from lm() (squared residual standard error). This is because there are only \(n - 2\) prediction errors left, and their standardised squares add up to the RSS.

title: State Space Models and Kalman Filter
text:
Reflection
What was most challenging: Getting the indices for \(G_t\) right in Question 1. The KF() function in the notes has constant \(F\) and \(G\), so it doesn’t matter there, but with time-varying matrices the prediction for \(\theta_{t+1}\) has to use \(G_{t+1}\). In Question 2, I had to realise that \(x_t\) is just an AR(2), so the starting variances come from the usual AR(2) formulas. For Question 4, the hardest part was storing the \(2 \times 2\) matrices, since the numeric vectors from the notes only work when the state is one number.
What I now understand: The difference between filtered values and one-step predictions. In Question 1 the one-step predictions were nearly flat, but the filtered values followed the state closely, because the update step uses \(y_t\). Question 2 showed me how much observation noise can hide: with \(\sigma_v = 10\) the ACF and PACF of \(y_t\) showed nothing, even though \(x_t\) has a strong cycle underneath. I also hadn’t realised that linear regression is just a Kalman filter with \(W = 0\), and that the linear growth model differenced twice is an MA(2), so it behaves like an ARIMA(0,2,2).
Advantages and limitations of the methods:

Advantages: The state-space form separates the process we care about from the measurement noise, and covers ARIMA, regression and structural models in one framework. The Kalman filter is a short loop that gives the filtered states, the fitted values, the likelihood and the forecasts all at once, and missing values and forecasts need no extra code. It also makes it easy to let parameters change over time.
Limitations: The Kalman filter only works for linear Gaussian models. The likelihood can be flat or have more than one maximum, so starting values need to be checked, and when the noise is large the state variances are hard to estimate (as with \(\hat W\) in Question 1). The results also depend on the prior for \(\theta_0\), especially early in the series.

Links: Project 4: Kalman filter.
